en: Preface to the Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment,
composed by Pei Xiu, Imperial Intendant of Jiangxi Circuit, Prefect of Hongzhou,
and concurrently Grand Master of Remonstrance (Yushi Dafu) of the Tang Dynasty.
Now, that which belongs to the realm of blood and breath must necessarily possess cognition; and all things possessing cognition must share the same substance.

This is what is called the true, pure, luminous, and wondrous, the void-penetrating and spirit-communicating, standing forth alone and enduring. It is the fundamental source of all sentient beings; therefore it is called the "mind-ground.
Because it is that which all Buddhas have attained, it is called "Bodhi. Because it thoroughly penetrates and harmoniously encompasses all, it is called the "Dharmadhātu."

Because it is eternally tranquil and blissful, it is called *nirvāṇa*; because it is unturbid and without outflows, it is called "purity"; because it is non-false and unchanging, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness);
because it is free from faults and transcends all that is contrary, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature); because it protects the good and wards off evil, it is called *dhāraṇī*;

because it conceals and encompasses all within, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Womb of the Tathāgata); and because it transcends the profound and the hidden, it is called the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyavimala-vyūha*), which presides over the multitudes.
Virtue is fully perfected therein; it illuminates the masses of darkness while shining alone, and thus it is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*Yuanjue*).

In reality, all of this is but the one mind. To turn one's back upon it is to be ordinary; to accord with it is to be a sage. To be deluded by it is for birth and death to begin; to awaken to it is for the cycle of rebirth to cease.
To seek it intimately, there are cessation, contemplation, concentration, and wisdom; to extend it broadly, there are the six perfections and myriad practices; to draw it forth...
To possess wisdom is then to possess right wisdom; to rely upon it as a cause is then to possess the right cause. In reality, these are all one and the same dharma.
Those who are perpetually in perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) yet have never realized that perfect enlightenment are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Those who seek to realize perfect enlightenment but have not yet reached its ultimate fulfillment are bodhisattvas. Those who are fully endowed with perfect enlightenment and abide in the maintenance of perfect enlightenment are Tathāgatas.
Apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no six realms; apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no three vehicles; apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there is no Tathāgata;

and apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there is no True Dharma. In reality, these are all but one single Way. This is what the Buddhas of the three periods have realized—they have realized this very thing.
It is for this reason that the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the One Great Matter. The Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—[are all for this purpose].
All the sūtras generally explain this; however, when the Tathāgata bestowed his teachings, there were distinctions between the manifest and the esoteric;

in establishing the principles, there were variations of breadth and brevity; in accordance with the times, there were sequences of before and after; and according to the capacities of those present, there were degrees of depth and shallowness.

Were it not for those of superior faculties and perfect wisdom, who could have fully comprehended them? Therefore, the Tathāgata secretly expounded and revealed this within the *Glorious Treasury* (*Prabhāsa-kośa*) to the twelve great bodhisattvas.
Manifesting a profound penetration that spread widely, he established its principles as the fundamental doctrine of all sutras.

Master Guifeng received the Dharma from the venerable Daoyuan, a direct disciple of Nanpin and a grand-disciple of Heze. One day, while following the assembly of monks for a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a local official, he took his place among the lower-ranking members.
As he received the scriptures in order, he encountered the *Nanyang Huizhong’s Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sutra*.
Before the scroll of the *Yi* (義) was finished, he was moved to tears of realization; upon returning, he reported his awakening to his teacher.
His teacher patted him on the back and said, "You shall greatly propagate the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun-jiao*). These sutras were entrusted to you by all the Buddhas.

Having received the secret seal of the Southern School and the prophetic prediction of the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuanyue-jing*), the Chan Master then read through the Tripitaka of Sutras and Vinaya, mastering the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Awakening of Faith*.
Having thoroughly studied these treatises, he then reined in his progress at the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm and sat in meditative repose within the wondrous field of *Samantabhadra’s Awakening*.
He investigated the moisture reached by the "single rain" and exhausted the distinct purposes of the five teachings; thereupon, he composed commentaries and exegeses consisting of:

the *Great Commentary* in three fascicles, the *Great Sub-commentary* in thirteen fascicles, the *Brief Commentary* in two fascicles, the *Small Sub-commentary* in six fascicles, and the *Meaning of Practice and Realization in the Ritual Hall* in ten fascicles.
These eight volumes circulate together in the world; their exposition of the teachings is perfect, their vision of the Dharma is penetrating, and their explanation of meanings is upright.
Their entry into contemplation is as clear as holding a torch, and their phrasing reaches the ultimate principle without frivolous flightiness.
Their prose supports the teachings without superficial ornamentation, and they do not allow their own strengths to become a source of affliction.
Thus, there is no doctrine of exclusion, for it does not depend on what has not yet arrived;

there is no doctrine of personal opinion, for it is vast and open—the very eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the marrow of the thirty-five patriarchs, the fundamental root of living beings, and the thorough path of the three periods of time. Even if there were authors in later generations, none could surpass it. (4)
Is this based on the direct hearing from one who has personally visited a Pure Land? How could it be that the flavor of its meaning is exhausted by such [a description]?
Someone said: "The Way is formless; those who look cannot see it. The Way is directionless; those who travel cannot reach it. How much less can it be captured by words?
It resides simply within one's nature; how could it be fully explained by a mere few tens of thousands of characters? He replied: "Alas!"

This is insufficient for discussing the Way. Did we not say previously that that which unifies all virtues and is fully perfected, which illuminates the masses of darkness and shines alone, is Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)?
For Perfect Enlightenment can give rise to all dharmas, and yet no dharma has ever been apart from Perfect Enlightenment.
Now, as for the texts of the Tripiṭaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—that have been transmitted to China, they number more than five thousand scrolls.
What is that which is expounded therein? It is nothing other than precept, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*). What is sought by practicing precept, concentration, and wisdom?
It is nothing other than Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). Perfect Enlightenment is a single Dharma; yet why do we seek it by unfolding myriad practices?

It is because the faculties and capacities (*indriya-bhājana*) of sentient beings differ. Thus, the entire Great Canon consists of sūtras of Perfect Enlightenment, and this commentary is [the commentary] upon the Great Canon.
To comment upon five thousand scrolls of text with only a few volumes of sub-commentary—is this not extremely concise?

Why then do you say it is prolix? When one cuts off the path of speech, stills the mind of conceptual thought, forgets subject and object, and extinguishes mental images, only then is realization attained;
it certainly does not reside in verbal expression. Alas, for all living beings!
Those who come and go are those of the six realms of existence. Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity and grief; birds and beasts harbor the sorrow of flight and panic;
the asuras are currently in a state of rage, while the devas are immersed in pleasure. To rectify the mind and incline toward Bodhi, only the human path is capable of it.
If one is a human and does not strive for this, I truly know not what to do with such a person. Cease worldly distractions and dwell constantly in dhyāna.
Having entered the master’s domain and received the eminent instructions of the Chan Master, I have no means to repay his kindness;
I shall simply extol his Dharma and announce it to the great assembly. All other details are fully contained in the original preface.
The Great Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment (Original Preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Mount Yuánzhōng.
“Yuan, heng, li, and zhen” are the virtues of Qian; “constant bliss, selfhood, purity, and permanence” are the virtues of the Buddha. Both originate from the single Qi (vital energy).
It is rooted in the single mind; by concentrating the vital energy (*qi*), one attains pliancy, and by cultivating the single mind, one perfects the *citta* of the Way.

This *citta* is profound, empty, wondrous, and pure; it is brilliant and luminous, without coming or going, darkly penetrating the three periods of time. It is neither center nor periphery, but transparently pervades the ten directions.
Being neither extinguished nor born, how could it be harmed by the four mountains? Detached from nature and detached from form, what need is there for the five colors?
It can blind those dwelling in the stream of birth and death; yet the black pearl shines alone amidst the blue sea, and the crescent moon of Nirvāṇa stands solitary and bright in the azure sky.
How great indeed is the source from which the myriad dharmas arise! The myriad dharmas are illusory, arising through the convergence of conditions;

yet the nature of these arising dharmas is fundamentally non-existent—all is but consciousness. Consciousness is like a phantom or a dream, being in essence nothing but the single mind. When this mind is stilled, [all phenomena are extinguished].
Knowing that the circular enlightenment of the eyes is all-pervasive and pure, with no room for anything else within it, its boundless virtues and functions are of one single nature.
When this nature arises as phenomena, object and wisdom are distinct yet clearly interpenetrating; when phenomena and nature are fused, body and mind become vast and open.
Compared to the ocean-seal samādhi, it surpasses even the great void—vast and brilliant, far beyond the reach of thought and speculation. Thus is my Buddha.

Realizing this and pitying those deluded beings, he sighed again, "How marvelous! Having fully contemplated the Great Matter and perfected the Ten Powers, he was able to crush the demonic armies beneath the tree;
thus, he gave rise to the Four Minds, wishing to reveal the treasure-trove within the house.

Yet, because losing one's head is easy while abandoning one's father is difficult, and because awakening is easier than remaining in delusion, he established the teachings at the Immortal Garden and the Site of Enlightenment through gradual stages. Accordingly, he set forth the distinctions of the Five Periods, wherein emptiness and existence alternate.
Alternately manifesting the non-duality of the sudden teaching and the two truths, where the profound spirit is beyond all dependence—does this present sutra not belong to the category of the Sudden?

Thus, when the Tathāgata enters the Land of Quiescent Light, where ordinary and sagely beings share a single source, he manifests the Body of Enjoyment; the principal and the retinue assemble together.
The Great Being Mañjuśrī first inquires into the cause of the original arising, and the Bhagavat first proclaims the ultimate fruit. This illuminates [the truth].

This true essence extinguishes those dream-forms; knowing there is no self or person, who is it that undergoes the cycle of rebirth? From various illusory transformations, birth arises within the awakened mind.

When illusions are exhausted, awakening is perfected; the mind penetrates all, and its principle pervades the Dharma. The mind is fundamentally Buddha; through the arising of thought, one drifts and sinks.

Though the shore does not actually move, it seems to rush past because of the boat’s motion. Suddenly eliminate the false ruler, and the empty sky will not produce flowers; gradually [the delusions] subside.
The source of craving is exhausted like gold that no longer requires smelting; the principle of cultivation and realization is severed, yet wisdom appears as if having gradations.
One realizes that what precedes is not the name of what follows, much less the arising and ceasing of delusion—how could this apply to those whose virtues are equal to perfect luminosity?

Nevertheless, even a fine horse from the stables shakes at the shadow of the whip, and a great treasure buried in dust requires a method of treatment; thus, the three contemplations become clear and bright, and both the provisional and the real are entered.
The various wheels, interwoven in single and double arrays, cultivate the four marks; the spirit is hidden within, beyond perception, yet it does not reject the four ailments when they manifest.
When the essence of the mind is revealed like a blooming flower, one further applies oneself to long, medium, and short-term periods of focused mindfulness and mental restraint.

Through these distinct and comprehensive practices, karmic obstructions and afflictive obstructions are eliminated, and the body of wisdom is perfected. At the ultimate limit of stillness, awakening pervades hundreds of thousands of worlds.

The Buddha-realm manifests before one through hearing these five names; this surpasses the merit of giving away lands and jewels. To explain even half a verse of its meaning is superior to the sands of the Ganges.

That the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle are truly unable to uphold it is because they lack the capacity to receive it. Alas! The *Bā-gē* harmonizes with the multitude, yet its measure-like principles soar upon the monkey-mind;
the *Xuě-qǔ* (Snow Melody) is rarely encountered, for its definitive meaning remains hidden in the Dragon Treasury. Zongmi was still a youth [when he encountered it].

I have specialized in the *Analects* and the *Book of Documents*, and studied the *Brahma-Scriptures*; yet I was equally immersed in the traps of words, tasting only their dregs. Fortunately, at Fushan, the needle and the magnet met;
my Zen practice encountered the Southern School’s teachings, and I met this scripture. With a single word, the ground of my mind opened; within a single scroll, the sky of meaning shone brightly.
Recently, realizing that "the Way is not a fixed way" and that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," I now understand the nature of the mind.

This Buddha’s mind is fixed; he shall surely become a Buddha. Yet, because the Buddha praised the cultivation of wisdom through the accumulation of extensive learning, I have traveled to a hundred cities to sit and explore the various scriptures.
Although my lectures may be superficial and my studies merely those of a student under Master An, I have been graced by his kindness as one who receives instruction.

Having received the seal of approval from a true son of the Buddha, I am moved all the more to feel the Buddha’s grace upon meeting a close friend again. For long I have lamented my own isolation and poverty, and now I wish to set forth [my thoughts].

The Dharma-gift gathers the threads of Prajñā, weaving them into the *Avataṃsaka*; it upholds the *Vinaya* and illuminates the *Vijñaptimātratā*. Yet, among the myriad prescriptions of medical arts, one must select those that provide specific counter-measures;

among the thousand treasures of the ocean, one first seeks the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Considering that the texts are rich and the meanings vast, I truly defer to the *Saṃpuṭa* (the *Avataṃsaka*) for its pointing to the essence;
yet for engaging the faculties according to their capacity, nothing compares to the *Awakening of Faith* (*Bodhicitta-śāstra*). Therefore, I have examined various treatises repeatedly.

The hundred schools have utilized their respective tools to provide detailed expositions; I have contemplated the profound intent of the Sage with utmost sincerity, researching and refining the meaning until its principles were fully realized.

I have integrated both the nature and characteristics (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa) as well as the gradual and sudden teachings, so that those who possess the skill of a master swordsman need not seek elsewhere, and those who practice inward reflection need not look at another’s face—this was my ambition.
On a grand scale, I have severed all boundaries and measures, making the square and expansive correct while embracing all within its inclusivity, and perfecting it through its circularity.
The virtues of this [Dharma] are all-pervasive; the spiritual source of the Awakened One is not obscured.

The term *sūtra* generally refers to all the various sections [of the canon], while "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*) specifically praises this particular text. Because it strings together the flowers of meaning and thereby gathers and transforms all classes of beings, it is called the *Mahāvaipulya-bodhivattāra-sūtra-nītārtha*.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
I take refuge in the one of wondrous form-body, With unimpeded eloquence and wisdom;

In the pure awakening that serves as the locus, And in the gates of cultivation and realization that flow from it— To the Honored One Samantabhadra of Wondrous Virtue, Together with his assembly of twelve hundred thousand.
I have made this profound and vast vow to adorn this essential abridgment of the sūtra.

May the Three Jewels, in their compassionate pity, secretly provide aid through skillful means and wisdom. May the ocean of all dharma-gates flow inwardly into my mind, so that the signs of the principles may manifest within my heart;
like a painting appearing in the wind across the void, let every stroke correspond to the sacred intent.

Every phrase accords with the capacities of all beings; body and mind enter the city of awakening. Together they enjoy the bliss of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the explanation of this sutra, there is a tenfold analysis:
first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, its classification within the Piṭakas and Vehicles (*yāna*); third, the distinction between the provisional and the real;
fourth, the profundity of its scope; fifth, the appropriate capacities of those to be converted; sixth, the essential nature of that which expresses it.
First, regarding the seven points of the general and specific intent (*abhiprāya*): first, the general;
second, the specific. The general refers to repaying causes, responding to requests, manifesting the principle, and delivering sentient beings throughout the Teacher’s entire lifetime.

The arising of the Teaching is entirely due to this. If one traces the Buddha’s original intent, it is solely because he appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*mahāntam artham*), desiring to enable sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and attain purity therein.
Although he speaks of the dharmas realized through the three vehicles and matters of discipline, these teachings are all for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
There are ten reasons for the distinctiveness [of this teaching], for which this sutra is expounded: First, it reveals that causal practice has a fundamental basis.

This refers to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the ground of the original arising of the cause, wherein the Buddha taught that all Tathāgatas rely upon perfect, illuminating pure awakening to realize the emptiness of ignorance;
based on this, they give rise to the pure mind and are then able to cultivate the pāramitās and so forth. Second, it merges... [text truncated]
Because the ultimate fruit is perfected through its absolute cessation, it refers to the total dissolution of the two modes of transformation—the basis of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Only this pure awakened nature constitutes the ultimate fruit, which is without beginning or end, neither increasing nor decreasing;

therefore, it is said that *nirvāṇa* is a dream from yesterday and the Buddha-land is like flowers in the sky. Thus, through these three definitive discernments, one should realize the principle and cultivate accordingly. Therefore, it is said:

Samantabhadra’s intention in questioning was this: "The nature of awakening is fundamentally perfect; all things are like illusions. Since illusions are empty and have no substance, who can speak of 'cultivation'?
If one does not cultivate, by what cause could one realize awakening? The Buddha replied: "One relies on the arising of illusory wisdom to eliminate all illusions.
When illusions are exhausted, wisdom subsides, and the mind of awakening becomes perfectly luminous. However, those who now speak only of emptiness and illusion are mired in nihilism.
Those who cultivate the practice are bound by the attainment of existence precisely because the intent of awakening and cultivation appears contrary yet accords;
thus, the principle is most difficult to clarify and requires decisive discernment. This is because it exhausts all four types of profound doubt, as expressed in the Bodhisattva’s difficult question:
"If sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, then since they currently possess ignorance, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions should subsequently become afflicted."

The Buddha’s intended meaning in his reply was that this very discrimination is itself ignorance; therefore, even seeing Perfect Enlightenment is the same as being subject to transmigration, like "the clouds moving and the moon following.
However, if for even a single moment non-arising occurs, then the past and future limits are severed, like the disappearance of flowers when a cataract is cured.
Sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, yet few are able to know this; those who know it have little faith, and those who believe in it are rare.
Even with understanding upon understanding, it is difficult to reach this state; yet now, through this sutra’s definitive resolution, one truly reaches the source.
If one can master this, all doubts will naturally be dispelled. The five [fetters] eliminate the root of saṃsāra: that which initiates karma and forms seeds has ignorance as its root;
that which moistens karma and leads to rebirth has craving as its basis. If one does not recognize their characteristics, they will immediately act as thieves.
Because if one does not penetrate their emptiness, they can never be severed; thus, the text answers that Mañjuśrī and Maitreya thoroughly investigated and exhausted their roots and sources.

This refers to the six searches for the hidden obstructions to bodhi: although the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span share names with those found in various teachings, their modes of activity are profound and subtle, making them difficult to eliminate as they progress from the coarse to the fine.
It is like the eyelashes, which are not reflected by a bright mirror; I am likewise such that I do not clarify [the truth] without the explicit teaching.

Therefore, in the chapter on Pure Practice, one searches through the layers of meaning, for seven brief phrases can encompass many significances, as stated in the treatise (wherever a citation from the treatise appears without its title, it is from the *Awakening of Faith*). Or there may be sentient beings who attain understanding through extensive hearing.

There are three types of individuals who can achieve understanding: first, those who hear little but possess extensive comprehension, or who delight in *dhāraṇī* and can grasp the vast meaning from brief texts;

second, those for whom both text and meaning are extensive, such as the *Avataṃsaka*; third, those for whom both text and meaning are concise, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*. Regarding these three categories, the first type may encounter texts that are extensive in wording but concise in meaning, like the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;

or texts where both word and meaning are extensive, like the *Avataṃsaka*; or texts where both word and meaning are concise, like the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*. As for the third category, the meaning is concise.
The *Guang* (Extensive Commentary) on that treatise and this sutra consists of twenty-eight sheets of text in a single fascicle.

Its meaning encompasses the Final Teaching (*jiao*) and the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*)—these two being precisely the core tenets it follows—as well as the School of Emptiness (*kong zong*), which includes the cultivation of the two types of emptiness and the revelation that the realms of objects and consciousness are each individually pure, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*;

the School of Characteristics (*xiang zong*), which concerns the distinctions among the five natures and the stages of cultivation and realization; and it also includes the Hinayana (*xiaosheng*), with its analytical examination of the four great elements, the contemplation of differentiation, and the contemplation of impurity, while simultaneously containing the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

[The text] distinguishes between the individual sense organs, consciousnesses, objects, the three realms, and the two categories—each explained through the three [aspects of] equality, immobility, and universal pervasion throughout the Dharma-realm, being neither destroyed nor mixed, like a thousand lamps in a single room;

furthermore, it explains the distinct cultivation of the three contemplations and how, based on a single dharma-nature, one manifests precept, concentration, and wisdom. It universally resolves and clarifies the meaning and intent of cultivation (for every dharma-gate is entered through realization and cultivated by relying upon the dharma);

thus, at the beginning of each contemplation gate, it states "realizing the pure *pariniṣpanna-bodhi*" (*jìng yuánjué*), and only then speaks of "cultivating such and such," and so forth. It fully encompasses both sudden and gradual approaches to the Chan gates, having extensively explored the entire Dragon Canon.

There is no preparation for these eight [sections] because the single Dharma skillfully applies to the three faculties. That is to say: the Gate of Universal Eye Contemplation applies to those of superior faculties;
the Three Contemplations of the Various Wheels apply to those of middling faculties; and the Three Periods of the Ritual Site apply to those of inferior faculties (both of these are gradual).
Regarding the "single Dharma," in every single passage there is nothing that does not cite the Perfect Enlightenment as its basis and conclude by entering into Perfect Enlightenment.

Ninth, because it causes one to cultivate profound meditation that accords with the nature [of reality], the various schools' gates of dhyāna-samādhi do not transcend the four formless [attainments] and the four emptinesses;

only the *Awakening of Faith* directly cultivates the samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This sutra, however, leads directly into the gate of the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Although there are differences between the three faculties regarding gradual or sudden entry, that which is entered is none other than Perfect Enlightenment. Tenth, it exhorts one to remain detached from phenomena and clarify their signlessness.

Because the teachings on the various secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) taught by the Master provide rules for practice that can be followed and traces upon which to rely, it is not necessarily required to follow a spiritual friend or teacher for a long time. This sutra states that delusion is fundamentally non-existent and further says there is nothing to be severed;
it states that the Buddha is primordially present and further says one must diligently cultivate all ritual protocols—all categories of such [teachings] are like this in the final age.
Later students find it difficult to rely upon and follow; they must instead seek out a master who is free from conceptual signs and who can provide clear instruction at every turn.

Therefore, one should draw near such a teacher, dedicating one's entire life and even sacrificing one’s body. Amidst the four modes of deportment, do not cling to their outward forms; do not resent them when they depart, nor be arrogant when they arrive.
Only by serving and taking refuge in this manner can one truly awaken to and enter Perfect Enlightenment. Thus, the youth Sudhana...
When the Master first encountered Mañjuśrī, as soon as he gave rise to the mind of awakening and development, Mañjuśrī immediately instructed him to draw near to virtuous friends;

this was because the principles of the Dharma-realm are difficult to clarify due to their alternating concealment and manifestation, and thus taking a teacher as one's guide was established as the subsequent standard.

Regarding the classification by way of the two collections (*piṭaka*) and vehicles (*yāna*): the three dharmas constitute three gates—first the collection, next the vehicle, and finally the division. "Collection" refers to the three collections (*tripiṭaka*).

As for the general designation of "collection" (*piṭaka*) for the two collections, it is because they contain and encompass [the teachings]. Regarding the first, the three collections: first is the *sūtra*, which in ancient translations is rendered as *qìjīng* (契經).
"Qì" (契) means to accord with principle and to accord with the capacities of beings; "jīng" (經) means to string together, penetrate, and gather those to be converted.

The *sūtra* (契經) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "a scripture that accords with principle and suits the faculties. As a *karmadhāraya*, it refers to the "Piṭaka" (藏). Its direct translation is "thread" (*sūtra*).

A thread can string together flowers, and a scripture can hold together the warp [of the Dharma]. Because the term for "thread" was not valued in this land [China], the word "scripture" (*jing*) was retained.

However, since in India the terms *sūtra* were used for threads, mats, scriptures, ropes, and even the holy teachings themselves, the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* translates it as [the following].

The ancient masters of the Holy Teachings observed that both Confucianism and Mohism refer to their own texts as "classics" (*jing*). Consequently, they borrowed the term "classic" from them to designate the Holy Teachings;

thus, the name encompasses two meanings and accords with both traditions. By adding the character "conformity" (*qie*) to assist the name—distinguishing it from the "classics" of the secular world—this usage is highly appropriate.

Regarding the third point, the comparative analysis of the provisional and the real: throughout the ancient and modern periods, the virtuous masters of both the Western Regions and this land have established various schools and categorized the teachings with differing views on their integration or separation—some maintaining that there is but a single flavor without distinction, while others open up distinct schools and conduct detailed discernment. First, because the single principle is fundamentally of one flavor and various paths return to the same destination; second, because the single voice universally responds and the two [aspects] universally nourish;
third, because the Buddha’s original intent was for the sake of a single matter; fourth, because the various understandings differ according to each individual text;

This is the meaning behind Kumārajīva’s establishment of the "Single-Sound Teaching" (ekasvara-dharma) during the Yao Qin period.

Second, as views gradually arise, the single flavor is gradually divided, with each establishing its own source and faction to disparage others.

During the third turning, the teaching was given universally for those setting out upon any of the vehicles; because it encompasses all three vehicles and the scope of those to be guided is exhaustive, it alone is of definitive meaning.
Second, regarding the completeness or deficiency of the verbal expression: during the first period, only the Hīnayāna was taught; during the second period, only the Mahāyāna was taught.

First, it is shown that the ultimate meaning (*nītārtha*) is realized only when the manifestation of conditions is exhausted through the realization of the principle of emptiness (initially consisting of the two vehicles of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, subsequently augmented by the addition of the Mahāyāna to form the three vehicles, and finally culminating in the Single Vehicle).

This is the gateway established by Jñānaprabha for making such determinations. Because these two types of gateways exist, the various scriptural teachings—each based on its own particular force—are either definitive or non-definitive, yet they do not contradict one another; this is explained in the subsequent section.

Among those who maintain the position that [all things] are both empty and existent, there are further two [subdivisions]: first, the presentation of divergent views; second, the reconciliation of these views to show they are not contradictory.

for if there were no mind or mental factors, what would be abandoned, what realized, what cultivated, or what beneficial? Thus the treatise says:

If there is a passage that speaks of dependent origination as empty, one should know that this is said with reference to the fact that dependently originated phenomena lack the two kinds of self (*ātman*) as they are conceptually imputed;

If they were thus non-existent, that would be a nihilistic non-existence, a view of wrongly grasped emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) which is truly terrifying. As the Sūtra says: "It is better to..."

for the profound *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* definitively teaches that [phenomena] exist, and this cannot be contradicted. Second, regarding this statement:
Phenomena arising from conditions are definitively empty, because that which arises from conditions necessarily lacks intrinsic nature, just like a magical illusion;

Even if there were a place where it was taught that the essence of phenomena arising from conditions exists, one should know that this is merely a conventional, provisional designation and does not mean that the essence of those phenomena is truly non-empty; for if they possessed an essence, they would not [arise from conditions].

Because [things] arise from conditions and do not arise without conditions, there is no seeing, abandoning, realizing, or cultivating; this destroys the two truths. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states:
"If all dharmas were not empty, there would be no Path and no fruit. The Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā states:

"If all dharmas were not empty, then the Three Jewels and the Four Truths would not exist—this constitutes a great false view. The Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra states: "One contemplates that all dharmas arise from causes."
That which arises dependently, arising from causes and conditions, lacks intrinsic nature; because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is ultimately and entirely empty.

Furthermore, if you say that this illusory object is not empty, I shall now ask you: regarding the rabbit [in the] illusory cloth, does the rabbit exist within the cloth, or does it exist outside the cloth?
Does it exist as the cloth itself, or does it exist apart from the cloth? Does it have fur and skin, or does it not?

Since its flesh and bones have both utterly perished, what reliance can there be? What, then, is there to grasp as existing? You should know that this rabbit perishes of itself without awaiting destruction;
it was fundamentally unarisen yet appears as empty. Therefore, it is only through the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) that the two truths can be maintained.

Furthermore, as for your claim that our school holds a "view of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), this fault belongs to you. Why? Because if you were to establish existence, it would not depend upon conditions (*pratyaya*).
If one does not rely on conditions, then cause and effect would be severed; is this not the view of emptiness? To stubbornly cling to the existence of dharmas—is this not the view of existence?
Since both views of existence and non-existence simultaneously undermine your own tenet, why do you not feel fear? The emptiness I speak of is free from the views of existence and non-existence;
your own view of emptiness is what is at fault, not my tenet. Furthermore, how can you say that a wise person acts to eliminate illusion?
Regarding the phrase "the enemies and so forth": in which Mahāyāna sūtras is it not taught that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations?
When a bodhisattva cultivates illusory wisdom, severs illusory delusions, accomplishes illusory practices, and attains illusory fruits—how could such teachings not be contradicted [by your position]?
Why do you not feel fear? Furthermore, your own master, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, followed the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* within his own system.
Since Nāgārjuna was honored as an Ācārya and you have already relied upon his teachings to explain other treatises, how could you, as one of his later followers, suddenly disparage them?

Within the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the Buddha stated that Nāgārjuna dwells on the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), is able to destroy the views of existence and non-existence, and will be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Since it is said he destroys the views of existence and non-existence, how could he ever hold to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) alone?
Since those who disparage others and contend with the Buddha as praised by the Buddha are not of the Śākya lineage, while in the second assembly there were none who opposed him;

and since all phenomena of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) have never possessed an intrinsic nature and have never been destroyed—being without nature, without destruction, non-dual, and unimpeded—they constitute dependent origination. Therefore, although Nāgārjuna and others spoke of the exhaustion of existence, [it is in this sense].
Emptiness does not destroy existence; since existence is not diminished, this is the emptiness of existence that is non-contradictory.
This is the true emptiness that is free from both existence and emptiness. Although masters such as Asaṅga speak of existence within the ultimate emptiness, they do not diminish that emptiness.
Since emptiness is not diminished, this is existence within emptiness that is non-contradictory. Therefore, it is also free from both emptiness and existence.
One should know that these two explanations—of existence as an illusion and of existence itself—are entirely interfused without any remaining boundary;

for although each describes a single meaning, they are fully and perfectly complete in their entirety, and thus there is no contradiction between them. Were it otherwise, one would likely fall into nihilism and fail to exert effort in establishing existence.
Failing to realize that this existence is an existence not different from emptiness, one consequently rejects that emptiness.

On the contrary, one loses what is inherently one's own because of grasping at existence (*bhāva*). Furthermore, if one fears falling into the state of having something to attain (*upalabdhi*), one might strenuously establish emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
yet, failing to realize that this emptiness is not a void distinct from existence, one consequently rejects that existence and instead loses what is inherently one's own—namely, emptiness itself.
One loses this inherent emptiness precisely because of grasping at emptiness; therefore, the entire substance [of the mind] is completely [lost].
Regarding the existence or non-existence of emptiness, masters such as Asaṅga teach that it exists as a whole in its entirety, while Nāgārjuna and others teach that it does not.
These two positions are not mutually contradictory; rather, because the two meanings are interdependent and mutually inclusive, they are non-dual. Question:
If this is so, why did later commentators such as Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla refute one another? Answer: This is...
They are mutually constitutive, not mutually destructive. Why is this? Because sentient beings of the final age possess faculties that gradually become dull;

when they hear it said that things exist as illusions (*māyopama*), they take them to be truly existent. Therefore, Bhāviveka and others refute existence until it is exhausted, so that only ultimate emptiness remains, at which point those illusory existences of dependent origination can be established.
If one does not reach ultimate nature-emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), then those dependently originated phenomena cannot be established.

Because illusory existence arises, it exists; therefore, in order to establish that it exists, one refutes [the notion of] existence. Furthermore, when others hear it said that the nature of dependent origination is emptiness, they take this to mean nihilistic non-existence.
Therefore, Dharmapāla and others refute [this view of] emptiness by maintaining the existence of illusionary existence.

Only when this illusory existence is preserved can one attain that true emptiness which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā*). If one does not fully arrive at this illusory existence, then [true emptiness] is not attained.
That emptiness which is their true nature is therefore the negation of emptiness for the sake of establishing emptiness.

If it were not so, later masters would find that as two principles mutually penetrate and their totalities cancel one another out, there would be no way to penetrate the profound depth of dependent origination.
Thus, what appears to be mutual negation is in fact mutual establishment, because the illusory existence and the true emptiness possess these two meanings.

First, extreme mutual conformity means merging into a single characteristic such that the entire substance is fully subsumed; second, extreme mutual opposition means each harms the other such that they are completely annihilated.
If there were no complete annihilation through mutual displacement, there would be no way for the entire substance to be fully subsumed;

therefore, what is extremely opposed is precisely what is extremely conformable. Because Nāgārjuna, Asaṅga, and others approach this from the perspective of extreme conformity, they do not [contradict one another].

Because Bhāviveka’s refutation of Dharmapāla is based on a point of extreme contradiction, they must refute one another; only when contradiction and conformity are without obstruction is there true dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Therefore, the preceding and succeeding [positions] do not contradict each other. One should reflect upon the rest accordingly: there are no phenomena that do not harmonize.
Third, regarding the succession in this land: it is truly because the time since the Sage departed is remote that the source and its currents have become increasingly [divergent].

Consequently, great virtuous ones have shouldered one another and eminent monks have followed in succession, continuing this tradition down to the Zhenguan era.
Names and signs proliferate, becoming increasingly corrupt through successive transmission; taking the provisional for the real causes the true path to be eclipsed by heterodox views.
Although the color of milk remains, its flavor is entirely absent; though the medicinal Dharma is disseminated, the maladies of delusion only increase.

Since the nature of reality and the teachings have thus been disparaged, the stream of the Way has become silent. If one does not carefully discern and select, how can one point toward the ultimate destination? Yet, this is the Mahāyāna.

Since existence and emptiness differ, the two truths have distinct essences; thus, the four aspects of the true and the conventional do not intermingle).

Because the cause ceases, it is not eternal; because the fruit arises, it is not annihilated. The four characteristics arise simultaneously: the characteristic of cessation manifests the absence of subsequent [arising], while the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms take objects and sever delusions.
This is explained as the simultaneous contemplation of both, yet they are determined to be distinct, for the former illuminates the conditioned.
The wisdom that realizes the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is said to be non-different [from it], yet in reality they are not one.

Since both mundane and supramundane wisdoms depend upon the seeds of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), the mental states of the four wisdoms are subject to transformation by their characteristics.

Consequently, the *dharmakāya* as the fruition body of a Buddha is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), for it is taught categorically that whatever arises as a phenomenon must necessarily cease. There are many such categories of meaning in great detail.

As fully explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and other such texts, those who establish the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong) maintain that the eight consciousnesses are all pervasive within the Tathāgatagarbha;
because these are established as True Suchness (*tathatā*) following conditions, it is said that True Suchness possesses the two meanings of immutability and following conditions.

Since the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is identical to the single principle of perfect completion (*pariniṣpanna*), it is said that the realm of sentient beings and the Buddha-realm are equal and uniform.

Neither increasing nor decreasing, the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) pervades both the true and the false (as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says "only one," and the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* says "non-dual").
Therefore, although it is empty, it is not severed; although it exists, it is not eternal. These four characteristics occur simultaneously, for their essential nature is itself cessation.

Thus, cessation and arising are simultaneous (as taught in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, and *Awakening of Faith*). To illumine that delusion has no root is itself the essence of wisdom; to illumine that this essence has no self-nature is itself the essence of liberation.

This is the realization of suchness; since both mundane and supramundane wisdoms depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is identical with the fundamental [awakening], the conditioned and the unconditioned are neither one nor different.
Therefore, the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is both eternal and the Dharma-body, and does not fall into the realm of numerical categories;

how much more so for the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is the very essence of wisdom and is not subject to the shifts of phenomenal characteristics? As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If one speaks of the Tathāgata..."
Those who likewise possess conditioned existence die and enter hell; such categories of meaning are also numerous.

Their sequence corresponds to that found in scriptures such as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and treatises such as the *Awakening of Faith*, and there is no contradiction when these are reconciled later. However, because the two schools each cling to their own respective authorities, they contradict one another.

If one understands the underlying intent and provides a harmonious interpretation, they do not conflict; this is because [the teachings] are directed toward the capacities of sentient beings (*yathā-yogam*).

Thus, regarding the three [types of grass], according to the Dharma they are one; regarding new conditioning (*navābhyāsa*), they are five; regarding original existence (*mūlataḥ sattva*), there is neither two nor one.

If one enters into principle, both are simultaneously swept away, and thus the three and the one are both extinguished. Now, judging the teachings based on the Buddha’s transformative ritual (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*), that which can be three and that which can be one exist;

therefore, those who contend over right and wrong realize there is no contradiction or dispute. Second, as for the refutation of the Proponents of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavādin*), there are also two parts; first, the analysis.

The differences are briefly distinguished in five ways: first, the distinction between the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*); second, the distinction between true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) and conventional knowledge; third, the distinction between the two truths and the three truths;
fourth, the distinction between the existence and emptiness of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); and fifth, the distinction between the existence and emptiness of the Buddha’s qualities.
Regarding these, the Niḥsvabhāvavāda school asserts that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, which is itself *tathatā*; one who can realize this is...
It is called "True Wisdom" (for those who have not yet realized the absence of intrinsic nature, there is no true wisdom). The dharmas and meanings explained therein do not transcend the Two Truths:

existence refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent), while emptiness refers to the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected). Although the Buddha-body is said to be found through fivefold seeking, such finding is merely illusory;
non-finding is the truth. Being free from all marks is called the merit of the Buddha. If one follows the Dharma-nature school (*Faxing zong*), it clarifies the purity of self-nature.
The pure, eternally abiding true mind is precisely the ultimate reality; therefore, the treatise describes the essence of *tathatā* as being "merely the one mind.

This one mind is the true reality that is inherently capable of knowing, penetrating both principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*), and pervading both defilement and purity (as stated in the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where the Buddha’s realm and wisdom, and the questions and answers regarding the Buddha’s realm and knowledge, are distinct).
The dharma-meanings thus expounded are complete with the three truths (*trisatya*); form and other phenomena are themselves emptiness.

The True Truth (*satyārtha*)—that the reflection in a mirror is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and that emptiness is itself form (*rūpa*), and so forth—is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). [In this state,] emptiness does not destroy the reflection. The single true nature of the mind (*citta-tathatā*), which is neither empty nor form, yet is capable of being both empty and form, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

[In this state, it is] like the luminosity within the mirror. Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): 1. The *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is existent from the perspective of deluded attachment (*sattva*) but non-existent in reality (*artha*); its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) exists, but its essence (*svabhāva*) is non-existent. 2. The *paratantra* (dependent nature) is existent in reality but non-existent from the perspective of deluded attachment; its essence exists, but its characteristic is non-existent. 3. The *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) is existent in reality and existent from the perspective of deluded attachment; both its characteristic and its essence exist. All these are present.
The essential bodies of all Buddhas are each endowed with the ten bodies, the ten wisdoms, the marks and signs of true merit, and the pervasive light;
each of these is inexhaustible, existing inherently from the beginning, not dependent upon conditions or opportunities. These five have been briefly explained;
the others may be understood by analogy. As for the subsequent "convergence" (hui), it means that since all phenomena are the manifestation of the true mind through conditions, they converge therein.
Because conditions lack intrinsic nature, they return to the true mind; thus, from the beginning, they do not differ from original gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*).

Outside of this, there is no separate wisdom; other truths and natures may be clarified by analogy with these examples. However, while teachings have distinctions between their beginnings and ends, the Dharma itself has no difference in depth. (This concludes the establishment of the three teachings according to the traditions of China and the Western Regions.

Third, during the two dynasties of Chen and Sui, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi established four kinds of teaching: 1. The Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭaka-yāna*); 2. The Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*); 3. The Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*); 4. The Perfect Teaching (*samantabhadra-yāna*).

The Tripiṭaka Teaching (for those of inferior faculties who follow the teaching from beginning to end) clarifies the principle of the Four Noble Truths regarding the arising and ceasing of dependent origination;

it is the direct teaching for the Śrāvaka vehicle and an incidental teaching for Bodhisattvas. The Two Shared Teachings (where the three vehicles equally receive the instruction) clarify that dependent origination is itself emptiness and non-arising;
the principle of the Four Noble Truths is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, being the direct teaching for Bodhisattvas and an incidental teaching for the two [Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha] vehicles.

(The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle should study Prajñā, etc. Third, this distinct teaching (*biejiao*) is not shared with those of the two vehicles;

therefore, it correctly elucidates the principle of the four noble truths as being infinitely provisional designations based on causes and conditions. It transforms bodhisattvas without involving the two vehicles, yet it is not called "unshared" (*bujung*).
It is termed "distinct" because it also intends to exclude [the teachings] that are not the Perfect (*yuan*), distinguishing them by means of a single cause that stands apart.
Because it produces fruits one by one without integration, practicing them in a sequential and distinct manner, it cannot achieve the perfect fusion of cause and fruit.

The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) correctly elucidates the inconceivable dependent origination, the Middle Way within the two truths, and the complete sufficiency of phenomena and principle; it is neither partial nor differentiated.

Because it transforms only those of the highest and sharpest faculties, it is called "Perfect. (In this teaching, the aspects of teaching, wisdom, principle, severance, practice, stages, cause, and fruit are all both distinct and perfect.)

However, these four teachings arise from the three contemplations (*san guan*). Because there are differences in the analytical and substantial approaches when entering emptiness from the conventional (*ru kong*), the first two teachings arise;
because there is a distinct teaching (*bie jiao*) for entering the conventional from emptiness and entering the middle from the conventional, the three contemplations arise;

and because they can be attained within a single moment of mind, the Perfect Teaching (*yuan jiao*) arises. Furthermore, these four teachings are not restricted to a single division (*bu*); within each division, they may all be present.

Furthermore, for this reason, they are again subsumed under four modes of teaching: namely, the Sudden, the Gradual (as previously mentioned by Master Liu), the Indeterminate (mutual knowledge), and the Secret (mutual ignorance).
Initially, in order to address non-Buddhists, the three matters of precepts, concentration, and wisdom were established;

because these three are distinct and different from one another, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls them the "Three Piṭakas," and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* is likewise so named. The intent of the Shared Teaching is to harmonize these three, and thus it is distinguished [from the others].

Because the teachings manifest the three [teachings] based on a single dharma-nature, the three and one of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are non-obstructive; thus, this master’s established principles are perfectly complete.
However, while he primarily elucidates the *Avataṃsaka*, he also incorporates other methods such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; though it is exclusively Perfect, it possesses minor deficiencies.
Fourth, the Master Xianshou, the patriarch of the *Avataṃsaka*, established five types of teaching, for which there is an extensive separate chapter.

The Great Same (Dàtóng) Tiantai school merely adds the Sudden Teaching (Dùnjiào) to [the fourfold classification]. What are these five? First, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teaching;
third, the Final teaching; fourth, the Sudden teaching; and fifth, the Perfect teaching. The first corresponds to the *Āgama* (Cángjiào) of Tiantai;

because it accords with the capacities of beings and follows the words of others, it explains the various categories of dharmas as being exclusively distinct, for its purpose is to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

The distinction between ordinary beings and sages is established through their respective inclinations toward joy and aversion, clarifying cause and effect; however, the number of dharmas taught therein is seventy-five.

It speaks only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and does not clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). (Although the *Āgamas* state that there is no such thing as "old age and death," this is likewise not explicitly stated.

Relying solely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to establish the roots of defilement and purity, it fails to exhaust the source of all phenomena; therefore, many disputes arise. (From the perspective of the Buddha’s intent, this is comprehensive; from the perspective of the literal teaching, it remains obscured.)

Therefore, those who study and practice this school adhere to the principles according to the words and grasp the essence according to the characteristics; they compose treatises and propagate them through an unbroken succession of transmission, as extensively analyzed in the *Zongqu* (The Essential Tenets).

Second, the Initial Teaching (*shijiao*) is also called the Partial Teaching (*fenjiao*), because it is identified with the second and third periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*. This is because [this teaching] uniformly accepts that those of fixed nature (*niyāta-gotra*) and those without nature (*agotra*) both fail to attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, these are now combined and categorized collectively as a single teaching. Since this has not yet exhausted the Great [Vehicle], [it remains incomplete].
Because it establishes the principle of the Vehicle of the Means (upāya-yāna), it is established as "initially existing" [but] not yet attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is called "partial.
It extensively explains the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) while pruning the superfluous and recording only the essentials; even so, there are still about one hundred [doctrines].

Because it briefly explains the nature of phenomena (dharma-dhātu), and because the nature of phenomena—the phenomena that are explained—is decisively determined and clearly distinguished, there is little dispute. Third, the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya) is also called the True Teaching (bhūta-naya) and the Teaching of Fixed Nature (niyata-gotra).
Because it establishes that those of the two vehicles and the icchantikas shall all attain Buddhahood, it represents the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna;

thus it is established as the "Final" (zhōng) and called "Real" (shí) because it accords with the true principle. It teaches few characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and much of the nature (dharmatā), for even the characteristics taught ultimately converge into the nature;
thus, there is no contention regarding its doctrines. Both of these preceding teachings rely upon the stages and positions (bhūmi).

The gradual cultivation and realization of the stages is collectively termed the "Gradual Teaching. As for the "Sudden Teaching," it holds that the mere non-arising of a single thought-moment is itself called Buddhahood;

because it does not rely on the sequential progression through stages and positions, it is established as "Sudden. (The *Sāṃkhyavikrīḍita-sūtra* states: "One who attains the true nature of all dharmas does not proceed from one stage to another. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"The first stage is itself the eighth, and so on up to the stage of nothingness—what sequence could there be? It does not teach the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) at all, but only elucidates the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
The nature of all that exists is nothing but conceptual construction; the entire dharma-realm is nothing but the transcendence of words. The five dharmas and the three self-natures are all empty;
the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of non-self are both discarded and negated. Teach the contemplation of detachment from signs of disparagement so that the mind is extinguished;
when the mind does not arise, it is itself delusion, and when it does not arise, it is itself the Buddha. Thus, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising.
"Birth is like the silent abiding of Vimalakīrti"—this is its intended meaning. Question: If this is the teaching (śāsana), what then is the principle (nyāya)? Answer:

Because it directly expresses this principle, it is called the Sudden Teaching (tongo). It is established as a distinct category because it addresses those whose faculties are free from discursive thought (nirvikalpa).

Furthermore, it serves as an antidote for those who are stuck in signs (nimitta), such as [the extremes of] emptiness or existence; thus, it accords with the Chan school. As for the fifth, the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), it clarifies that a single stage is...

All stages are, in every respect, a single stage; therefore, the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) subsumes the five stages and the attainment of perfect enlightenment, wherein the primary and its attendants are fully present.
For this reason, it is called the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which is the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

What is taught therein is exclusively the inexhaustible nature-ocean of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), a perfectly interfused and unimpeded dependent origination, like the overlapping jewels of Indra’s net.
Although this judgment is profound and its principles are exhaustive and comprehensive, Master Qingliang took it as his standard;

I now likewise rely upon it. Furthermore, I shall proceed from the "One Sound" of Zhi Dun and Kumārajīva to the "Four Teachings" of Tiantai, correlating them in sequence to demonstrate their completeness.
First, they are collectively treated as one, meaning that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) subsumes each of the preceding four.

First, regarding their commonality in being "round" (just as the hundred rivers in the sea are nothing other than the sea): this refers solely to that which is expounded by the Tathāgata’s single great skillful means and single voice.
Second, regarding the distinction between the "half" and the "full": the first [of the two] is the half, while the latter four are all full;

the former four are winding paths, while the last one is the level path. Third, regarding the distinction between the gradual and the sudden: the first three are gradual (within these, they correspond respectively to the three periods of Jñānaprabha, the first two of which are the three periods of Śīlabhadra); the fourth is indeterminate.

The fifth is the Sudden [teaching] (as both Master Ci'en and Master Liu judged the *Avataṃsaka* to be the Sudden teaching). Fourth, the first [of these four], the *Āgama* teachings, constitutes the Tripitaka Teaching; the second, the emptiness [of the *Prajñāpāramitā*], constitutes the Shared Teaching;
the third and fourth are both the Distinct Teaching; and the fifth is named the Perfect Teaching. It is already known that these five teachings permeate all scriptural expositions.
However, it remains uncertain which of those [five] this present sutra is subsumed under. Now, to clarify this meaning, it is divided as follows:
Regarding the three gates: first, "that fully encompasses this, while this partially encompasses that" refers to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

This means that the various meanings—such as the sovereign and unimpeded great functions of the Buddhas regarding both their primary and secondary fruits (*dharmakāya* and *rūpakāya*), the myriad subtle functions like grains of sand on the shore, and the fact that all phenomena naturally interpenetrate one another in layers of mutual fusion and inclusion—are not taught in this sutra. However, if one considers only the direct revelation of the essence of the single true Dharma-realm (*ekasatyadharmadhātu*) and the meaning of the non-obstruction of the one and the many within contemplation, then this sutra is identical [to the Perfect Teaching].
Second, "this partially encompasses that, while that does not encompass this" refers to the first two teachings (the Separate and Shared Teachings).

(The text states that by severing self-attachment and practicing the two types of emptiness contemplation, one removes craving; it further says that because it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice gradually, it is able to include them. However, these are all merely provisional expedients established based on the perfectly luminous awakened mind.

Since the beginning and end of their cultivation have no substantial reality and each is nothing but the luminous clarity of awakening, they are not truly encompassed by those [gradualist] categories. Third, regarding the mutual subsumption of their essential natures and total characteristics, this refers to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao).

(This sutra also relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, as the text says, "Knowing illusion is itself liberation," etc., and it is called the "Sudden Teaching Mahayana. This concludes the comparative analysis of the provisional and the real.
[End. The Great Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, Volume One, Part One.
