Regarding the authoritative nature of the sacred word (*āptavacana*), which does not depend on other discourses, the *Śāstra* says:

"Within the two types of Buddha-fields—the Enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) and Transformation (*nirmāṇa*)—to which category does this present Buddha-field belong? And what kind of body is the Buddha who preached this sutra? [Below this, there are four sections: first, the erroneous view;

second, the correct view; third, the inquiry; and fourth, the perfect realization. First: One interpretation holds that this land is subsumed under the Transformation Land (*nirmāṇakāya-kṣetra*), and the Buddha who preached this sutra is a Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

[Regarding the body: An external objection states: "If this is so, why does the Sūtra say that [the Buddha] 'dwells in the most excellent realm, which transcends the sphere of activity of the three realms'? Is this not a defiled land? The response below says:

"In order to inspire those prior to the stage of the grounds (*bhūmi*) and others to joyfully cultivate the causes, the Buddha temporarily manifests a pure land and a wondrous body, and through his supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*), he empowers the assembly so that they may temporarily behold it.
[Next it says: There is an interpretation that this land is subsumed under the Enjoyment Land (*saṃbhogakāya-kṣetra*), and that the Buddha who preaches this Sūtra is [a Sambhogakāya Buddha].
Regarding the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the extent of this pure land is boundless. (To address the first objection:

If it were merely a temporary transformation created for the sake of allowing the assembly to see it, it should appear as clearly as in other sūtras [such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the three transformations of the pure land, or the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* where Vimalakīrti presses the earth with his toe;

in these texts, it is stated that "it is by the Buddha’s supernatural power," etc.]. Since the sūtras do not state this [regarding the present case], and since the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* is not like this, it is therefore the land of the Enjoyment Body. (Conclusion: If that is so, this belongs to those on the stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding what Bodhisattvas ought to see and hear, for what reason is this Dharma assembly compiled and circulated within this manifested Buddha-land?

It is because the Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma intends to manifest the Omniscient One (the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya), as well as his dwelling place (the Pure Land), as transcending the mundane world (the Transformation Body’s defiled land).
By manifesting them in this way—[hereafter, the intent of this manifestation is explained; there are four points: he desires to... [let it be known].

(1) Because the sentient beings to be converted take delight in it; (2) in order to cause them to make the vow to be born in such a pure land, to see such Buddhas, and to hear such Dharma, so that they may cultivate those causes;

(3) in order to produce great joy in sentient beings who possess vast and superior resolve, as well as in all Bodhisattvas—therefore it was compiled and disseminated. (This concludes the three points above. (4) Furthermore, this is a supreme Dharma.
In this regard, it is appropriate to hear that while the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) is not supreme, its coarse characteristics cannot be fully proclaimed (*concluding the preceding point*).

Therefore, the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) dwells in the *saṃbhogakāya*-land and teaches the various bodhisattvas on the first stage and above, so that those who transmit the Dharma may compile and circulate it (*summarizing the conclusion of the correct doctrine*).
Next, [the author] provisionally sets forth an external objection: "If that is so, why does he not teach only that [the *nirmāṇakāya*]?"

Regarding the Dharma that was taught: why not simply designate Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and other locations by means of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and then, within the sutras themselves, praise and explain the sublime and wondrous qualities of the true body (*dharmakāya*) and its pure land—as is done in texts such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*?
Furthermore, [the text] points out the fault of not designating the place of teaching, saying:

"If neither the place nor the speaker is mentioned—if there were no physical form, name, transformation body, or transformed land, such as Śākyamuni at Jetavana and so forth—one would not know where this Dharma was spoken or who spoke it."

Because all [beings] harbor doubts—due to the absence of a presiding lord and the lack of the six accomplishments—it is necessary to provide a complete explanation (this is the conclusion). Later, the principle of ultimate exhaustion is harmonized and explained as follows:
"In terms of the true meaning (*yathārthārtha*), when Śākyamuni preached this sūtra, it was not that he was anything other than the World-Honored One Śākyamuni himself;

rather, the great assembly prior to the stages saw the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) dwelling in this defiled land and preaching the Dharma for them, while the great assembly on the stages saw him receiving [the teaching]."

Using their bodies, they dwell in the Buddha’s pure lands and he preaches the Dharma for them (thus there are also cases where both the pure and the impure are indicated, as in the *Samādhi-rāja-sūtra* and others).
Although what they hear is the same (they hear the same essential meaning of the Dharma), what they see differs individually (some see him in Śrāvastī, Magadha, or the Jeta Grove;

some see him with a body one zhang and six chi tall, possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; some see him in the Boundless Pure Land of Radiance as the body of Vairocana, pervading the Dharma-realm, with eighty-four thousand marks and characteristics; and so forth). Some see Vairocana.

Within each and every atom of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) and the infinite worlds, his bodies possess as many marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) as there are atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Although all rejoice together, believe, accept, and practice [the teachings], each believes in what they themselves see regarding their own body and land, and what they hear regarding the Dharma;

thus, while their understanding has varying depths and their practices differ accordingly—each cultivating their path according to what they see and understand—the one who transmits the Dharma does so in order to cause sentient beings to hear of the supreme and rare aspirations, so that they may diligently cultivate those causes.

Because one is born in the Pure Land and realizes the merits of a Buddha, the compilers—speaking from the perspective of those who perceive the supreme—record that "the Bhagavān dwells in the most excellent [state]," and so forth.

(This indicates the intention that while the names, marks, and titles of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) dwelling in an impure land are concealed, only the realm of the true body (*dharmakāya*) in the Pure Land is revealed. This is the case in all other scriptures as well;

because they benefit beings according to their capacities, each scripture merely reveals the transformation body in an impure land while concealing the true body in the Pure Land, in accordance with its own specific intent. Therefore, it was said previously that there is concealment and revelation depending on the capacity of the recipient. [End of] Exegesis.
It is said that the commentaries are clear and explicit, requiring no further deliberation; when verified against the preceding scriptures and other analogous examples, the correspondence is evident.

As for the ten scriptures listed previously (including the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*), which all expound upon extraordinary matters and profound, subtle principles, those capable of receiving, collecting, and transcribing them without omission are none other than Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*). Only such individuals are qualified for this task.

Because it was entrusted [to them], the Pure Land was proclaimed; only when Bodhisattvas personally received it and transmitted it in succession did all classes of beings universally receive its benefits.
Regarding the essential purport of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: it is vast and profound. Its Buddha-land is the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-lokadhātu*), and its Buddha-body is Vairocana.

Yet, even he manifested within impure realms, appearing in seven locations among humans and devas (the first assembly at the Kingdom of Magadha, the second, seventh, and eighth [at the Dragon Palace], and so forth).

(Question: Since the Universal Radiance Hall (Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala), the three Trāyastriṃśa heavens, the four Yāma heavens, the five Tuṣita heavens, the six Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, and the Jeta Grove are all not apart from the Desire Realm, why is it that the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other such texts do not [mention them]?
(Answer: The Great Sage established his teachings through many gates of both provisional and ultimate truth. In sum, all sūtras do not exceed three intended meanings.

That is to say, as for the various other sūtras, they are intended to lead those who follow their consciousnesses to enter [the path]; therefore, they mention only the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) and the defiled lands.
Because scriptures such as the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* intend for the wise to receive and realize the truth, they specifically cite the true body (*dharmakāya*) and its pure land.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, consciousness and wisdom are interfused, the pure and the defiled penetrate one another, and the entire dharma-realm is encompassed; it speaks in accordance with the nature of reality (without being constrained by the capacities of sentient beings).
Therefore, Śākyamuni is entirely Vairocana, and without destroying the Sahā world, he manifests the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava*). For this reason:

To state the general outline: Anāthapiṇḍada (the nine assemblies in Magadha; the first assembly in the same impure world; the four locations in the desire realm heavens—all are within the sphere of the five turbidities);
Jambudvīpa (three locations in India). To explain the characteristics: the Golden Ground (the Sūtra says of Magadha that its ground is solid, composed of diamond);

the Lotus Throne (the Sūtra says one sees the Buddha seated upon a lotus-treasury lion throne, surrounded by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten Buddha-lands, and likewise within each atom). Each and every one pervades the entire Dharma-realm (each part of the Buddha’s body...).

Every single limb, joint, hair-tip, Buddha-land, and atom of dust pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Since these two categories each have their own fundamental tenets and purposes, why do you cling to one and find fault with the other?
For the Buddha’s transformative manifestations differ in their hidden and manifest traces; his single body appears in diverse responses, and his single voice is heard differently by various beings.

Thus, the ocean of his teachings is boundless, and the distinction between the provisional and the ultimate is unfathomable. Moreover, even among the followers of the Hīnayāna schools in India, there were those who did not believe in this [Mahāyāna] as a whole.

How much more so for the Mahāyāna sūtras! In this degenerate age—considering that even a hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Kāśyapīya masters who upheld the Vinaya were not equal to those during the Buddha’s lifetime, and the taste of milk was not as it was when the Buddha was present, let alone now that nearly two thousand years have passed—the circumstances are different (for China and India are separated by vast distances). How could one avoid the flow of doubt?

Now, by clearly manifesting the words of the Sage, I hope to dispel these delusions and allow direct entry into the True Vehicle. Furthermore, the introduction of a single sūtra must rely upon the "Certification of Faith" (*saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).

One must resolve [these points] through thorough understanding and not weary of the prolixity of the text. This concludes the preceding section on the comprehensive explanation of doubts and difficulties.

The Great Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, Volume One, Part Three, composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cōngtáng Monastery on Zhōngnán Mountain.

From this point downward is the formal explanation of the main text, which is divided into two sections: first, subsuming phenomena back into the ultimate reality; second, manifesting from that ultimate reality.
Section One: The Initial Exposition of the Source of the Function of Entering Wisdom. Section Two: Clarifying that [the Tathāgata] Shares the Same Essence as Ordinary Beings and Sages. Section Three:
Generally Manifesting that the Designation Accords with the Perfect Pervasiveness of the Essence. Now, for the first section:
He entered the Great Radiant Treasury of Supernatural Powers, the Samādhi of Right Reception.
The commentary states: "Treasury" (*garbha*) refers to the *dharmadhātu-garbha*, the nature of the jewel. When faith arises, suchness is the fundamental source of both Buddhas and sentient beings;
its spiritual and wondrous functions are unfathomable, its pervasive reach is unimpeded, and its luminous nature embodies countless meritorious functions within it.
Since hundreds of thousands of penetrations and radiances all arise from this, it is called a "treasury. It is also termed "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
The "Land" is also called the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; when various conceptual discriminations cease and wisdom merges with principle, it is termed "entry.

However, all Buddhas possess constant light and radiated light. If we consider the constant light, this light is itself the *garbha* (womb-treasury), meaning that the nature of the mind is fundamentally luminous.
When delusion causes it to appear dark, yet once false thoughts are exhausted, its brilliance manifests boundlessly. Thus, the Treatise says: "The nature of the mind..."
The non-arising [of thoughts] is itself the great wisdom-light that universally illumines the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

If one refers to the light emitted and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) produced, it is the treasury of the light of supernormal powers (the analysis of the compound as *karmadhāraya* and *tatpuruṣa* may be understood accordingly). Furthermore, both the supernormal powers and the lights are immeasurable in number.
To speak by way of analogy: the supernormal powers are either six or ten, while the lights consist of bodily light and the light of wisdom.

Regarding "the samādhi of the light of right reception" (āśraya-parivṛtti): this is expressed in both Chinese and Sanskrit. Abiding within the *tathāgatagarbha* while not receiving any further sensations is termed "right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*).

Furthermore, *samādhi* is translated here as "right contemplation" (*samyak-manasikāra*), because when one is in meditative concentration, one carefully and correctly contemplates the object of focus. Thus, "right" (*samyak*) distinguishes it from discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), while "contemplation" (*manasikāra*) distinguishes it from mental dullness (*styāna), as Master Xiao Gong explained.
Second, regarding the identity of essence with ordinary beings and sages: since one has entered its source, one is identical to its essence. Therefore, the Treatise states:
The various illusions of karma, including both outflow-free states and ignorance, are all identical in their nature and characteristics to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also says: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Furthermore, the *Candrottarā-dārikā-paripṛcchā Sūtra* says: "I also know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are all of one and the same essence, awakening to the single Dharma."

The essence of true suchness is non-dual; immeasurable sentient beings equally share in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). In this passage, there are two parts: first, it clarifies the sameness of the sages.
All Tathāgatas abide in the majestic maintenance of light.
The commentary states: "All" refers to the ten directions and the three periods of time. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body;
their single mind, single wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are likewise so. True Reality, which is primordial awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), is called "Thus" (*tathā*);

the wisdom that realizes it, which is initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), is called "Come" (*āgata*). Since the original and the initial are non-dual, they are termed "Tathāgata. This is precisely what is meant.
Sentient beings have a fundamental beginninglessness; this Suchness is the Light-Adorned One (*Prabhāvyūha*), whose layered and interpenetrating radiance shines forth with brilliant clarity.

"Abiding" means dwelling securely, forever severing all攀緣 (*ālambana*, cognitive clinging); "sustaining" means maintaining support so as not to lose or destroy it. The subsequent passage clarifies that [this] is common to all.
"This is the ground of pure awakening for all these sentient beings.

The commentary explains: "Delusion of the truth gives rise to delusion; through delusive vision, there are sentient beings. Yet the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty, being entirely the ground of original awakening.

As the *Treatise* says: 'All sentient beings are originally and eternally abiding, having entered into nirvāṇa. Because delusion cannot defile it, it is called 'pure' (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: 'Though stained...')."
Though unstained, the Sage realizes this realm directly as "abiding and maintaining. Ordinary people do not know they share this state; it is simply pointed out as the ground of enlightenment.
These three aspects collectively clarify that its essence is perfectly pervasive:
body and mind are quiescent and extinguished, abiding in the equal primordial limit, perfect throughout the ten directions, non-dual, and compliant with reality.
The commentary states: Whether ordinary or sagely, the grasping at the similarities or differences of body and mind is entirely illusory; in its very substance, it is quiescent.
Because it is quiescent, it is equal, all being of one single limit—this is the primordial limit of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Since it is no different from the essence of enlightenment, it is, in accordance with that essence, perfect and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. As Daoxiao said: "Śūraṅgama praises the smallness of empty space."
The Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra praises the vastness of the dharma-nature, comparing it to common talk of the ocean versus the hoofprint of an ox;
"non-duality" refers to conforming to this non-duality. As for the inversion of the Western (Sanskrit) language, it is because a literal reversal of the characters cannot fully convey the meaning.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are treated as two: ordinary beings follow birth-and-death, while those of the Two Vehicles seek nirvāṇa; now, [the Bodhisattvas] abide in neither.

Therefore, it is said that one should "accord with" [reality]. Regarding the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), purity and defilement are non-dual; regarding the primary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*), sentient beings and Buddhas are non-dual.
When examined in their essential nature, body and mind are non-dual; when universally encompassed, self and others are non-dual. To be in accord with this is what constitutes "accordance.
Furthermore, the equality of ordinary beings and sages has many meanings; for now, following the Buddha’s teaching, we shall establish the equality of all Buddhas.

Because the Dharma-body and Wisdom-body are without increase or decrease; if one relies on sentient beings, their births and deaths are equal, and their afflictions, karma, suffering, and the links of dependent origination are all equal.
If one compares them with Buddhas, the ordinary person’s present state is equal to the Buddha’s past state of practicing toward the attainment of the fruit;

the [ordinary person’s] future attainment of the fruit is equal to the Buddha’s present state of attaining Buddhahood; and the ultimate perfection of Buddhahood is equal to the Buddha’s eternal abiding. This is based upon...
When the three periods of time are viewed in relation to one another, afflictions are originally present in the Buddha but now absent; sentient beings are originally absent but now present;
bodhi is originally present in sentient beings but now absent; and all Buddhas are originally absent but now present.

If one speaks in terms of the distinction between delusion and awakening, then the nature of nirvāṇa is neither encompassed by nor within the three periods of time; thus, we know that there are dharmas existing throughout the three periods.
It is impossible that [the Buddha and sentient beings] are identical in their essential purity alone;

for if they are explained as being pure by nature, then while the Buddha and sentient beings are currently equal, this does not preclude the distinction between delusion and awakening. Therefore, the Three Vehicles possess both difference and non-difference.
The quiescence of sentient beings is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and the Dharma-body following conditions is itself sentient beings; thus, quiescence is not...
Sentient beings who lack [inherent nature] are eternally non-different from the True [Dharma-realm], yet they establish the Dharma-body that follows conditions as being non-existent;

this body is eternally non-different from phenomena, yet it manifests [within them]. Furthermore, as previously cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are the three that are without distinction;
they are thus equal. Therefore, all dharmas of the three periods of time, whether defiled or pure, are without exception equal.

How much more so for one who understands that these [realms] mutually encompass one another in accordance with their true nature; such a person is said to be "well-established in the ground of the mind of equality.
When both names manifest as the land in accordance with reality, all pure lands appear within the non-dual realm.

The commentary states: First, the meaning is explained, followed by a structural analysis of the text. Regarding the initial section on the meaning of the Pure Land, it is analyzed through four gates:
first, explaining its characteristics; second, revealing its essential nature; third, the means of adornment; and fourth, the identity or difference between the body and the land.

Within the first gate, although there are many types of lands, they do not exceed three: first, the *dharmatā*-land (the land of the true nature of phenomena); and second, the land of enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Regarding the three transformation lands (*nirmāṇakṣetra*), if one distinguishes between the enjoyment lands (*saṃbhogakṣetra*) that are self-produced and those produced by others, they constitute four lands;

however, when subsumed, there are only two types: the pure and the defiled. Alternatively, the nature (*svabhāva*) and the appearance (*lakṣaṇa*) may be fused into one. This differs from other schools:

[in their view] a single substance cannot simultaneously be both pure and defiled, nor can it possess deficiency and fullness; if they were distinct substances, they could not form a single principle of uniformity, and thus a substantial reality would be untenable.

If one searches for their source, they are dark and without substance; yet they do not fail to arise as the conditions for the myriad forms. Thus, form subsumes perfect fusion (yuanrong) without any obstruction. Next, regarding the determination of essence (*tǐ*):

in the Small Vehicle, it is the eight subtle particles (*aṣṭau paramāṇavaḥ*); in the provisional teachings, it is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*); in the true teachings, it is the "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, distinguishing the essence and nature according to each of the four lands is considered provisional, while the comprehensive integration of them is considered real. These three aspects constitute the distinctions between the provisional and the real.

"Convenience" means that whether it be the sūtras or the accounts of origins, all are due to the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus, and because of the karmic actions of sentient beings.
Thus, these lands encompass both the pure and the defiled; yet, as the Buddha should guide and gather in beings according to what is appropriate, they are all called "Buddha-lands.
If considered in terms of actual practice, they are exclusively pure and not defiled. Furthermore, there are two kinds of purity: first, mundane purity.
Because they are free from the defilements of desire, the six practices serve as the skillful means (*upāya*); the two upper realms constitute the pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*).
There are two types of supramundane purity: the first is the supramundane, which refers to the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) taking the Truths (*satya*) as their skillful means;

this is explained according to the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), for there is no separate pure land in that sense. Speaking according to the ultimate reality (*nītārtha*), there exists a distinct [pure land] outside the three realms.
Regarding the Pure Land as the dwelling place of the Two Vehicles, there is a passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* stating that it is "supremely pure among all supramundane realms.

This refers to the Buddha-land of the Bodhisattva, which takes the myriad practices performed through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) as its skillful means (*upāya*), and the immeasurable adornments of the seven treasures of the True Reward (*vipāka*) as its land.
This, in turn, has two aspects: first, the aspect of the ultimate reality, the self-enjoyment of the Buddha.

The two types of "simultaneous forgetting" (*yì jiān wàng*) serve as skillful means because they have not yet reached the ultimate state of Equal Enlightenment (*sámjué*). Thus, the *Renwang jing* states:

"The three stages of worthies and the ten stages of sages abide in the retribution of their fruits; only the One Buddha dwells in the Pure Land. Within this state of non-ultimate attainment, there are again two kinds:
first, from the eighth stage upward, one is exclusively pure, for having forever severed the burdens of form, the illuminating essence shines alone.
Because the deities have no fixed location, the color and characteristics of their pure lands are difficult to clarify.

From the second through the seventh stages (*bhūmi*) downward, because one has not yet transcended the triple world and the untainted observational wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is subject to interruption, they are not exclusively pure.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is only upon entering the first stage that one’s realm becomes a pure land; the abodes of the three levels of worthies (*tri-kṣānti*) are all termed "impure. This is the partial acceptance [of this view].

This is because they are distinguished by their transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*). However, according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), even Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages of Faith (*śraddhā*) already possess a Pure Land.

Regarding the identity or difference between the subsequent body and the land, there are two parts: first, a brief correlation based on the Provisional Teachings; second, a detailed explanation based on the ultimate meaning.

In the first part, it is said that the *svabhāvakāya* (Self-Nature Body) relies upon the *dharmatā-bhūmi* (Land of the Nature of Phenomena), while the remaining three bodies all rely upon their own respective lands. As for the mirror-like [wisdom]: [The text continues with the analysis of the four wisdoms and their corresponding lands.]

The consciousness purified by wisdom, through the maturation of causes and conditions cultivated in the past, transforms continuously from the moment of initial enlightenment until the end of the future, becoming a purely pure Buddha-field that is boundless, perfectly circular, and adorned with various jewels;
the self-enjoyment body constantly dwells therein. Through the power of equanimous wisdom and compassion cultivated in the past, it manifests according to the needs of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages.

For the sake of purifying the buddha-fields, which undergo transformations—small or large, inferior or superior, and earlier or later—the *parśubhogakāya* (enjoyment body for others) dwells therein, having achieved the power of wisdom and compassion.

Based on what was previously cultivated, it manifests as a buddha-field—pure or impure, small or large, and earlier or later—in accordance with the needs of sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*). The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) dwells therein, and subsequently expands.
The commentator asks: Are the *dharmatā-kāya* and its lands distinct or not? If they are distinct, they cannot be called *dharmatā*, for the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is non-dual.

If they are not distinct, there can be no relationship between that which depends (*āśrita*) and that upon which it depends (*āśraya*). Answer: The sūtras and śāstras offer differing explanations; however, when subsumed generally, there are ten types of *dharmakāya*.
Since the lands manifest according to the body, there are five levels. First, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is held that...
The pure *dharmadhātu* constitutes the *dharmakāya*, and it likewise takes the *dharmatā* as its land-nature (*kṣetradharmatā*).

Although their nature is of a single flavor, they are distinguished into two based on the characteristics of the body and the land. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "When reckoned among sentient beings, it is called *buddhadhātu*;
when reckoned among non-sentient things, it is called *dharmatā*. Though conventionally designated as subject and object, in reality there is no difference between them.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states: "Although there is no difference in the essence (*tattva*) of these bodies and lands, they are so designated because their dharmatā and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ.
That is to say, when the dharmatā belongs to the Buddha, it is called the Dharmatākāya; when the dharmatā belongs to the Dharma, it is called the Dharmatābhūmi.

This is said because the nature [of the dharmatā] varies according to its characteristics. It further states: "These bodies and lands of the Buddha are both not subsumed under form (*rūpa*); although they are not..."
One may speak of its size and dimensions in terms of its phenomenal characteristics, yet its magnitude is boundless, for it is like space, pervading all places.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says that Samantabhadra dwells in reliance upon the Truth, and so forth; for all Tathāgatas realize this same state.
As the preceding passage states: "All Tathāgatas abide in the majesty of light, their bodies and minds being quiescent and equanimous."
The equality of the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is perfected throughout the ten directions; non-dual yet conforming to duality, it takes great wisdom alone as its *dharmakāya*.
That which is realized as *tathatā* (suchness) is the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (dharma-nature land). Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:

"Stainless and unobstructed wisdom is the *dharmakāya*. Thus, the third [aspect] is both wisdom and suchness, constituting the *dharmakāya*, as stated in the Liang translation of the *Saṃgraha-bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, both the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and other texts state that only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain, which is designated as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Thus, the "body" contains both suchness and wisdom, while the "land" consists of suchness alone. When the four objects and the wisdom [that perceives them] are both extinguished, this constitutes the Dharma-body.
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither mind nor object; the land is likewise. Based on this principle, all...
The sūtras all state that the body and land of the Tathāgata are non-dual (5). These four preceding phrases together constitute one unimpeded *dharmakāya*;
whatever is spoken is obtained as the land, which is likewise so (6). These five phrases—both general and specific—are mutually fused and mutually negated;
these five modes of expression vanish, leaving nothing to rely upon, such that even the *dharmakāya* and the land are likewise so.

Furthermore, this section above has distinguished the seven penetrations (*saptābhijñā*) based solely on their objects and wisdom; however, these fully encompass the five parts [of the path], as well as the ocean-like merits cultivated through compassion and vows, all of which are subsumed within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This is because merits produced through cultivation necessarily realize the principle (*tattva*); thus, they are harmoniously integrated without obstruction.
This very essence of the Greatness of True Suchness (*tathatā*) that is realized constitutes the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), serving as its support.
Regarding this meaning, the body and land are entirely distinct from the eightfold [retribution and transformation bodies].

Since there is no aspect of color-form or merit that is not subsumed within this Dharma-body, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the thirty-two marks and so forth are all subsumed under the Dharma-body. Nevertheless, there are three senses to this:

first, because they are identical with suchness (*tathatā*), they are subsumed under the Dharma-body of principle; second, because they are manifested by wisdom, they belong to the Dharma-body of wisdom.

The three bodies and the three wisdoms are both dharmas of merit; therefore, they are called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Its supporting land, moreover, is unimpeded in its pervasion of both essence and appearance, as well as purity and impurity.
While my own land is pure, you do not see it; sentient beings perceive it as being consumed by fire. This purity of the land is indestructible.
Form is itself the mark of Suchness (*tathatā*), and that mark is non-mark. Body and land, phenomenon and principle, interpenetrate and rely upon one another.

The "Holding of the Penetrations" (dhāraṇī-abhijñā) consists of four propositions: namely, that the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) each rely upon the land of physical characteristics and the land of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), respectively (considering them both individually and in relation to one another). This aforementioned penetration applies to all Mahāyāna teachings.

The ninth [penetration] subsumes the three kinds of worlds, all of which constitute one great Dharma-body, as explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, because it possesses the ten Buddhas; thus, the three bodies and so forth are all this.

Because it is subsumed within the middle-grade wisdom of correct enlightenment, its lands are likewise so; thus, regarding the ten higher grades, the provisional and the real are exclusively assigned to the ninth [grade] as belonging to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).

The essence [of this] is that from the self-enjoyment body one enters the dharma-nature land; this corresponds to the various bodhisattvas, for it is from the dharma-nature that the other-enjoyment body manifests.

This refers to the profound and wondrous wisdom and virtue known as the Path Accomplished in a Previous Kalpa, who was already extolled as the Honored King of the Dragon Lineage;

If such is the supreme virtue, how could it not be called "wondrous"? As for Samantabhadra, there are briefly three interpretations. First:
1. Regarding the essence itself: it is called "Universal" (*pǔ*) because its nature is all-pervasive; it is called "Worthy" (*xián*) because it accomplishes virtues in accordance with conditions.

2. Regarding the various stages: it is called "Universal" because it is comprehensive and leaves nothing out; it is called "Worthy" because it is adjacent to the ultimate, being a near-sage (*ārya*). 3. Regarding the virtues of the specific stage (the Stage of Equal Enlightenment):

it is called "Universal" because there are no virtues that are not pervasive; it is called "Worthy" because it is harmonious, gentle, and compliant. This is based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s text on the "Perfectly Interfused Contemplation of the Three Sages."

Wen-shu (Mañjuśrī) specifically represents understanding (*prajñā*), while P’u-hsien (Samantabhadra) represents practice (*caryā*); that understanding and practice are of the same essence is Vairocana. These constitute the Three Sages;

thus, this Bodhisattva [Vairocana] constantly forms a pair with them. Now, the first [section] thoroughly investigates the true and the delusive to establish correct understanding, which corresponds to Wen-shu.
The second [section] examines the illusory phenomena to clarify correct practice, which corresponds to P’u-hsien. This is indeed excellent.
Because this sutra is spoken from the perspective of the true body that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), it perfectly reveals the awakened nature;

By means of this dharma-gate, one contemplates that the body and mind lack intrinsic substance, and that the faculties, consciousnesses, objects, and realms—whether mundane or supramundane, one's own body or the bodies of others—are all pure and pervasively fill the Dharma-realm as one.
When all sentient beings universally attain the accomplishment of the contemplative practices of the Buddhas and suddenly perceive such a realm, this is the true Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*).
This encompasses both compassion and wisdom: to universally see that all phenomena are pure is the Great Wisdom Universal Eye;
to universally see that all sentient beings achieve Buddhahood is the Great Compassion Universal Eye. As for the four Vajragarbhas, they are so named by way of metaphor.
It is called "Vajra-like," being both firm and sharp. Being firm means that no object can destroy it;
being sharp means it can destroy all things. This wisdom of the Bodhisattva is likewise: it is firm because afflictions cannot invade it and external Māras cannot move it;
it is sharp because it can shatter all obstacles and sever the doubts of people. Therefore, three layers of profound difficulties are raised to test and eliminate [any remaining attachments].
Regarding the doubt of those in the final age: once such doubt is absent, one is endowed with inexhaustible merit; therefore, he is further called "The Treasury.

although the Buddha uses a single voice to accommodate the myriad classes of beings, while this section generally clarifies the three contemplations, they differ according to individual capacity as being either singular or combined.
The twenty-five wheels each realize and enter this state because this Bodhisattva is well able to distinguish the perfect, adaptive voice according to the various types [of beings].

Having already abandoned all faults and further removed the four characteristics, yet within the mental application of the functioning mind, there still remain the maladies of effort, cessation, indifference, and extinction;

since awareness has not yet reached universality, one must now resolve these four maladies. By realizing that the nature of awareness is flawless and universally aware of all maladies, one arrives at this point.
To specify fully: it is universal awareness of the beginning and the end, and universal awareness of the coarse and the subtle.

furthermore, this section specifically opens up skillful means through the three-period *dharmadhātu* (the three-month retreat), whereby those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities universally return to Perfect Enlightenment.

Second, because the preceding stages of practice and understanding have already been perfected, reaching this point is termed the "ultimate realization. This refers to the state of ultimate realization.
There is no separate essence; it is solely Perfect Enlightenment. First, the initial pointing toward Perfect Enlightenment as the *dhāraṇī* gate:

this refers to arising from the fundamental source to manifest the phenomenal. Now that the exposition of the meaning is complete, returning to Perfect Enlightenment signifies the reintegration of the phenomenal back into the fundamental.
These three points are expressed for this purpose. Regarding the "Twelve Worthy and Virtuous Leaders" (*śreṣṭhin*) here: they are harmonious, gentle, virtuous, and compliant.

It is said that there is no distinction between "honoring the worthy" (*xianxian*) and the intention of "goodness and righteousness" (*shanyiyi*). "Worthy" refers to those who are nearly-sages (*yasheng*);
"good" refers to those who accord with principle. The former are the leaders; they desire that all virtues arise together and accord with true reality to attain the stage of the correct cause.

Those who are next to the fruit of sagehood must rely upon the scriptures and teachings. Since the circulation of these scriptures and teachings is the foremost task for the worthy and the good, they must circulate them.
In this section, there is a threefold general praise of these Bodhisattvas:
they, together with their retinues, have all entered samādhi and dwell together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma.
The commentary explains: Now, a Great Being must surely honor virtue and expand their deeds, emptying the mind and casting aside the self. Because they honor virtue, they advance.
Because he equalizes the vast karma of the Buddha-fruit, his practice pervades the Dharma-realm; because his mind is empty, his wisdom encompasses all things without regarding them as external;

and because his merit flows to the limits of the future without being for himself—this present passage merely praises the virtue of the principal and the retinue entering meditative concentration together with the Buddha’s assembly, extolling the orthodox teaching that harmoniously subsumes all things to constitute perfect enlightenment.
This is because all the various sūtras that praise his virtues likewise speak according to what is appropriate for each case.

When they mention "retinues," it refers to assemblies that accord with the nature of reality, which must necessarily possess both a principal and its attendants (as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*). Therefore, each of these hundred thousand [teachings] has its own retinue (consisting of external followers and internal practitioners of the Dharma).

Because he enters meditative absorption, they dwell together within the Buddha’s realm (unlike the previous Buddhas, who were merely said to maintain their presence without being described as entering absorption). At that time—

those who hear and compile it are Mañjuśrī and others; the master who preaches the sutra is the Buddha’s Dharma-body; the time when preaching and listening coincide is the fusion of mind and object;

Thus concludes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From here on, within the second major section, the Main Body (*samyak-siddhānta*), there are eleven sequential inquiries by Bodhisattvas regarding various Dharma-gates, each answered by the Buddha;

Having established the true cause through faith and understanding, the subsequent ten questions and answers direct one toward practice based on that understanding, leading to realization according to one's faculties;

Now, one who wishes to direct the mind toward practice must first take correct faith and understanding as the foundation.
If that which is practiced is not correct, everything will be erroneous; even if one exerts oneself with diligence, it will be nothing but toil and hardship.

Many provisional schools of teaching say that one should first practice gradually, and once merit is perfected, sudden enlightenment will naturally follow. However, in this scripture of the *Avataṃsaka*, both the doctrinal characteristics and the ritual procedures are...

Nevertheless, it describes the gradual cultivation through the stages of the three worthies (*tri-piṭaka*) and ten sages (*daśa-ārya*). (Regarding this apparent contradiction, etc.

Therefore, within this section on Mañjuśrī, the realm of faith and understanding is revealed all at once; subsequently, the ten bodhisattvas beginning with Samantabhadra display these stages in their respective order, showing both the general and the specific.

Regarding the practice of contemplation (as in the initial inquiry of Samantabhadra: "Having heard of this realm of Perfect Enlightenment, how should one practice?"), first, concerning "true faith and understanding":
the *Huayan Sanqing Guan* states that "to have faith without understanding increases ignorance;
to have understanding without faith increases false views; only when faith and understanding are complete and penetrating do they become the foundation for practice."
Now, to suddenly believe that perfect enlightenment is inherently present and that ignorance is inherently non-existent, and to suddenly transcend birth and death—this is called "true and correct.
"True" distinguishes it from the deluded common person who merely uses false thoughts for practice;
"correct" distinguishes it from those who cling to heterodox views, different schools, and various non-Buddhists. Furthermore, the *Three Sages’ Contemplation* says:
If one has faith yet does not believe in the *dharmadhātu*, that faith is false; furthermore, to speak of "accomplishing the original cause" is to become attached to the initial cause of arousal.
However, the meaning of the "cause" taught in this sutra is profound while the phrasing is concise;

if one does not synthesize it with the various teachings but merely peers through a narrow opening, it will be difficult for faith and understanding to arise. Therefore, I shall now provide a preliminary exposition before the text, seeking the root source.
In conclusion, there are three stages: first, realizing the nature of Perfect Enlightenment; second, generating the Bodhicitta; and third, practicing the Bodhisattva path.
Regarding the realization of the enlightened nature: the four elements are not the self, and the five aggregates are all empty; even the emptiness of illness is empty.

Thus, one clearly realizes for oneself that while the states of sage and ordinary being appear distinct, such distinction is not true; yet the essence of the living being and the Buddha is identical—how could it increase or decrease? It is simply based upon this.

This awakening and understanding are ultimately no different from the beginning to the end; yet, while one may be capable of resolving to arouse the mind and study the bodhisattva practices, what is real and what is unreal regarding these manifestations seen and heard?

How is it known that the right path is [obstructed] by the increase of all evils through perverted wisdom? Furthermore, it is said:

One who does not believe, comply with, or realize this cannot be called a true Bodhisattva;

Therefore, in the treatise, two types of awakening are first revealed, followed by the instruction to give rise to the three minds.

Subsequently, one should cultivate the five elements (corresponding respectively to these three layers; however, regarding the first gate among them, since its meaning is most difficult to accept and apply, it is crucial that this be clearly understood so as not to hesitate).

Second, those who have resolved their minds toward Bodhicitta, having already awakened to Perfect Enlightenment (Pariniṣpanna-bodhi), are capable of generating the Great Mind, which serves as the foundation for the myriad practices.
Therefore, among the two thousand methods of practice in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Bodhicitta is first established as the basis.
Regarding the essence, characteristics, and virtues of the mind: as for the essence of the mind, it consists of three types of mind—great compassion, great wisdom, and great vows.
The great vow is the general [aspect], while compassion and wisdom are the specific [aspects]. As for the vow, it is a longing; what is the object of this longing?

It is solely the aspiration to resolve the mind (*cittotpāda*) so as to penetrate all phenomena and rescue and deliver sentient beings. Thus, compassion and wisdom are accomplished. Therefore, the Treatise says:
"The arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith is briefly explained in three ways: first, the direct mind, because of being correctly mindful of the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*)."
First is Great Wisdom, which is characterized by non-attachment; second is the Profound Mind, which delights in cultivating all virtuous practices;

and third is the Great Vow, referring to the Four Great Vows (in correspondence with the Four Noble Truths). Third is the Great Compassionate Mind, which rescues and protects all suffering sentient beings.
Regarding the characteristics of the mind: the mind thus generated must be without limitation, particularly in terms of its compassion.
Aspiration is the Great Compassion that exhaustively delivers all sentient beings; the Great Vow is the exhaustive cultivation of all practices.
When one contemplates True Suchness through Great Wisdom, there is no Bodhi above to be sought, no sentient beings below to be delivered, and no myriad practices in between to be cultivated.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "You should cause these sons of heaven to abandon their discriminating views regarding Bodhi."
All these are without limit. As for the merit of the mind, if one relies on the merit of a single thought-moment of the aforementioned resolve, it surpasses empty space;
all Buddhas praise it together, and even through many kalpas it would not be exhausted.

Thus, when a good friend returns a prostration to a youth, or an Arhat offers respect to a śrāmaṇera, although there is no difference between the beginning and the end, the initial resolve is difficult to achieve. For this reason, Maitreya... [text continues].
Two hundred and twenty-two parables are provided here to extensively manifest its functional power:

Third, regarding the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices: since one has already resolved the mind [for enlightenment], one must cultivate all practices; therefore, this is what Sudhana beholds.

Each of the spiritual friends said, "I have already set my mind on Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, yet I do not know how to learn the bodhisattva practices or cultivate the bodhisattva path. However, when facing those who have attained awakening, one cultivates according to principle;

These three preceding causes, together with their fruit, constitute four; therefore, my Master Qingliang, in his response to the questions of Emperor Shunzong regarding the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the various sūtras, synthesized them from beginning to end, exactly corresponding to these four:
first, clarifying the inconceivable realm of consciousness so that faith and understanding dwell within one’s heart; second, truly and correctly generating the bodhicitta.

and it dedicates toward Bodhi so that cause and fruit are perfected (4). Thus, the original cause of this treatise is precisely these first two [points], while cultivation and realization according to faculties are precisely these latter three or four.
