To have a point of return is itself called "detachment"; it is not said that one must wait until the end of life to be called detached.
Thus, the *Aṅgīrasī-bhāryā-nītārtha-sūtra* explains the meaning of birth and death, saying:

"If one can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind are ultimately unobtainable as independent entities, yet can speak according to what is appropriate based upon their harmonious combination."

To consider the meaning of "life" as being such that one knows earth, water, fire, and wind ultimately cannot be found as something substantial, yet is able to manifest according to what is appropriate—this is the meaning of "death.

This intent precisely clarifies that union is itself dispersal and dispersal is itself union; therefore, the passages concerning union and dispersal both state that the deluded body cannot be found as a self.
As for their locations: earth has form and resistance and is heavy and stagnant, while wind has no form and is light and buoyant; they are diametrically opposed.

Water and fire likewise mutually overcome and seize one another (the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* also states: "The two serpents of earth and water are by nature heavy and downward-tending, while the two serpents of wind and fire are by nature light and upward-tending").
Thus we know that the four great elements are mutually opposed and distinct from one another; I do not yet know to which of them my body belongs.

If the "Great" were collectively identical with the four [elements], it would be the self; if it were not collectively identical with the four, then there should be a self-body distinct from those four—this is why it is said thus.
Subsequently, one contemplates according to reality.
One immediately realizes that this body is ultimately without substance, appearing as a composite phenomenon and being truly identical to a magical illusion.

The commentary explains: "This means that through the preceding investigation and analysis, one perceives the principle of reality and definitively knows that the four great elements are not the self;
it is only by way of a composite that they are conventionally designated as a 'body,' yet they possess no substantial reality. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle 14, asks: "If [it is] oneself..."
If one who perceives a self in what is not-self in one's own body should likewise perceive a self in the bodies of others, this response presents a parallel difficulty:
if one were to perceive a self in another's body, one would further have to be challenged as to why one does not likewise give rise to the perception of a self within one's own body.

Furthermore, there are those who perceive a self within the possessions of others, such as non-Buddhist practitioners who, while practicing dhyāna, enter into earth-contemplation (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*).

At that time, seeing the earth, one thinks, "This is me"; and it is likewise with water, fire, wind, and space. Furthermore, there was a man traveling far who stayed alone overnight in an empty house;
at night he saw one ghost carrying a corpse, and another ghost came to dispute [with him] (as described at length—this is a matter of conventional, provisional combination).
Moreover, it is precisely because of the calculation of a "self" that one takes this body as oneself, and consequently regards other bodies as "other."
Therefore, birth is difficult to transcend. Later, one contemplates that the mind is without self. For the mind has no intrinsic characteristic; it arises only by relying on objects.
The nature of objects is fundamentally empty, yet they manifest because of the mind. When the sense organs and their objects harmonize, there appears what seems to be a "conditioned mind.

Whether one searches internally or externally, what is its substance? One remains long immersed in birth and death because of failing to understand the mind. If one can truly understand it, perfect enlightenment will naturally manifest.
Because it manifests, the *Śūraṅgama* says: "The nature of madness ceases of its own accord; this cessation is itself Bodhi, the supreme, pure, and luminous mind, which is not obtained from others.
In this passage, there are two parts: first, the contemplation through investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*).

The four conditions combine provisionally to give rise to the delusive existence of the six sense faculties. These six faculties and the four great elements combine internally and externally to produce the delusive existence of the objective conditions (*ālambana-vāyu*).
Within this accumulation, that which appears to have the characteristics of an object of perception is conventionally designated as "mind.

The commentary states: regarding the "four conditions" and so forth, it means that the four great elements (mahābhūta) combine to form a single material form (rūpa)—[the first seven days being like thin curd].

It is only upon this form that the six sense faculties (indriya) arise—[the sixth and seventh days being the opening of the six emotions]. Apart from this physical body, the sense organs have no inherent substance; they are each distinct divisions [of that form].
If even the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not exist as substantial forms, what cavities could the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) possibly rely upon?

As for this body, which is a composite of the internal four great elements and the external six sense organs—formed through their conjunction—it is a false construction. Regarding the phrase "delusory conditions and vital energies" (*pratyaya-vāyu*):
because one relies on the conjunction of the four great elements and the six sense organs to form the body, there subsequently arise the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
It is a false manifestation. From this, the internal faculties and external objects give rise to a deluded mind whose discursive contemplation is unceasing;
it arises and perishes from moment to moment, never stopping for even an instant. When conditions conjoin, it exists; when conditions disperse, it vanishes.

Upon investigating its own essence, it is found to be utterly unobtainable; therefore, it is said that "mind" is a provisional name. Although this deluded mind arises provisionally through conditions, it does not exist apart from them.
Because it is a portion of the true mind’s vital energy, it is called "conditioned energy" (*yuanqi*); saying it "seems to exist" clarifies that it is not substantially existent.

As for "conditioned marks" (*yuanxiang*), these are the marks of conditioned deliberation. Master Sengzhao said: "It is like a *wangliang* (a mountain sprite) that seems to have thoughts; though one examines and investigates it thoroughly, there is nothing to point to or grasp.
One should subsequently contemplate this according to reality.
Good son, if this deluded mind were without the six sense objects, it could not exist; for when the four elements are analyzed and dissolved, no sense objects can be found.
Within that state, as the conditions of the objects each return to their dispersal and extinction, ultimately there is no perceiving mind to be seen.

The commentary states: The mind relies upon the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and these objects depend upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Since the four great elements have no substantial essence, the six objects are empty;

therefore, it is said that "conditions and objects each return to dispersion and extinction. "Conditions" refers to the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*), and "objects" refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Since both conditions and objects are extinguished, the essence of the mind is itself empty; thus, the definitive judgment is made: "Ultimately, there is nothing at all. That which is called the "conditioned mind" (*ālambana-citta*) is precisely the aforementioned conditions.
Question: Since it says "the mind is devoid of objects," the following three phrases also explain the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

How can you categorize this exclusively as the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)? Answer: This refers to the fact that when the conditions and objects (*ālambana*) disperse individually, it precisely manifests the emptiness of the mind.

Therefore, it concludes by stating, "there is no mind to be seen. Both body and mind are collectively categorized under the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). The *Vajrasamādhi* also states: "It causes... [and so forth].
Question: All those sentient beings are free from a self of mind; all minds of mine have been originally empty and quiescent.
If a real self does not exist, how can there be such matters as memory, cognition, recitation, study, and the recording of enmity and gratitude? Answer:
Each and every sentient being possesses its own fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which continues as a single stream, maintains the seeds, and acts as a mutual cause for all phenomena.
Question: By the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), such phenomena as memory and cognition are possible. But who is it that performs karma, and who is it that experiences its fruit? Answer:
It is through the causal power of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of all sentient beings that the continuum remains uninterrupted;
thus, performing karma and experiencing its fruit is not contrary to reason. Question: Who attains *nirvāṇa*? Answer: One who cultivates the realization of selflessness (*anātman*).
Because the continuity of characteristics is extinguished through the power of causes and conditions, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

From this, one knows that there is certainly no real self, but only various consciousnesses which, from beginningless time, have arisen in succession—preceding moments ceasing as succeeding ones are born—in a causal continuity.

Due to the perfuming of delusion, they appear as if possessing the characteristic of a self; the foolish among them falsely grasp at this as a self. Second, regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*):
Good son, because that sentient being’s illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease;
and because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion itself also ceases.
The commentary states: Previously, by searching within body and mind and finding no self, it was called "emptiness of self" (pudgala-śūnyatā).
This [present section], however, holds that body, mind, and their objects are each empty of intrinsic nature; thus, it is called "emptiness of phenomena" (dharma-śūnyatā).

Since the body and so forth are fundamentally empty and were not only extinguished now, the Sūtra says: "Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form is extinguished to become empty. It is simply that during delusion, one clings to existence, and now...

The exhaustion of grasping is what begins the meaning of "cessation. When it is said that "even the extinction of illusion is extinguished," this means that when one views through emotional conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), one sees the arising of illusion;

whereas when one views through wisdom (*prajñā*), one sees the extinction of illusion. Since the phenomena of extinction correspond to arising and wisdom corresponds to emotion—these being all relative phenomena—they are all dependently originated.
Being dependently originated, they are empty; therefore, they are all extinguished. As the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* says: "There is no eye-element."
...up to the point where there is neither ignorance nor attainment. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "All phenomena are like illusions;

they are far removed from mind and consciousness, and wisdom cannot find them. (The triple destruction of illusion: first, the destruction of illusion; second, the destruction of the destruction of illusion. Yet, one should give rise to the mind of great compassion.

Now, the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna; in order to cause others to realize it, the matter must be explained in detail. Regarding what is called "emptiness," all [phenomena]...

Because the external dharmas grasped by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the various sectarian tenets do not exist according to reason, "ordinary beings" refers to all sentient beings within the four modes of birth and six realms of existence.
All such beings, apart from their minds, lack any fixed, real dharmas; these are not necessarily acquired through study or inherited from a teacher, but are co-emergent with beginningless time.
Upon encountering objects, they grasp at them; yet the dharmas thus grasped exist in reality only as mental constructs and have no objective existence.

From this, it is definitively known that none of these can be apprehended. That which exists only as a mental projection is what the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* calls "arising based on the transformations of consciousness," and what the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* calls "relying solely on deluded thought" (the dharma of the arising and ceasing of the mind). The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Consciousness-only has no objective realm;
because there are no external objects, one falsely perceives them, like a person with a cataract seeing hairs, moons, and other such things. Question: If they do not exist...
If external objects were merely false perceptions, why would one not see forms at all times and in all places, or conversely, never see them at all?

Furthermore, why is it that when form exists in a particular time and place, the eye sees that form, yet does not see it when form is absent in other times and places? Moreover, why is it that many people in the same place and at the same time all equally see or do not see it? The verse of that treatise answers this: [The verse follows: "Because of the power of karma, the sense organs are distinct; Therefore, there is seeing and non-seeing. This means that due to the specific force of individual karma, the sense faculties differ from one person to another; hence, there is both seeing and not seeing. Thus, even though the object is the same, some perceive it while others do not. This explains how external objects can be established as real despite the existence of such variations in perception.
Regarding the time and other such factors, there are no external phenomena such as form; they are like dreams and the [perceptions] of hungry ghosts, which arise from the false seeing based on karma.
Question: Seeing hair, moons, and various objects in a dream while suffering from cataracts is entirely useless, whereas the objects seen by one with clear vision upon waking are all functional.
How can it be said that these are like what is seen in a dream by one with cataracts? The verse answers: "Just as in a dream..."
Question: If there are no women, how can one lose one’s body through impurity? Furthermore, worldly dreams vanish immediately upon waking; yet now we perceive forms as if they were real.

How can it be said that perceiving forms is like a dream? Answer: If one attains supramundane remedial wisdom (*pratipakṣa-jñāna*) that is free from conceptual differentiation (*avikalpa*), one realizes things as they truly are:
that all external phenomena of the world, such as form and so forth, are entirely illusory. It is in this sense that perceiving forms is like a dream.
This meaning is no different from a dream; for these many reasons, it is said that "phenomenally they exist" (*yǒu qíng*) while "in principle they do not exist" (*lí wú*).

Regarding this, there are three points: first, analyzing form to reveal emptiness—this means using conceptual wisdom to analyze form until it reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), at which point form and so forth are empty.

Furthermore, when one investigates whether these ultimate atoms possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*) or lack them, neither can be apprehended; thus, the ultimate atom [is found to be non-existent].
Regarding the proof and explanation of the two natures in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, it clarifies that form is empty because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature;
that is, because there is no possibility of arising from self, other, both, or without cause. As the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states:

"There has never been a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions; therefore, there is no dharma whatsoever that is not empty. Among the three types of emptiness, this is necessarily...
Because it is formless, space is said to be without boundaries, indestructible, and unmixed. Thus, within space there can be no form;
if there were a substantial entity of form, space would be destroyed and mixed. Since form cannot destroy space or mix with space, form and all other phenomena are empty.
(This includes the four gates of the meaning of emptiness regarding the existence of objects as conceived by sentient beings. Therefore, the real dharmas grasped by ordinary worldlings...
Although this may seem reasonable, upon thorough investigation it is found to be without wisdom. One should therefore oppose sentiment and conform to principle.

The various sectarian tenets—namely those of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the other vehicles (*yāna*), Confucianism, and Taoism—are as follows: the various phenomena (*dharma*) adhered to by the non-Buddhists and the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) are not of a truly existent nature, distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because they are objects of apprehension (*grāhya*);
thus, just like the mind and mental factors which can apprehend them, [those phenomena] do not exist as real entities.
Cognition (*buddhi*) likewise does not take that [object] as its objective support (*ālambana*), because it is a grasper (*grāhaka*), just like the cognition that takes this [subject] as its support.

The heterodox tenets and sectarian calculations of the Hīnayāna and non-Buddhist schools in the Western Regions are exceedingly numerous; since these do not exist here in this land, there is no need to trouble ourselves with their refutation.

As for the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism, which are followed in this country, although their attachments to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) diverge along different paths, they ought to be thoroughly refuted according to reason. Although the two founders established their teachings differently, yet...

All [these schools] take emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as the foundation of the Three Powers (*trika*), the myriad things, and the universe. Laozi says: "There was something undifferentiated and complete, born before Heaven and Earth.

He further says: "The Dao gives birth to the One; the One gives birth to the Two; the Two give birth to the Three; the Three give birth to the myriad things. He also says: "Man models himself after the Earth;
the Earth models itself after Heaven; Heaven models itself after the Dao; the Dao models itself after spontaneity. The *Yi* says: "In the *Yi* there is..."
"The Great Ultimate gives rise to the Two Polarities; the Two Polarities give rise to the Four Images; the Four Images give rise to the Eight Trigrams;
the Eight Trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune; and good fortune and misfortune give rise to great undertakings.

If one takes the naturally omnipresent Way as the cause capable of producing the myriad things, this is a false cause. If a dharma can produce [something], it must not be eternal; and whatever is not eternal must necessarily...
Because they are not pervasive, and that which is not pervasive is not real, how could a single cause that is originally without distinction produce many distinct effects?
If it could so produce them, they should arise simultaneously and pervasively.
If, however, they can only arise by depending on time and conditions, this contradicts the principle of a single cause; for time and conditions themselves would likewise have to arise simultaneously.
Because [the cause] is permanent, if one claims that all things arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*), this is equivalent to having no cause;

furthermore, since there would be no restriction of time or place, all things would have to arise at all times. If one claims that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way" and that these transformations can produce all things, this likewise does not escape the refutation of either a false cause or no cause, as previously analyzed. However, this merely refutes erroneous attachments regarding the *māyā*.

The arising of things does not depend on [external] causes; the diligent practice of the five constant virtues and the Way and its Power (moral virtue) is, when analyzed by the superior [wisdom], found to lack any rational basis.
Therefore, no phenomena exist apart from one's own mind. Since all minds and mental factors are dependently originated, they are like illusory phenomena and do not truly exist.
To dispel the attachment to minds and mental factors as having real external objects, it is taught that "only [mind] exists."
If consciousness were to grasp at the true existence of "consciousness-only," it would likewise be a grasping at dharmas (dharma-grāha), just as grasping at external objects is.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "All mental characteristics (the eight consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors) are originally non-existent;

their seeds are originally non-existent, and their original locus is empty, quiescent, and unborn. If the mind is unborn, one enters into emptiness and quiescence; this ground of emptiness and quiescence is [the stage] next..."

The mind-as-such (tathatā) manifested by the preceding section is precisely the emptiness of mind; when the aforementioned attachments are exhausted, both mind and objects are empty, which is termed the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
(The refutation of the two attachments is complete.)
The second major section reveals the principle: it is the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness. Because the preceding attachments have been exhausted, this principle manifests;
it is like the moon appearing when clouds disperse, or a mirror becoming clear when dust is removed. This does not mean that the absence of clouds is itself called the moon;
rather, the moon is seen in the place where there are no clouds. Likewise, this does not mean that the absence of illusion is itself the truth.
It is as if one perceives the ultimate truth only where there is no illusion. In this passage, there are two parts; first is the principle.
Because illusion is extinguished through extinction, that which is not illusion does not undergo extinction.

The commentary states: the first phrase follows from what preceded, while the second phrase correctly reveals [the truth]. It reveals that the nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally pure, perfectly luminous, and unique.
The essence is complete in its reality and is not attained through cultivation; although all illusions are extinguished, the self-nature constantly abides.
Because it does not depend on conditions for its arising, it is called "non-illusory. The Vajrasamādhi is also described as: "If one attains the empty mind, the mind is not illusory.

However, in contrast to the preceding explanation regarding the exhaustion of delusions, it is said that suchness is, according to our own school, simply named Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue). This is the subsequent metaphor.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, its brilliance appears. The explanation says:
although it is called "polishing a mirror," it is actually polishing away the dust; what is termed "cultivating the Way" is merely the removal of delusion.

Now, the nature of the mirror is inherently luminous and is not obtained from without; when covered by dust, it is obscured, but when polished, it becomes manifest. Although there is this obscuration and manifestation...

The distinct clarity of nature is not different from what is now called the person. Grasping at phenomena and grasping at a self are defilements; investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*) are as they truly are.
The fundamental awakening of the true mind is clarity; the emptiness of both person and phenomena is manifestation. (The contemplation of the two emptinesses is concluded.)
From here begins the second major section, which clarifies the contemplation of the *dharmadhātu*. This section has three parts: first, confirming the preceding and revealing the subsequent;

second, erasing traces to enter the profound mystery; third, perfectly manifesting the *dharmadhātu*. Regarding the first part—confirming the preceding two emptinesses and revealing the subsequent perfect and pervasive *dharmadhātu*—there are again two sub-sections: first, the heading.
"Good son, you should know that both body and mind are entirely illusory defilements (*mala*). When the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure.

**Explanation:** The first two phrases correspond to what preceded [the main teaching], while the latter two phrases reveal what follows. First, regarding "illusory defilements": "illusory" means empty and unreal, lacking any substantial entity;
"defilement" is so named because it refers to the dust and grime that soils and pollutes. This arises from being deluded by illusory appearances and clinging to them.

Because grasping and attachment defile the pure mind, they are called "illusory stains. Although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess bodies and minds, because they understand them to be like illusions and do not grasp at their marks, there is no sense of defilement; thus, they are not "stains. Because they understand that illusions are empty, they are not "illusions.
To manifest the latter [the non-illusory] means that the faculties, objects, all dharmas, and the ten directions of the Dharma-realm are universally pure. This...

Because one clings to self and other through the cataracts of defilement in body and mind, one becomes obstructed and limited; now that the self is empty and phenomena are quiescent, what could possibly be unpenetrated?
The subsequent explanation of the text has two parts: first, the analogy.
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects five colors, appearing differently according to the direction;
those who are foolish perceive that the maṇi actually possesses these five colors.
The commentary states: Because the metaphors of the mirror and the mani-jewel differ, he again addresses the "good son.
This means that the essential nature of the mani-jewel is luminously pure and free from flaw, entirely devoid of color-form.
Because its nature is pure, when it encounters all manner of colors, they appear within it; the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—each manifest according to their respective directions.
However, this single metaphor also illustrates what precedes the seal and what follows its manifestation.

Regarding "what precedes the seal," the five colors represent the five destinies, and "according to direction" represents according to karma. The foolish person does not understand the substance of the pearl; they see only the entirety of the blue and yellow.
Because they see the blue and yellow, they do not see the substance of the pearl. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Ordinary beings see all phenomena as..."
Following along with various characteristics and failing to realize that phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one does not see the Buddha. If these are correlated with the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):
the jewel is a metaphor for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the principle revealed previously;

the manifestation of colors is a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the aforementioned illusion; and the fool seeing them as definitely blue or yellow is a metaphor for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
"Nature" refers to the defilements of the preceding sensory objects (*viṣaya*). If one takes it from a distance, it refers to the characteristics of the preceding body and mind.
This passage serves to confirm the meaning of the preceding text; therefore, it points back to what was before. As for saying it "reveals what follows":

this perfect pearl is grasped by that foolish person as having a fixed color, and thus the cause for destroying that color is assigned to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to confirm the preceding text. If...
For one who is free from conceptual grasping, these various colors of this pearl are each individually pure, yet each is of the same single essence;
they are all perfectly round pearls, manifesting through wondrous function without any substantiality that could be destroyed.

This serves as a metaphor for the subsequent passage, wherein the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm are all pure, perfect, immovable, interpenetrating, and unobstructed; thus it is said to clarify what follows, even while referring back to what precedes.

The analogy of the mirror illustrates only one aspect of clarity; furthermore, it is said that [clarity] manifests through polishing, which represents the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).

It is only by breaking through attachments that [the nature] is revealed, and thus it receives its name in opposition to attachment. Now, the *maṇi* jewel is fundamentally pure and fundamentally luminous, illuminating all ten directions simultaneously;
therefore, it is used to manifest the doctrine of the ultimate Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This refers to the latter Dharma.
Good son, the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind.
To those who are deluded, it is said that this pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such physical and mental self-characteristics; the case is likewise for them.
The commentary states: "To say that there is a real body and mind due to ignorance is to reveal that although Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) manifests, it is not its fixed reality.
Thus, the treatise says: "The essence of wisdom cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena; it is immovable, fully endowed with the untainted (*anāsrava*), and permeates sentient beings.
Other meanings have already been explained in detail through their corresponding metaphors, as can be understood from them. Therefore, it is said:
It is also like this: the second [stage] sweeps away the traces and enters the profound.

Because of this, one cannot remain distant from illusion and transformation; therefore, I say that the illusory defilements of body and mind are countered by the departure from illusory defilements, which is termed "Bodhisattva.
When defilements are exhausted, they are countered by their removal; thus, there is no counter-object for defilement, nor is there a speaker who designates it.
The commentary states: Within this section there are two parts. First, it explains the reason for the "traces" (the provisional teachings);

second, following the exhaustion of defilements, it proceeds to directly eliminate those traces. Now, these are explained in continuous succession. As for those traces, they arise one after another and are likewise eliminated one after another.
Because sentient beings falsely cling to illusory transformations, the Buddha spoke of them as "illusory defilements."
Because sentient beings rely on the teaching to become free from defilement, they are further called "Bodhisattvas.

Since these illusory defilements are like colors within a jewel—know that they are fundamentally non-existent—it is said that "defilements are exhausted. Since the defilements to be abandoned do not exist, how can the wisdom that abandons them be established?
Thus it is said that there is no "removal through opposition. Since there is no wisdom of abandonment through opposition, how could there be a person who gives rise to such wisdom? Deeply...

In the shallow [stage], since the fundamental is originally non-existent, there is no one who expounds the teaching; therefore, it is said that "non-existence itself is the counterpart. Regarding "defilement" (*rajas*) and "the name of the teaching":

"defilement" refers to the Bodhisattva, and "the name of the teaching" refers to the Buddha. Since even the Buddha who responds to the capacities of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one then perceives the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
that the preaching of the sūtras resides within the Dharma-body is precisely this point. Now, the dharmas of the superior person are each threefold, making nine in total.

These six categories are all traces of what has been swept away; that is to say, regarding phenomena (*dharma*), there are those with attachment and defilement, those free from defilement, and their respective enumerations.

Regarding persons (*pudgala*), there are sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. Question: Since persons inherently possess distinctions while phenomena are fundamentally without difference, why are three names spoken? Answer:

Although in terms of their essential substance (*tattva*) they do not exist [as distinct entities], in terms of conventional meaning (*artha*) they do exist. This is because they are established in opposition to one another: persons and phenomena are each distinct.

This is because of the differentiation between the subjective (the perceiver) and the objective (the perceived). Third, the section on the Perfect Manifestation of the Dharma-realm consists of two parts: first, the single True Dharma-realm; second, the threefold Dharma-realm.
Regarding the "single true" [Dharma-realm], it does not yet clarify the relationship between principle and phenomena, nor does it discuss existence or emptiness;

it points directly to the numinous source of original enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Below, in contrast to all phenomena, through their perfect dissolution and perfect inclusion, one then explains the distinctions of the threefold [Dharma-realm] and so forth. Now...
First: "Good son, because this Bodhisattva and sentient beings of the final age have realized that all illusions are extinguished and their images vanish,
they then attain a directionless purity, manifested by the awakening within boundless empty space."

The commentary states: To announce and point toward that which is realized by the respective faculties, and because the realm to be further revealed is inconceivable and superior to what preceded it, he refers back to the preceding application of effort to clarify the reason for his entry and to initiate the momentum of the subsequent text.
As for "realization," it refers to the perfection of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); as for "extinguishing images," it refers to the *paratantra* [nature] as well.

"Exhaustively merging into directionless purity" refers to taking the body as the primary locus while externally perceiving east and west (as Master Zhaogong explained). Since the mark of self (*ātman*) no longer exists, what further direction or location could there be?
"The awakening to the manifestation of empty space" means that even though empty space is distinct from consciousness, it is not substantially real.
If one were to say it exists, would it be one or many? If its substance were one, it would pervade all places and would accordingly merge with whatever it encounters.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) would have to be manifold, because where one [phenomenon] is conjoined, others would not be;
if this were not the case, all phenomena would have to be mutually pervasive. If you claim that space is not conjoined with phenomena, it would follow that it cannot contain them.

Furthermore, since space exists within form (*rūpa*) and other [phenomena], it would either be intermingled with them or fail to be pervasive. If its substance were manifold, it would possess distinct categories (*jāti*).
Since it cannot universally contain things like form and so forth, one should know that space, too, is a manifestation of mere consciousness. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:
"If there is a person who gives rise to true realization and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will vanish all at once.

This means that what is perceived as space is merely a shadow of dust within the locus of awakening obscured by deluded sentiment; once these shadows are eliminated, space is fundamentally awakening itself. (When a person is deluded or awakened, the nature of water and wind is empty.)

"Manifestation" means emptiness dissolves and awareness appears; "arising" means delusion is exhausted and the mind opens. Examining them from both sides, neither has a limit. Thus, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra further says:
"When hearing is restored, the cataracts of the faculties are removed; when dust is dissolved, awareness becomes perfectly pure.

When purity reaches its ultimate, light penetrates everywhere, and tranquil illumination contains the void. Returning to observe the world, it is like an event within a dream. (Emptiness arises within awareness.)
Thus it is known that the dual negation of emptiness and existence is simply the solitary discernment of the awakened mind—a luminous, spiritual awareness that is never obscured.

The three subsequent levels of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are: first, the contemplation of true emptiness devoid of marks; second, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;

and third, the contemplation of universal interpenetration. The meaning and intent herein are entirely identical to the three stages of the *Huayan* "Contemplation of the Dharma-realm" (*Fajie guanmen*).
Regarding the method of classification based on these aspects, I shall first present the gates of contemplation and subsequently explain the meaning of the sutra passages;

each gate is treated with primary emphasis. First, concerning the "Contemplation of Returning Form to Emptiness" (*zhēnkōng guān*), there are four propositions within this gate (the first two each having four, making eight, which together with the latter two make ten).
The first is the contemplation that form is not identical to absolute emptiness (*duànkōng*), but rather its entire substance is [emptiness].
Because this is true emptiness, the two—blue and so forth—are not the principle of true emptiness;

since that which lacks substance is without exception entirely empty, (1) form is not identical to emptiness, for within emptiness there is necessarily no form; (2) yet it is identical to emptiness, because one realizes that form has no substance.
(The first three phrases use the Dharma to eliminate attachment to phenomena. (3) All dharmas of form are necessarily not different from true emptiness, because they are necessarily non-existent.

Because of their nature (*dharmatā*)—since emptiness is thus for form, it is so for all things. Second, the contemplation that emptiness is identical to form also has four parts: first, because the true emptiness that severs [all] emptiness is not identical to form, yet it is identical to form;
second, because the principle of emptiness is not blue and so forth, this true emptiness that is not blue and so forth is necessarily not different from blue and so forth;
third, because emptiness is the basis (*āśraya*), it is not identical to form, yet if it were not the basis, it would have to be identical to form.

Because it is form (the first three phrases also use dharmas to distinguish from the emotional mind): the four emptinesses are themselves form, because this principle of the selflessness of dharmas is not annihilationist.

(Since emptiness and form are thus, all things are likewise. Third is the contemplation of the non-obstruction of emptiness and form: when form, in its entirety, is entirely true emptiness, then form is exhausted and emptiness manifests;
when emptiness, in its entirety, is not different from form, it is entirely the exhaustion of form and the manifestation of emptiness.
Form is empty; this non-concealment constitutes the fourth dharma of a single flavor: the contemplation of the ultimate cessation and lack of reliance.
This means that the true emptiness which is the object of contemplation cannot be said to be identical to form nor different from form, nor identical to emptiness nor different from emptiness.
All dharmas are neither "not" nor "not-not," and even this very statement is not accepted. It is utterly transcendent and without reliance, beyond all words.

That which is reached is not what the intellect reaches; this constitutes the sphere of practice. For as soon as the mind arises or a thought moves, one deviates from the essence of the Dharma and loses right mindfulness.

(The first two phrases distinguish the mundane for the sake of revealing understanding as one enters the gate; the third phrase marks the end of understanding and the movement toward practice; the fourth phrase establishes the very substance of practice. Practice is accomplished through understanding, and when practice arises, understanding is transcended.
The exposition of the Gate of Contemplation is hereby concluded.

In the subsequent explanation of the meaning of the scripture, there are two parts within the text: first, the emptiness and purity of form-characteristics; second, the identity of emptiness and form as being like suchness.

Within the latter, there are seven further points: first, the internal body’s faculties and consciousnesses; second, the external objects, the six sense-fields; third, the internal and external four great elements;

fourth, all mundane phenomena; fifth, all supramundane phenomena; sixth, one’s own and others’ primary retributions (the bodies); seventh, the many and single secondary retributions (the environments).
However, the "Gate of Contemplation" states that "all dharmas are likewise," which refers precisely to these seven sections. One should say:
"The faculties and consciousnesses are empty, not empty," and so forth; among these seven, the first is as follows.

Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind is revealed as pure; because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure; because the objects of perception are pure, the eye-faculty is pure;
because the eye-faculty is pure, the eye-consciousness is pure; because the eye-consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure;
because the objects of hearing are pure, the ear-faculty is pure; because the ear-faculty is pure, the ear-consciousness is pure; because the ear-consciousness is pure... [and so on].
The objects of perception are pure; likewise, this applies even to the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The commentary states: "From here on, all that is called 'pure' refers to using the two preceding gates of emptiness-observation to eliminate emotional attachments and reveal understanding.
Subsequently, by erasing traces and extinguishing shadows, one acts while understanding is severed; thus, all are pure as true emptiness."
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ultimate emptiness is itself ultimate purity. Because people fear emptiness, it is described as "pure.
This means that when people first hear of emptiness, they fear its annihilation; thus, other passages speak of it as "pure.
As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, all [versions] speak of it as "pure," while the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) speaks directly of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). Emptiness and...
The meaning of "purity" is that all signs are utterly severed. If explained from the perspective of the mind, it is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

"Delusive thought is defilement; the absence of delusive thought is purity. The absence of delusive thought is precisely the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); therefore, this emptiness is described here as "purity.
Since the previously mentioned illusory defilements have already been exhausted and the observing wisdom has also vanished, one is in union with the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*); thus, all [is pure].

Regarding "Because it is pure," the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "Because the Bodhisattva, within phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), practices contemplation to sever [delusions], they attain such purity;
therefore, it is called the 'purity of form. This purity can shatter all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within all phenomena, and because awakening is perfectly luminous, [it is so named].
This refers back to what preceded to reveal the cause of this purity; it is attained by means of sweeping away and dissolving [all attachments].
Regarding the phrase "the perfectly manifest, luminous mind is pure," etc.: this refers to the deluded awakening-mind that grasps at phenomena within the mind;
now, seeing the *dharmatā*, all phenomena are empty, and thus it is called "pure. It is like a person who does not recognize the substance of a pearl but merely grasps at its blue or yellow colors;
once they see the *maṇi* jewel, those colors become pure. The meaning of the text throughout these seven sections is identical to this. However, as for the unfolding...
The meaning of "turning back upon the preceding to reveal purity" will be explained later.

For now, we shall explain the names, entities, and mental aspects of the categories of dharmas. Regarding the general characteristics, it clarifies that my "self-mind" is the very essence of the *ālayavijñāna*.
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are four types of various alternative names for the eighth consciousness among these.
The name "mind" (*citta*) applies universally across all stages; it is one and the same. (The other three—namely, the *ādāna*, the *āśraya*, and the seed-consciousness—are the same as this.
During delusion, because it is that which is grasped and stored (*ālayati*), and because it is that which stores both the grasper and the grasped, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*.

Now, when the wisdom of contemplation is perfected and the nature of awakening is fully luminous, it is simply termed "mind. Since the mind is thus purified, it is identical to the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*); therefore, from here on...

The sudden realization that the perceived objects are identical to the Buddha-realm occurs because one perceives all objective forms (*rūpa*) through the mental construction and grasping of one's own mind;
it is due to this grasping of signs that seeing, hearing, and so forth constitute "objects" (*viṣaya*).

Thus, one does not speak of external forms alone as "objects," nor does one speak of the sense organs and consciousness alone as "objects," for there are scriptural passages concerning the triad of organ, object, and consciousness. Following this, [one investigates] these perceived objects of vision.
Its essence is actually the mind of self-clinging; it is merely designated by a distinct name based on the point where it arises in grasping at form and so forth.
Furthermore, its essence does not exist separately from the triad of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness.

Just as the phenomena of the five aggregates and the "self" within those aggregates are neither different nor identical, this is likewise the case. If one were to assign these according to their meaning:
That is to say, the evolving aspect (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) within the ālayavijñāna and the seventh consciousness together constitute this "view" and so forth.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the arising of the ālayavijñāna must necessarily be associated with two consciousnesses.
Furthermore, when the sixth and seventh consciousnesses perceive external objects, they must internally rely upon the manas as their defiled root (*kliṣṭamūla*) in order to arise.

In Sanskrit it is called *kliṣṭa-manas*, which is translated here as "defiled mind" (*rǎnwù yì*). Because it is associated with the four afflictions, it is termed "defiled"; because it constantly and thoroughly deliberates, it is termed "mind" (*yì*). This deliberation is the function of the mind; thus, it is explained by the *karmadhāraya* compound.

Therefore, among the mental factors (*caitta*) listed here, there is no separate manas. The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* likewise, immediately after explaining the *ālayavijñāna*, proceeds to explain the *manovijñāna* without mentioning a separate seventh consciousness.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* is also like this; as that sūtra states: "Briefly stated, there are three kinds."

"Consciousness" refers to the true consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), and the discriminating object-consciousness (*viṣaya-vikalpa-vijñāna*). The first is the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*);
the second is the eighth [consciousness], the manifesting [consciousness]; and the latter refers to the preceding six. Therefore, that sūtra explains its own meaning by stating:

"Grasping at external objects gives rise to the aforementioned object-consciousness. This shows that the object-consciousness is not the *manas*. However, this is according to that sūtra and the *Awakening of Faith* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*).
The reason why the essence of the *manas* is not separately presented in all [treatises] is based on two points according to the explanation of Master Xianshou:

first, as previously stated, the sixth and eighth consciousnesses must necessarily coexist; second, when ignorance moves the true mind to form the *ālayavijñāna*, external objects draw the mind to give rise to grasping, and since this defiled or pure seventh consciousness does not exist in such cases, it is not mentioned separately. Furthermore, it is said that [the *manas*] conceives of a self (*ātman*).

Thus, it accords with the aspect of transformation (pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa) in conceiving "mine" within the sense-consciousness (*viṣaya-vijñāna*)—this does not contradict the mode of operation of the *manas*.
If one were not to connect what precedes with what follows, then the meaning of the mental factors (*caitta*) arising in succession would not be easily demonstrated.

As for the faculties such as the eye, because they are the supports (*āśraya*) of consciousness and are capable of producing consciousness, the first five [consciousnesses] each arise from their own seeds and their own actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) has as its essence the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements; it is the seventh consciousness, for by grasping this [seventh consciousness], the mental consciousness arises.

As for the visual and other [sensory] consciousnesses, their names are established according to the faculties because they differ in kind according to the six faculties and their respective objects. This is due to five reasons:
first, it is the consciousness that depends on the faculty, for consciousness does not necessarily arise from the object of form (*rūpa*), as is the case with the blind.
The consciousnesses produced by the two types of faculties, such as the eye-faculty, necessarily undergo transformation when the faculty undergoes transformation;

this is not like the case where the perception of blue appears as yellow due to a defect in the eye-faculty, which does not mean that consciousness itself is destroyed when the object (color) is impaired.

Thirdly, consciousness belonging to the faculty arises because the seeds of consciousness follow along with the faculty; it is not the case that the seeds of the object (color) follow the seeds of consciousness.

Fourth, the consciousness that assists the faculties causes benefit or harm to the faculties through its union with them; it is the consciousness that experiences what is received by the faculty, not the object-field.

Fifth, just like the faculties, both the faculty and the consciousness are of the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), whereas those material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are certainly non-sentient (*asattvākhya*);

because the faculty possesses these five superior qualities, it is said to be the basis (*āśraya*). Although all six groups of consciousness depend upon the mind (*manas*), [the first five] are specifically designated as depending on their respective faculties.

Alternatively, they are named according to their specific objects—ranging from the consciousness of form (*rūpa-vijñāna*) to the consciousness of phenomena (*dharma-vijñāna*)—because these names accord with the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

(This is explained in terms of the stage where one has not yet attained mastery. However, if based on the arising of faith, all are termed "mental consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*), because all six arise in dependence upon the mind (*manas*) and are thus the consciousnesses of the mind.

Therefore, the treatise explains the causal conditions for arising and ceasing, saying: [the passage]... *(Note: The final phrase "所" indicates that the source text was likely truncated; the full citation would typically conclude with a verb or further explanation of the causal conditions.)*

This means that because sentient beings evolve based upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), "mind" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* itself, while "thought" refers to the five types of mentation.
Because the two meanings of the *ālaya* include the sense of "non-awakening," it arises from non-awakening:

it is able to see (*karmavijñāna*), it is able to manifest (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it is able to grasp objects (*jñānavijñāna*), and it gives rise to the continuity of conceptualization (*santativijñāna*). As for "consciousness," it is...

This *saṃtati-vijñāna* (the evolving consciousness, though its coarse and subtle aspects differ, is nonetheless a single consciousness without a separate essence; thus it refers to the aforementioned fifth consciousness) functions through deepening attachment based on ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

They falsely calculate [it] as "self" and "what belongs to self" (*ātman* and *ātmīya*). Not only do they calculate external objects as sensory realms (*viṣaya*), they also calculate the body as the self and the objects as what belongs to the self.

Through various such deluded attachments—whether calculating the self as being identical with the aggregates (*skandha*) or distinct from them—they grasp at objects according to circumstances and differentiate the six sense-fields; this is called the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).

It is also called the "discriminating consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), because it relies upon the six consciousnesses to individually apprehend the six sense objects; as the Sūtra says, "it is divided into the six harmonious unions.

Furthermore, it is also termed the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastu-prativikalpa-vijñāna*), because it can further discriminate the various characteristics of phenomena across the past, future, and present. The commentary states: These five [consciousnesses] comprise eight when combined with the first three, and six when combined with the latter two.

By this, the explanation of the preceding [consciousnesses] shows that their essence does not arise in isolation. Moreover, there are many other categories regarding the meaning and characteristics of the eight consciousnesses.

Now, briefly pointing out fifteen points: first, in general discussion, all eight [categories] are termed *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*; specifically, however, there are eight *cittas* and seven *manas*, while the first six are all *vijñānas*.

Second, according to their respective characteristics, each takes its own name as its essence (in the three categories, this refers to the aggregate of consciousness, the sense-base of mind, and the seven mental elements as the essence).

Third, in terms of reality, they are ultimately subsumed within the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya*). Third [point], the five conditions and the five objects (direct perception is the reality); the six conditions...

All [cognitions] (the three types of valid cognition, both provisional and real) have seven conditions that rely upon the ālayavijñāna (non-valid cognition is provisional); the eighth condition consists of the sense organs, the body, seeds, and the receptacle world (actual reality).

The fourth [category] possesses all four; the third and second possess two parts each; the fifth has eight pervasives that are not considered [afflictions], while the seventh consists of those that are considered [afflictions] but are not pervasive;

the sixth is associated with both; the first five are associated with neither. The sixth [category] consists of the fundamental afflictions arising simultaneously (four dull and two sharp), which are divided [into these groups].

The first [obstruction] possesses all ten; the eighth lacks them entirely; the sixth possesses them all; and the seventh consists of the four co-emergent delusions and the three poisons of the five co-emergent afflictions.

Regarding the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the number of factors is the same [as the afflictive obstruction], though their functions differ (the text regarding the two obstructions follows below and will be explained there).

As for the seventh, the karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*), the seventh [category] lacks it entirely, while the eighth possesses its seeds; for the remaining six, it consists of active manifestations (*samudācāra*). As for the eighth, the retributive obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*), it pertains to all eight.

Only the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is the collective retribution for the six [senses], while the nine [remaining aggregates] are the individual retributions for the mental factors (*caitta*).

Because mental factors always arise in dependence upon the mind, because they are associated with the mind, and because they are bound to the mind, the mind takes the general characteristics as its object, whereas mental factors take both general and specific characteristics as their objects—just as a master painter provides the outline and his disciples fill in the colors. The eighth [aggregate, consciousness], possesses five [mental factors], namely: the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), which are contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). The seventh [aggregate, formations], possesses eighteen, namely:

the five universals, the four afflictions (*kleśa*)—delusion (*moha*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and pride (*māna*)—the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—sloth (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), negligence (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and incorrect resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*)—and the three wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*)—faith (*śraddhā*), conscientiousness (*apramāda*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). (Note: *styāna* is omitted from the list in the source text, but it is traditionally included among the secondary afflictions.)
1) Knowledge (*jñāna*), along with wisdom (*prajñā*), constitutes the sixth [category] which possesses all five [factors]; there are thirty-four [mental factors], namely:

the universal (*sarvatraga*) and the specific (*viniyata*) [factors], the wholesome (*kuśala*) in their entirety, the three root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), [the two—] shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), the ten major derivative afflictions (*mahābhūmika-kleśa*) [as above], the eight and seven [factors] of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and the six that pervade the three natures (*tridhātu*).

2) Eleven [categories] consist of eight that are substantially existent (*dravyasat*); [in terms of nature, they are all conventional (*prajñapti*)]. 3) Twelve [categories] consist of the eye, ear, and body [faculties], which are present in two realms (*dhātu*) [but not in their entirety]. 4) Two [categories].
1. Regarding the levels (*bhūmi*): the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue belong to one level; six, seven, and eight consciousnesses pervade all levels;

thirteen [factors] all pervade both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). 2. Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*): they depend upon the conditions of cause, object, and predominance (the five [consciousnesses] depend on the five sense organs;

the sixth, seventh, and eighth depend on the sixth, seventh, and eighth respectively; and these three are mutually dependent); as well as the condition of equal-immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*). 3. Regarding the arising of eye-consciousness: it arises from nine conditions—namely, space, light, the sense organ, and the object.

The mental application (*manasikāra*), the fundamental [afflictions], the distinctions of defilement and purity, and the seeds; the ear-consciousness arises solely from eight [factors] (excluding clarity); the nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses from seven (excluding space);

the latter three (the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses) from five (further excluding the distinctions of defilement and purity); and from three (further excluding the faculties and objects). Externally, there are the six objects of the sensory fields.
"Good son, because the faculties (*indriya*) are pure, the object-field of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is pure; because the object-field of form is pure, the object-field of sound (*śabda-dhātu*) is pure;
and the same applies to the objects of odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).

The commentary states: Briefly, three gates are opened: first, the explanation of names and meanings; second, the discernment of essential nature (*svabhāva*); and third, the manifestation of categories. First: [the explanation of names and meanings].

There are both general and specific [classifications]. The general refers to the objects (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, there are other names, namely the six decays (*ṣadāyatana*) and the six meaningless things (*ṣad-anartha*);

these all pertain to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). They are also called the six spheres (*ṣad-viṣaya*), which applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*). The specific [classification] refers to what is grasped by the eye and the other [faculties], thus they are called "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Because they clarify the spheres in relation to the faculties, they are termed "form" and so forth. Next, regarding the determination of their essential nature (*svabhāva*): as previously stated, the six faculties each constitute their own respective nature.

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the category of "form" (*rūpa*): form has both general and specific aspects. (The general aspect refers to the five sense organs, the five objects, and the form included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), all of which are termed "form" because they possess the characteristic of being obstructive and resistant.

What is discussed here, however, is the specific aspect; that is, that which is specifically designated as "form" by the eye is called "form with visibility and resistance," because it possesses the most coarse and manifest characteristics of obstruction and resistance.
(The form of the *dharmāyatana* is invisible and non-resistant, while the other four objects and the [first] five organs are invisible but resistant. Briefly stated, there are three types:
Manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) refers to blue, yellow, and so forth; [specifically] red, white, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, and space.

Shape (*saṃsthāna*) refers to long, short, and so forth; [specifically] square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, regular, and irregular. Intimation (*vijñapti*) refers to walking, sitting, and so forth; [specifically] standing, lying down, bending, stretching, taking, and discarding.

Sound refers to that which arises from appropriated [matter], as well as false or correct teachings, and that which is agreeable and so forth. Odor refers to the pleasant and the foul (based on the object and based on the mind); "equal" refers to that which is neither of the above two.

Intrinsic (co-arising with the substance), combined (composed of many factors), and transformed (unripe and non-fragrant) tastes refer to bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland, as well as intrinsic [tastes] and so forth.
As for touch, it refers to earth, water, fire, wind, cold, heat, roughness, smoothness, pain, itchiness, hunger, satiety, and other such phenomena;
among the one hundred categories, excluding only the five sense objects (which have already been individually listed), all others are "phenomena" (*dharma*). 3.
Regarding the four great elements of the internal and external:

O son of good family, because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is utterly pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element are likewise utterly pure.
The commentary states: This means that one does not grasp at the sense of consciousness arising and the mind being drawn toward the faculties and objects;

rather, one directly grasps the substance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* explains that each of the four great elements has two aspects, namely internal and external (both of which come from nowhere and go nowhere).
Regarding the two aspects of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), the internal refers to whatever is solid and firm within one's own body or the bodies of others, such as the hair.
The external [elements] such as hair, nails, and teeth refer to all that is hard and solid outside the body, namely earth, stones, grass, trees, and so forth.
Regarding the water element (*āpas-dhātu*), there are two types: internal moisture within the body, such as tears and secretions; and external moisture, such as rain and dew.
Regarding the fire element (*tejas-dhātu*), there are two types: internal heat within the body, characterized by warmth and capable of digesting food and drink; and external heat.
The heat-element (tejas) has the characteristic of maturation and so forth; the wind-element (vāyu-dhātu) consists of two types:

the internal wind-body, which is named "swift-moving" and resides in the four limbs and other parts of the body, and the external wind-body, which resides in the atmosphere and so forth. These four great elements (mahābhūta), from their very inception through their duration, are empty in their essential nature (svabhāva);
they are naturally detached from an essential nature, and their nature of cessation is likewise detached. The commentary states: "They are all empty."

This is merely another way of expressing the same meaning as "pure covering" (*viśuddha-āvāsaka*). Nevertheless, although the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) exist both internally and externally, the manifestation of external phenomena must necessarily arise through the internal transformation of the four [elements] that constitute all worldly dharmas.
"Good son, because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are pure, the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), and the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) are pure.

The commentary explains: "The twelve bases refer to the six sense organs (*indriya*) and the six sense objects (*viṣaya*). They are called 'bases' (*sthāna*) because they are the locations where consciousness arises;

they are called 'gates' (*dvāra*) because they are the doors through which [consciousness] arises; and they are also called 'entrances' (*praveśa') because the mental consciousness is constantly obscured as the organs and objects mutually enter into one another—or alternatively, because they are simply enumerated as six."

Regarding the eighteen *dhātus* as explained through their mutual relationship: within each sense-faculty (*indriya*) gate, there are three distinct domains—the faculty, consciousness, and object—each having its own specific sphere (for example, the eye and its consciousness constitute one domain, while consciousness and its object, form, constitute another). Furthermore, they carry the meanings of "cause" and "lineage.

As for the previous two interpretations regarding the six [internal bases], the first explains them as the causes of karma; this third interpretation views them as the antidotes to the five types of self-clinging.
The *skandhas* (aggregates) comprise the three categories (*triskandha*); there is no school of either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna that does not rely upon these to elucidate various doctrines.

What was previously stated regarding the false identification of the body and mind as the "four great elements" and the phrase "the combination of internal and external," etc., refers precisely to the meaning of the five *skandhas*;

therefore, they are omitted here. However, regarding these three categories, which do not possess separate entities but are explained through various modes of expansion and contraction, there are three interpretations. First:
The faculties are of three grades: superior, intermediate, and inferior; or alternatively, inferior, intermediate, and superior. There are three grades of pleasure:

concise, intermediate, and extensive. There are three types of delusion: first, delusion regarding mental factors while not deluded regarding mind or matter, which is why the five aggregates are taught;
second, delusion regarding material phenomena while not deluded regarding mind or mental factors, which is why the twelve bases are taught; third, delusion regarding both matter and mind.
The eighteen *dhātus* (realms) spoken of by the non-deluded mind take these three categories (*skandha*, *āyatana*, *dhātu*) to subsume the one hundred dharmas:

the *rūpa-skandha* (aggregate of form) subsumes eleven; *vedanā* (feeling) and *saṃjñā* (perception) each comprise one; the seventy-three [mental factors] comprise one; the eight consciousnesses comprise eight;

and only six are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which are not subsumed under the aggregates. As for the *āyatanas* (bases), the five faculties and five objects each comprise one, while the mind comprises eight consciousnesses and the mental objects comprise eight dharmas.
Regarding the twelve *dhātus*: the five faculties, the five objects, and the six consciousnesses each comprise one [category], while the mental faculty (*manas*) subsumes two consciousnesses;

thus, there are eight [categories] and twenty-five existences (*bhava*). These twenty-five existences consist of the four continents, the four realms of misery, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the non-percipient beings, the Pure Abodes, and the six heavens of the desire realm.
All of these are "existence" (*bhava*) insofar as they pertain to actual retribution (*vipākaphala*), and are not subsumed under correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
Therefore, although the Brahmā King resides in the First Dhyāna and the Pure Abodes of Non-conception reside in the Fourth Dhyāna,

these are singled out within the category of the Fourth Dhyāna because the Brahmā King possesses views while the Non-conception Pure Abodes are exclusively for noble ones (ārya), thus distinguishing them from other devas.

Because that is pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure; likewise, everything up to the eighty-four thousand gates of dhāraṇī is entirely pure.
The commentary says: Question: Worldly phenomena arise from the transformations of deluded sentiments; once these delusions are exhausted, one admits that the myriad dharmas are entirely empty.

But how can it be said that supramundane dharmas, which are real and true, are also empty? Answer: If viewed in terms of the opposition between ordinary beings and sages, there is indeed a total distinction between superior and inferior.
However, if one contemplates them according to the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), both are equally illusory transformations, all arising from conditions.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, it is like having one mirror that manifests various impurities, shards, and rubble, while another mirror manifests various sublime and wondrous jewels.
A foolish child does not understand the vast difference between the noble and the base, but a wise person realizes they are in no way different.
For those whose wisdom-observation is perfected and whose mental consciousness is pure, it is likewise so; they see both the mundane and the supramundane.
Whether sages or ordinary beings, all in the world are empty, for they are entirely the essence of awakening;
thus the text below states that seeing the Buddha-world as like flowers in the sky is solely because it accords with the principle of equality, which is why they are called "sages.

If one were to value the sage while disparaging the ordinary person, or rejoice in the true while loathing the deluded, then even if one were to practice cultivation, how could one realize the true source? As stated in the text: [The passage continues...]
This section has three parts: first, the fruit-dharmas of all Buddhas; second, the causal dharmas of the two vehicles; and third, the summary.

Regarding the first, the ten powers (*daśabala*): although the Tathāgata possesses only the single power of wisdom regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, because this power has ten kinds of functions, it is spoken of as ten.
It is called "power" (*bala*) in the aggregate sense because it can crush adversaries and cannot be overcome.
Therefore, one comprehensively understands that all dharmas consist of causes, conditions, and karmic retributions.

Regarding what is possible (*sthāna*)—where cause and effect correspond—and what is impossible (*asthāna*)—the opposite of the above, such as a woman becoming a wheel-turning monarch, two kings [coexisting], the pleasant retribution for evil karma, the five hindrances cultivating the seven factors of awakening, a Buddha transgressing the noble path, or severing fetters while still born [into saṃsāra], and so forth—one thereby subdues the notions of no-cause and evil causes.

One knows who is capable of being saved (through preaching the Dharma) and who is not (due to lack of conditions). Second, one knows the past, present, and future (past karmic retributions exist across the past, present, and future, whether singularly or in combination).

...and so forth; the same applies to the present and future. idānīm kartṛ-pudgala-pratītya vipāka-pratigrahaṇe kevalam sthānam eva vyākhyāyate; api ca pūrvaṃ sāmānyena, idaṃ tu viśeṣataḥ*). Third, one knows the defilements (*rāga-dṛṣṭi-mānādayaḥ*) and the purity (*anāmiśratvam rāgādibhiḥ*) of the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis.

He is liberated from doubt and likewise knows that the outflows of sentient beings have been exhausted and they have attained *nirvāṇa*.

However, because the Buddha’s power is immeasurable, here we speak only of the ten powers in relation to the causes and conditions for delivering sentient beings, thereby clarifying his activities: (1) knowing those who can be delivered and those who cannot; (2) knowing those with obstacles and those without;

The first power is summarized as the means for delivering sentient beings; within this, nine powers are distinguished. Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*):

first, the correct knowledge of all phenomena—wherein the Buddhas truthfully declare, "I am one who possesses perfect wisdom," and so forth (this is because they speak the two truths with sincerity, because they do not contradict worldly convention, because they speak according to the true discourse, and because it is known by the mind; therefore, it is indestructible). Second, the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).

Furthermore, he habitually declares, "I have exhausted the outflows," and so forth; these three constitute the teaching that all factors obstructing the Path are [fully understood]. (Truly, he says they are unwholesome and that even wholesome states can obstruct liberation from the outflows.

Fourth, he teaches the Path for escaping suffering (the Noble Path which can transcend the mundane world and exhaust all sufferings). The Buddha makes this solemn declaration regarding these four dharmas with absolute fearlessness:

"Whether it be Śakra, Māra, Brahmā, or any other assembly, were they to speak according to reality that I do not know or do not see [these things], there would not be even the slightest sign of fear; therefore, I dwell in peace, having attained the state of nothing to lose."

The first two [of the four] reveal one’s own merit, while the latter two benefit sentient beings; furthermore, the first three speak of wisdom (*jñāna*) and the second four speak of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). However, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in its ninth stage (where this stage is attained spontaneously from the first stage; as the Sūtra says: "one never for a moment departs from the Buddha-ground"), speaks of ten kinds [of characteristics]: (1) self-characteristic, (2) common characteristic, (3) characteristic of activity, (4) characteristic of teaching, (5) characteristic of wisdom, (6) characteristic of selflessness, (7) characteristic of the vehicle, (8) characteristic of cause, (9) characteristic of fruit, and (10) characteristic of sustaining.

First, second, and third: body and speech. (Because he has perfected precepts, meditative concentration, sublime wisdom, and great compassion over many eons;

Answer: Because within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, his concentration never declines; furthermore, within the desire realm there is concentration, and it can be said that he enters concentration [when necessary]. Sixth, he has no relinquishing without full knowledge.

Sentient beings with dull faculties mostly perceive painful and pleasant sensations, yet they fail to perceive or know [the nature of] neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and thus possess a state of equanimity while being driven by the latent tendencies of ignorance. The Buddha, however, within the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, knows the moments of arising, abiding, and ceasing; therefore, in every thought-moment of his mind...

When he suddenly abandons the assembly to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), some people doubt the Buddha.
