This skillful means is called *dhyāna*.

The commentary explains that this refers to the meaning of "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), as previously interpreted: because it is contemplative while being calm, there is no distraction or movement, which corresponds to the meaning of "concentration" (*samādhi*);
because it is calm while being contemplative, it is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), which corresponds to the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*). Therefore, it constitutes the four *dhyānas*.
Question: Since concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are equal, why does the commentary state that the numinous mind is "transcendent" (*juedai*)?
Answer: It is precisely because one does not linger in these two, but proceeds directly to the source of the mind, that concentration and wisdom are said to be equal.

This meaning of transcendence is very clear within the explanation of their characteristics; there is certainly no doubt about it. Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is termed "the relinquishing of marks" (*shexiang*).

In the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is shown that the practitioner forgets their emotions and applies the mind, thereby manifesting the "double negation" (*ubhaya-apoha*) that transcends all dependence;

subsequently, the conclusion is made solely by way of its meaning, thus adopting the "double affirmation" (*ubhaya-siddhi*). Since both "double affirmation" and "double negation" are equally integrated and equally transcend dependence, both are the Middle Way.

Therefore, the explanation of the characteristics and the name of the conclusion mutually clarify these three. Regarding the initial text of the third manifestation, each instance first indicates the one who has attained awakening.
Because of having heard the preceding scripture, it is evident that the initial "Samādhi of Contemplation" corresponds to the commentary on the Mañjuśrī chapter;

the subsequent "Samādhi of Illusion" corresponds to the commentary on the entire Samantabhadra chapter and the first half of the Samantacakṣus chapter; and the final "Samādhi of Quiescence" corresponds to the commentary on the latter half of the Samantacakṣus chapter and the entirety of the Vajragarbha chapter.
When these are aligned with the preceding scripture, they can be clearly seen.
However, these three contemplations are largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the "three marks" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (T. 374, vol. 12).
That sūtra states that because it is devoid of the ten marks—namely, form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, arising, abiding, destruction, male, and female—it is called Great Nirvāṇa.

If a bhikṣu periodically cultivates and accumulates concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the mark of equanimity (*upekṣā*)—which are precisely those three marks—then he severs the ten marks and his concentration is definitively termed *samādhi*. If not...
To grasp at the marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) and be unable to contemplate the marks of permanence or impermanence in form is called *samādhi*.

To be able to contemplate the marks of permanence and impermanence in form is called the mark of wisdom (*prajñā*). When *samādhi* and wisdom are equal—like the speed of a team of four horses—one contemplates all phenomena;

this is called the mark of equanimity (*upekṣā*). (In the Two Vehicles, *samādhi* predominates; in Bodhisattvas, wisdom predominates; because the World-Honored One has both equally, he clearly perceives the Buddha-nature. One who perceives the Buddha-nature is said to possess the mark of equanimity. As for *śamatha*:
That which is called "capable of extinguishing" (as cited above) is therefore named the characteristic of *samādhi*.

That which is called *vipaśyanā* is named "right view" (seeing universally, seeing in sequence, seeing specific characteristics). That which is called *upekṣā* is named "equanimity" (neither agitation nor contemplation, neither active engagement nor withdrawal).

If a bodhisattva well understands the time for *samādhi* (giving rise to great arrogance when it is not the time for cultivating wisdom), and the time for wisdom (exerting diligence when it does not yet bring benefit)...

Therefore, the mind of regret is not the time for practicing concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the time for equanimity (*upekṣā*): when concentration and wisdom are unequal, it is inappropriate to practice equanimity; one should instead practice that which is needed. As for knowing the improper time, each point is as explained in the preceding notes.
This is called "practicing the path to Bodhi. As for the slight differences in terminology: in that [other] system, concentration comes first, followed by wisdom, and finally equanimity;

here, all three gates contain both concentration and wisdom. As for the general similarities: this initial stage is named *śamatha* (calm abiding), which involves taking up stillness and clarifying the spirit through concentration.

Regarding the "superiority of the marks" (*xiāng zēngshèng*): in that [text], it says "merely not grasping at the marks of form," whereas here it says "taking stillness as the practice. Both refer to the objects of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, in the subsequent passage of that [text], it says, "One who cultivates and accumulates concentration can perceive the marks of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)," whereas here it says, "By clarifying all thoughts, one awakens to the agitation of consciousness.

Next, regarding the "superiority of the wisdom-mark that realizes the roots and objects arise as illusions and eliminates those illusions": subsequently, when they are "absolutely non-referential and mutually fused," this is entirely identical to that [text].
That [text] says, "Equanimity (*samatā*) is called the mark of relinquishment (*upekṣā*). (In this context, "equality" refers to mutual fusion, and "relinquishment" refers to...)
Although those [three gates] are initially designated as "concentration" and subsequently as "wisdom," these are spoken of in terms of their predominant characteristics;

how could there truly be a concentration that is exclusively concentration or a wisdom that is exclusively wisdom within the teachings? Furthermore, while the meaning and principle of these three gates are identical to the Three Contemplations (*trividha-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of Tiantai (based on the *Ratnakaranda-sūtra*), their approaches differ.

As for the similarities: first, the contemplation of emptiness through the mutual identity and dissolution of all phenomena; second, the contemplation of the provisional through the arising of illusions.
Furthermore, these two forms of "transcending dependence" (*juedai*) constitute the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). The difference lies in this:

the former clarifies the skillful means for practitioners to apply their minds, whereas the latter investigates the nature and characteristics of all phenomena. Because the former primarily establishes practice based on the mind, it does not posit an object of contemplation;

because the latter primarily generates understanding based on doctrinal meaning, it posits the three truths (the conventional, the ultimate, and the first principle) as objects of contemplation. As the *Mūlamahāyānasaṃparigraha-sūtra* states: "There is no truth."

The Middle Way of the ultimate truth within the Four Truths is likewise entirely identical. Furthermore, the reason these [texts] do not establish three types of cessation—namely, cessation through realizing the true nature (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*), cessation in accordance with conditions (*suíyuán zhǐ*), and cessation that stills dualistic discrimination (*xī èbiān fēnbī zhǐ*)—is because each individual gate already contains both cessation (*zhǐ*) and contemplation (*guān*).
(In the *Śāstra* as well, one first cultivates cessation, then cultivates contemplation, and finally cultivates them together; this is largely the same, differing only slightly.

Nevertheless, the number three appears in these various sutras and in the Tiantai teachings; the *Śāstra* and the *Benye jing* should also follow this pattern in their enumeration, as it is due to the nature of the Dharma.

The essence of nature fundamentally possesses the three great elements (the relationship between substance and function). Delusion gives rise to the three paths (afflictions, karma, and suffering). Now, by relying on the three great elements, one manifests the three Buddha-natures (the *jñāna-hetu*, *pratyaya-hetu*, and *samyak-hetu*);

one cultivates the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation, contemplates the three truths, and purifies the three clusters of precepts (the precepts for restraining misconduct, the precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas, and the precepts for benefiting sentient beings).
One extinguishes the three paths and dedicates [merit] toward the three destinations (the limit of reality, sentient beings, and bodhi), thereby accomplishing the three wisdoms (all-... [omitted]).

[The three wisdoms: *jñāna*, *mārgajñatā*, and *sarvākārajñatā*] are endowed with the three virtues (*prahāṇa-jñāna*). One attains the three types of *bodhi* [the *bodhi* of the true nature, the *bodhi* of skillful means, and the *bodhi* of true wisdom].

One realizes the three types of *nirvāṇa* [intrinsic purity, purity through skillful means, and perfect purity]. Because one dwells securely in the three secret treasuries [the *prajñā*, liberation, and the *dharmakāya*], [it is so].

Question: If this is so, then a single person should cultivate all three contemplations simultaneously; why does the scriptural text permit both the singular and the plural? Answer: This is in consideration of...
Since entering the principle gradually according to one's capacity through the gate of cultivation and attaining perfect realization only then constitutes the ultimate, the subsequent text states,
"These three dharma-gates," and so forth, citing these three examples to manifest its perfection.
Good son, these three dharma-gates are all the direct approach to and conformity with Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

It is because of these that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained Buddhahood, and it is upon these three types of practice that the various skillful means of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions—whether diverse or identical—all depend.
If one attains perfect realization, one immediately accomplishes Perfect Enlightenment.
The commentary states: These three gates all arise from the realization of the pure, perfect *bodhi* (*yuanjue*).

Since the contemplative practices (*guanxing*) also lead toward and enter into this *yuanjue*, they remain inseparable from it from beginning to end; thus, it is said that one "draws near to" and "accords with" [the teachings].

While Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize and cultivate them together, the manifestations of their practice vary according to individual capacities and specific circumstances. Sometimes many people may collectively cultivate a single gate (of the myriad practices).
(Section One) Alternatively, a single person may cultivate many practices—whether three, five, a hundred, or a thousand.
Whether they are identical or different, it is difficult to standardize them according to their specific types; however, they must all rely upon these three kinds of karma.

Within these three kinds of karma, one may rely on all three, or only one, or two, whether simultaneously or sequentially, in simple or complex combinations, intermingled in various ways, as detailed in the "Twenty-five Wheels."

This clarifies that these are the practices of practitioners. To realize and perfect the state of a Buddha, although one may enter through a single gate, once success is achieved, all three are fully realized.
If one practices only a single aspect in isolation, it is merely called "approaching";
if the three matters are perfectly integrated, it is called "realizing Perfect Enlightenment. Fourth is the comparative evaluation that reveals their excellence.
Good son, even if someone were to cultivate the teachings of the noble ones and bring to fruition the fruits of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of arhats and pratyekabuddhas,
it would not equal a person who, for a single kṣaṇa, hears this unimpeded Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment and practices in accordance with it.
The commentary states: First, the inferior is raised up, and subsequently, by not being like them, the superior is revealed.
For instance, according to the various teachings, if one were to encourage even a single person or two to uphold the five precepts or the ten precepts, the merit would already be immense;

how much more so when causing as many as hundreds of millions of people to achieve the state of a Pratyekabuddha or Arhat, fully endowed with the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations, forever transcending the three realms and the ten fetters?

This is not even equal to someone who practices *Amitāyus-saṃbodhi* for a mere moment—the briefest duration being but a single *kṣaṇa*—let alone one who practices the wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) over a long period.
It is truly said that the footprint of an ox and the great ocean cannot be compared.

Those who hear these words and accord with them through hearing-wisdom (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), those who contemplate through reflection-wisdom (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and those who practice through cultivation-wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) constitute the first three [sections] within the verse of praise.
The seven phrases provide the topical outline.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Vīradeva, you should know: The mind of the Unsurpassed Great Enlightenment Is, from the primordial limit, devoid of dual characteristics."
The various skillful means that accord with reality are immeasurable in number; the Tathāgata has summarized and revealed them as being of three types.
The subsequent six lines concern the three contemplations.
Quiescent *śamatha* is like a mirror reflecting all images; The *samādhi* of illusion is like a sprout gradually growing;
*Dhyāna* is solely cessation, like the decorative rings within a vessel.
The final seven lines cite these as examples.
These three kinds of sublime Dharma gates are all in accord with awakening;
by means of them, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas have attained the Way. Because these three matters are perfectly realized, it is called ultimate nirvāṇa.
The subsequent verses on the comparative measurement that reveals superiority conclude the three preceding contemplations mentioned above.
From here below begins the second section, which clarifies the single and combined modes of cultivation; this text consists of four parts, and this is the first of those three.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśvabhāṣin rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The explanation is as follows: First, the expression of praise for what has preceded.
"The Great Compassionate World-Honored One, such a Dharma-gate is most rare"—the explanation of this may be understood accordingly.
Second, the request for what follows, which has two parts: first, an inquiry regarding that which is practiced.
"Bhagavān, regarding these various skillful means, how many practices for the gate of Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-avabodha) do all Bodhisattvas have?

The commentary explains: "These various skillful means" refers to the three preceding contemplations (*vipaśyanā*). "The gate of Perfect Enlightenment" refers to the fundamental practice upon which the preceding ones depend.
"How many practices" refers to the fact that although the three contemplations previously explained have clearly defined characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not yet known [how they are integrated].
Regarding the practice cultivated by a bodhisattva: does one person possess all three [perfections], or do three people each possess one?
Are they practiced sequentially, simultaneously, in regular order, or by skipping stages? This second section clarifies the purpose of the practice.
"I pray that you will provide skillful instruction for the sake of the great assembly and sentient beings of the future age, enabling them to realize the true nature of reality.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
2. Praise and Permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have been able, for the sake of this great assembly and for the sentient beings of the final age, to question the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation. You now..."
"Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you.
They listened in expectant silence three times.
Then, the Bodhisattva Viśvaghosa, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

Regarding the fourfold correct exposition within the prose section, there are four parts: first, stating the intention and indicating the number; second, observing the interlacing web; third, establishing the primary cause;
and fourth, providing a general demonstration of cultivation. Now, for the first.
"Good son, for all Tathāgatas, the Perfect Enlightenment is pure and fundamentally devoid of both cultivation and a cultivator.
It is only because all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon the power of illusion due to their lack of awakening that they engage in cultivation;
at that time, there arise twenty-five kinds of wheels of pure samādhi."

The commentary states: Within this, first the intention is raised, and subsequently the number is indicated. Regarding the former, there are two parts: first, clarifying the fundamental basis; second, from "All Bodhisattvas...
onwards, correctly clarifying the general meaning of the various wheels. The meaning of "cultivation without cultivation" is the same as in the preceding section.

Subsequently, from "At that time... onwards, the number of wheels is raised. "Wheel" (*cakra*) has the sense of crushing and rolling over; it is able to crush the obstacles of affliction so as to bring about correctness.
Because wisdom transforms, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Second, regarding the interlacing of the nets of the three contemplations within this [system]:

first, there are three wheels for the single cultivation of the three contemplations; next, there are twenty-one wheels for the interlacing of the three contemplations; finally, there is one wheel for the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations.
In the *Jiaku shu* (Sincere Commentary), these twenty-five contemplations are each given a name based on metaphors, excluding the first three.
Regarding the remaining wheels, they are not explained individually here; I have adopted them in their entirety while also elucidating their underlying meaning.

As for the first three wheels among the initial three groups, they are in fact the same as the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) mentioned previously and do not differ from them. However, because they are categorized to constitute the total number of twenty-five, they are explained briefly here to manifest the characteristics of the "single" and "compound" practices.
To speak of "single cultivation," the heading indicates it with the word "only" (*kevala*), and the concluding phrase uses the term "single" (*tan*). This is intended to clarify [the distinction].
Not combining it with the other two [insight] or three [applications], one first clarifies the turbid mind and brings its activity to rest through contemplation.
If bodhisattvas take only extreme stillness as their object and, by the power of that stillness,
permanently sever the afflictions and ultimately achieve fulfillment such that they enter nirvana without rising from their seats, these bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha alone.
The commentary states: Below this, all twenty-five wheels have headings and conclusions;

each should likewise be headed as "Awakening to Pure Perfect Enlightenment as the Basis for Initiating Practice," because they serve as the preceding context. The Sūtra omits them here out of fear of excessive prolixity.
"Clarifying the turbid and ceasing activity" means clarifying the turbid so that it becomes pure, and ceasing activity so that it becomes still. Only...

Regarding the phrase "taking up the ultimate stillness," this does not include other forms of contemplation. The next three phrases mean that by the power of the tranquil mind, one realizes that the characteristics of body and mind are empty;
when even a fleeting thought does not arise, what basis is there for afflictions? That afflictions do not arise is itself the awakened mind;

therefore, it is said that "ultimate accomplishment" is achieved. The final two phrases mean that without rising from the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), one enters directly into nirvana.
Nirvana is like the butcher Ding who wields his blade with ease.

If bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, then by the power of the Buddha, they manifest various transformations within worlds and fully practice the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva;
through dhāraṇīs, they do not lose their tranquil mindfulness or their various profound wisdoms.
This Bodhisattva practices *samāpatti* alone.
The explanation states that "Pao-t'ing" was a butcher during the Jin dynasty who, for nineteen years, used a single blade to dismember oxen without dulling the edge;

this serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s skillful cultivation of the myriad practices to benefit sentient beings, entering the secular world in accordance with conditions while remaining free from self-centered wisdom.
Prior to the injury, he manifested an assembly of illusions and internally gave rise to great compassion;

by the power of the Buddha, he immediately manifested a world of great wisdom, just as he previously transformed various illusions. His various activities encompass both adverse and favorable actions, as well as those performed for himself and others.
The phrase "fully practicing" and so forth refers exclusively to favorable practice. Below the *dhāraṇī*, this generally clarifies the movement.

Yet, by constantly maintaining a state of profound stillness and recollecting tranquil wisdom— which is precisely samādhi and prajñā— one brings forth the sound of the threefold manifestation and penetrates the barriers of contemplation.
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions and do not grasp at functional activity, severing afflictions alone until they are completely exhausted,
thereby realizing the true mark of reality, such bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* alone.

The commentary states: "Taking up the previous sound from the *huáng* (the metal ring on a bell), one produces it externally; this contemplation is called 'that which arises spontaneously. He himself explains it thus:

"When the substance of the vessel and its sound are fused, they respond to the *jiàn* (the clapper) like an echo; while the form is constrained, the nature is quiescent. Its wondrous function is boundless, and its wisdom and virtue are profound and subtle.

When the realized path remains as a relic, the light of its nature shines perfectly, and the dust of afflictions is forever stilled. As for 'only cessation' and so forth, the illusory realms are limitless."

Because it is difficult to fathom its depths, one must directly extinguish [it]—“extinguishing” meaning the cessation of thought. Furthermore, because active engagement and purposeful action obstruct meditative stillness (*dhyāna*), it is said that one does not grasp at them.
The *Sūtra on Entering the Buddha’s Realm* states: “All phenomena are like illusions; as illusions, they cannot be apprehended.

One should depart from all illusory phenomena. Therefore, I pay homage to the one who has nothing to observe and who alone cuts off afflictions, without depending on various conditioned practices (*saṃskāra*).

"Solitude" (*du*) precisely signifies the Middle Way that transcends all dependencies. "To exhaust and thereby realize" means that once that which is to be severed is exhausted, the faculty of severing itself becomes empty;

this is what constitutes realization. Yet, whenever the characteristics of these contemplative practices are explained, it is said that they sever afflictions because they are the aspect of quiescent *nirvāṇa*;
for when birth and death have ceased, it is called "quiescence. Thus, it is a penetrating, numinous illumination.
Because the mind exhausts the source of delusion, one next interlaces the three contemplations, taking each contemplation in turn as the primary focus while combining it with the others;
thus, by forming seven sets of three, there are twenty-one cycles. When combined with the three preceding single contemplations and the final complete fulfillment, they total twenty.
Fifth, each contemplation consists of seven sections, each of which contains four phases: the first two sections are paired together (each combining one);
the next two sections follow a sequential order (the latter combining the remaining); the next section begins with one and ends with the simultaneous (the simultaneous combining the other two);
and the final two sections begin with the simultaneous and end with one (the simultaneous combining the one). Now, for each contemplation:

Within the introduction, only seven sections are established; furthermore, for each contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), their sequence must be distinguished and the name of each contemplation cited one by one.
However, as the wording would become too prolix, only the single-character designation of each contemplation is provided:

the first is called "Contemplation of Stillness" (*jingguan*), the next "Contemplation of Illusion" (*huanguan*), and the last "Contemplation of Quiescence" (*jiguan*). The distinction between "quiescence" (*ji*) and "stillness" (*jing*) has already been fully explained in the preceding text.

Regarding the three sets of seven wheels: the first set of seven takes the contemplation of stillness as primary while incorporating both illusion and stillness; the middle set of seven takes the contemplation of illusion as primary while incorporating both stillness and silence;
and the final set of seven takes the contemplation of silence as primary while incorporating both stillness and illusion. Within the first of these, the seven contemplations are:
first, the contemplation of the ferry that carries all across together.
If bodhisattvas first attain profound stillness and, with a mind of tranquil wisdom, illuminate all illusions,
thereby giving rise to the practices of a bodhisattva within that state, such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated śamatha and subsequently cultivated samāpatti.
The commentary states: When a Bodhisattva cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to transcend the mundane, they are like setting a boat in motion;

when they exercise wisdom (*prajñā*) to transform sentient beings, they provide universal salvation. First, "attaining ultimate stillness" marks the beginning of the movement; "stillness" is the mind, and "wisdom" is the boat.

"Illuminating all illusions" refers to the subsequent cultivation of the contemplation of illusion. To illuminate and thereby transform these illusions is what constitutes universal salvation. If there were no... [text ends]
If one’s own wisdom is quiescent, how can one who dwells within an illusion illuminate those who are illusory and deliver them? It would be like a boat that sinks by itself;
how could it save those drowning? This is the Contemplation of the Two Profound Stillnesses, the Ocean-Clear-Space.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, realize the nature of tranquility and thereby sever the afflictions to transcend birth and death forever,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated śamatha and subsequently cultivated dhyāna.
The commentary states: "The profound sea" refers to the waves being unmoving; first, through calm observation (*śamatha*), one reverses the flow [of consciousness].
"The clarified sky" refers to the clarity and purity of the nature of water; subsequently, through tranquil observation (*vipaśyanā*), one manifests this nature.

The phrase "by means of calm wisdom" marks the beginning of the realization of the nature of ultimate stillness, while the phrase "the nature is itself tranquility" follows upon that stillness to indicate the concurrent cultivation of both calm and insight. The final two lines describe the efficacy of these two types of observation.
Using the severing of afflictions as the cause, one loses birth-and-death as the fruit; this is the observation of the three heads and three eyes of Śrīla.

If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings, and subsequently sever afflictions to enter nirvana—such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and then cultivated [the subsequent stages].
After *samāpatti*, one cultivates *dhyāna*.
The commentary explains: cultivating all three contemplations together is like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara;

"calm" (*jing*) indicates stillness through tranquil wisdom, "again manifesting" (*fuxian*) below refers to illusion (*māyā*), and "finally severing" (*houduan*) below refers to tranquility (*śānti*). Thus, the four [aspects] and the three points are cultivated simultaneously.

Contemplation: If a bodhisattva, having severed the afflictions through the power of supreme tranquility (*śamatha*), subsequently gives rise to the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva to deliver all sentient beings—
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha*, then cultivated *dhyāna*, and finally cultivated [vipaśyanā].

*Samāpatti*. The commentary explains that "three points" refers to the Sanskrit letter *i*; it means that when a single person fully cultivates the three contemplations, this is called "simultaneity," though it does not imply they occur at the exact same moment.
This is designated by the power of ultimate stillness once afflictions have been severed.
"Quiescence" refers to that which arises subsequently; "below" refers to illusion. This encompasses the two benefits: namely, pure conduct and the saving of sentient beings.
Since afflictions have been stilled and craving and views are no longer present, there is nothing impure about the practices initiated; thus, sentient beings can be saved.
The five grades consist of single and dual contemplations of the characters.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of ultimate stillness, sever afflictions with the mind and further deliver sentient beings while establishing worlds,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and then to be practicing *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* in equal measure.

The commentary states: The upper single [character] clarifies stillness and contemplation as in the first mouth; the subsequent double [characters] clarify both tranquility and illusion as in the lower two mouths;
thus it is called "single and double" to mark them by the power of stillness. The three phrases below "the mind cuts off" are equal and simultaneous in encompassing both illusion and tranquility.
The first phrase represents illusion: internally eliminating afflictions and externally delivering sentient beings, thereby possessing both compassion and wisdom. Thus, Vimalakīrti...
It is said that it is possible for one who is themselves unbound to be able to untie the bonds of others; this is the sixth contemplation on the single-footed and double-headed.

If a Bodhisattva, having first aroused transformative power through the force of supreme stillness (*śamatha*), subsequently cuts off the afflictions (*kleśa*), such a Bodhisattva is said to practice *śamatha* and *samāpatti* together, followed by the cultivation of *dhyāna*.
The commentary states: In the *Bai Ze Tu* (Diagram of Bai Ze), there is a mountain spirit with a head like a drum that has two faces visible both front and back.

This is a metaphor for the simultaneous illumination of stillness and illusion, where the two benefits operate in unison, like having two heads. To be solitary and tranquil is like having only one foot. This differs from what preceded it;
in the former case, the upper was single and the lower was double, whereas here the upper is double and the lower is single. This refers to the first two [stages].
The first phrase uniformly indicates stillness and illusion; by means of the power of ultimate stillness, one assists, supports, and stimulates the power of transformation to deliver sentient beings.
The subsequent phrase, "quiescence," encompasses the two benefits mentioned previously; thus, one enters the Middle Way. At the seventh fruition, the petals fall and the contemplation unfolds.
If a bodhisattva, having first utilized the power of ultimate stillness to support quiescent extinction, subsequently gives rise to activity and manifests transformed realms,
this bodhisattva is said to practice śamatha and dhyāna in tandem before practicing samāpatti.
The commentary states: By means of the tree of tranquil concentration, one first bears the fruit of the Middle Way of quiescent extinction;
subsequently, by means of illusory contemplation, one enters the realm of sentient beings to deliver all living beings, causing them equally to attain the fruit of nirvana.
The first two lines concern quiescence, while the latter two lines concern illusion. Next, beginning with the seven wheels of illusory contemplation, each is individually designated.
Illusion is first, followed by the other two; now, for the first, there is the sequence of martial [power] followed by civil [cultivation].

If bodhisattvas, through the power of transformation, adapt in various ways to attain ultimate stillness, these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*.
The commentary states: After King Wu succeeded Zhou, he melted down his spears and halberds to forge agricultural implements;

this is a metaphor for this Bodhisattva who first manifests various transformations and subsequently enters quiet contemplation. The two lines refer to the initial illusion, and the one line refers to the subsequent stillness—these two constitute the "retirement from observation" once the task is accomplished.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, attains cessation through various realms of experience,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated samāpatti and subsequently cultivated dhyāna.

The commentary states: When a Bodhisattva gives rise to wisdom to benefit sentient beings, this is the accomplishment of merit; practicing tranquility through internal cultivation is called "retiring from office.
This refers first to the illusionist (two phrases), and subsequently to tranquility (one phrase)—the third [section] is the contemplation of the illusionist’s mastery of arts.
If bodhisattvas perform buddha-work through the power of transformation, abide in tranquility, and sever afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced samāpatti, then cultivated śamatha, and finally cultivated dhyāna.
The commentary states: First, one initiates the methods of transformative arts; subsequently, one returns to the quiescence of the empty essence. Thus it is said:
"Resolving the arts, first the illusion" (two phrases), followed by "stillness" (one phrase), and finally "quiescence" (one phrase). This is the fourth contemplation: the Dragon Concealed in the Sea.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, sever the afflictions and abide in ultimate tranquility,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti* and cultivated *dhyāna*, followed by the cultivation of *śamatha*.
The commentary states: "Arising through illusory transformation is like a divine dragon spreading clouds and rain; returning to the essence and entering stillness is like disappearing into the sea.
First is "illusory" (two phrases), next is "quiescent" (one phrase), and finally "still" (one phrase). This is the Five Dragon Tree Penetrating Reality Contemplation.
If a bodhisattva, through the power of transformation and skillful means, acts in such a way that both [activity and] tranquil extinction are mutually accordant,
this bodhisattva is said to have previously cultivated samāpatti while practicing śamatha and dhyāna simultaneously.
The commentary states: First one employs provisional illusions, and later one returns to emptiness and stillness.

This is like Nāgārjuna, who initially practiced illusory arts to extensively convert those on heterodox paths, and later studied the True Vehicle to personally attain the fruits of sainthood. The first stage is illusion; the second stage is the simultaneous cultivation of both [skillful means and wisdom] along with stillness and tranquility.
(2) Sixth is the contemplation of signs as displayed by Śāṇakavāsin.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, employ various manifestations to support ultimate stillness and subsequently sever afflictions,
such bodhisattvas are said to practice samāpatti and śamatha in parallel, followed by the cultivation of dhyāna.
The commentary states: Śāṇakavāsa was the teacher of Upagupta. First, he used his supernormal powers to manifest signs and subdue the arrogance of Upagupta’s disciples;
subsequently, he entered meditative absorption and passed into parinirvāṇa. Initially, he attained stillness (*śamatha*); later, he combined this with tranquility (*praśama*).
Although he transformed sentient beings, he did not give rise to the thought of transformation; thus, he relied upon ultimate stillness. (7)
The Great Penetration of Silent Contemplation:
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, support their state of quiescence and subsequently abide in pure,
effortless meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), such bodhisattvas are said to practice *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of *śamatha*.
The commentary states: The Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū first employed transformative power to benefit sentient beings, and subsequently returned to quiescence.

First, he was equal to quiescence; second, he combined both [quiescence and activity]. Later, among the seven wheels, the contemplation of quiescence is primary. In each case, "quiescence" is designated as the first; in the second, it is combined with the others.
This is the initial contemplation of the ocean of emptiness of precious clarity.
If a bodhisattva, by the power of cessation, gives rise to supreme tranquility and abides in purity,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated śamatha.
The commentary states: "Buddha-Usnīṣa" refers to the text. "Treasure-brightness" (*ratna-prabhā*) is wisdom; "void-ocean" (*śūnyatā-samudra*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

As the Sūtra says: "Together they enter the Tathāgata’s treasure-bright void-ocean. Now, the contemplation of the numinous mind is like the brightness of the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), which is like the "treasure-brightness";
subsequent quiet contemplation is like the "void-ocean. First is quiescence (1), followed by combined quiescence (2); these two constitute the contemplation of the wondrous function of empty space.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence, initiate activity within all objects while remaining in accord with this quiescent functioning,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated samāpatti.
The commentary states: The substance of the numinous mind is like empty space; when it arises as transformation, it is the wondrous function.
Initially quiescent (1), subsequently encompassing illusion (3), the three *śūnyatās* manifest their divine observation.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation, abide in meditative concentration through various intrinsic natures and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated *dhyāna* while practicing *śamatha*, followed by practicing *samāpatti*.
The commentary states: Śūnyatā is the deity of space; when encountered by the radiance of the sun, it briefly manifests in this manner.
First quiescence, then emptiness, then illusion—first quiescence, then stillness, then illusion (one). Fourth, Kāśyapa returns to meditative concentration and observes.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation and the unconditioned nature of their own being,

give rise to functional activity within a pure realm and return to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *dhyāna* and subsequently practiced *samāpatti*,
followed by practicing *śamatha*.
The commentary states: This refers to Mahākāśyapa. First he realizes the essence, next he manifests supernatural powers, and finally he returns to meditative concentration.
Initially quiescence (2), then illusion (2), and finally stillness (1). Fifth, the manifestation of supernatural powers by Prabhūtaratna.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence and through various forms of purity, abide in meditative concentration and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated dhyāna and concurrently practiced śamatha and samāpatti.
The commentary states: The Buddha Prabhūtaratna first attained the Way and realized the essence of Suchness;

subsequently, within his stupa, he manifested the *Lotus Sūtra* as the non-obstruction between stillness and illusion—first quiescent (the two), later unified and encompassing both stillness and illusion (the two). Thus, the transformation of the six directions was observed.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation, support ultimate stillness and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to practice dhyāna and śamatha simultaneously, followed by the cultivation of samāpatti.
The commentary states: This refers to the Bodhisattva of the Lotus Sūtra, sixty thousand Ganges-sands in number, who manifest from below;
first they are aligned with stillness (II), later they are combined with illusion (I), and the seven types of deep-blue [gems] contain the contemplation of transformation.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), empowers their transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) to give rise to the wisdom of an utterly tranquil,
pure, and luminous state, such a bodhisattva is said to practice *dhyāna* and *samāpatti* simultaneously, followed by the practice of *śamatha*.
The commentary states: The *indranīla* jewel contains the images of all things; when confronted by them, it transforms and responds, yet upon responding, it returns to emptiness.

This is like the contemplation of the numinous mind (*lingxin*), which achieves a state of encompassing virtuous functions. It responds to conditions to give rise to illusions, yet subsequently returns to stillness.

First, it aligns with illusion (1); later, it incorporates stillness (2). Finally, there is the "single wheel" (*yilun*) of the wish-fulfilling gem, which perfectly gathers and perfectly cultivates the three contemplations.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly unify all things with the nature of enlightenment such that no phenomena deviate from that enlightened nature,
these bodhisattvas are said to be practicing the three kinds of pure self-natures in accordance with them in a perfectly integrated manner.

The commentary states: This is called the "Contemplation of the Perfect Cultivation of Wishes-Granting. It means that just as a wish-fulfilling jewel illuminates all four directions simultaneously, so too does great wisdom suddenly awaken to the simultaneous cultivation of the three contemplations.
One who possesses the wisdom of perfect enlightenment is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*) because they give rise to wisdom through this perfection.

"Perfectly encompassing all things" means that it perfectly integrates and harmonizes all phenomena—both principle and matter, nature and characteristics, truth and falsehood, form and emptiness, and so forth.

Categorizing by way of essence and correspondence constitutes "perfect integration" (*yuanhe*): because perfect enlightenment (*yuánjué*) is identical to principle (*lǐ*), it is not distinct from principle;

thus, it is entirely identical to phenomena (*shì*). Furthermore, because this enlightenment integrates phenomena, phenomena are not distinct from phenomena; thus, they are entirely identical to principle. Other characteristics such as nature (*xìng*) and marks (*xiàng*) are all explained in the same manner.
The meaning of the Middle Way (*zhōngdào*) and ultimate truth (*yìdì*) thus manifests herein: it is neither principle nor phenomenon, transcending both.

Within the simultaneous illumination of negation and manifestation, principle and phenomena are both revealed; this simultaneous illumination of negation and manifestation is what is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Regarding the statement that among all natures and characteristics there is nothing apart from the nature of enlightenment: "nature" refers to the contemplation of stillness (*śamatha*), "characteristics" refers to the contemplation of illusion (*māyā*), and the "nature of enlightenment" refers to the contemplation of the Middle Way of quiescent extinction (*madhyamā-pratipad-nirodha*). Therefore, it is said that one practices the three contemplations in a perfect manner. Furthermore, by means of Perfect Enlightenment...

All things arise from the essence; in their nature and characteristics there is no difference. The nature of awakening is the convergence of function back into the essence, where essence and function are unimpeded and stillness and illumination occur simultaneously.
This constitutes the perfect, unsurpassed, wondrous awakening—the primary cause for the realization of the three bonds.
"Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva; all bodhisattvas practice in this manner.
By understanding this, one can see the four general indications for cultivation."

If Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon this wheel, they should maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), contemplate in stillness, and seek compassion through repentance for twenty-one days.
They should place a marker at each of the twenty-five wheels and, with a sincere heart, seek compassion;

Non-arising (*anutpāda*):
