"To loathe the flow of consciousness and suppress the thoughts to clarify the spirit, seeking stillness within the void—this 'City of Transformation' is not real. These two points contradict the awakened mind.

"Because of this, one cannot enter pure awakening; it is not that awakening rejects those who seek to enter, but rather that there are those who seek to enter who do not enter by way of awakening. The commentary states:
This passage is precisely the conclusion answering the previous question. The previous question asked: "For what reason is one confused and distressed, failing to enter? Now [the answer is given].

The answer states: "Because of the recognition of the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one successively gives rise to errors; even if one leaves the six realms of existence, one falls back into the two vehicles (*yāna*).
Therefore, one does not enter [the ultimate state]. It further states: "It is not that awakening (*bodhi*) rejects them and causes them not to enter.
This means that it is not that awakening resists and prevents them from entering; rather, it is solely due to their recognition [of the four marks].

"I therefore do not enter. This means that as long as the dream-body has not yet been forgotten, one can certainly not merge with the original body; it is because the non-original body resists that [entry] occurs.

Regarding the phrase "there are various [objections]" and so forth, this explains the meaning of the non-awakened state resisting entry. It says: if at the time of entry one were in a state of awakening, then there would be no entry;
if there is no entry, then it is the awakened state that rejects it. Since entry does occur, it is the very nature of the realizing wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) that constitutes the essence of awakening.

Originally there is neither entering nor not-entering; why then hold the awakening (jue) accountable? Furthermore, if one understands that the seeing-awakening can enter, then that awakening itself becomes a non-attainment.
Thus we know that it must be through the forgetting of emotions and the absence of thought that one is called true entry. Therefore, Guo said: "To carry capacity is not realization.

This demonstrates the error and reveals the non-attainment when the three movements have not ceased; both [states] are delusions. [The commentary on this passage has two parts: first, the direct clarification.
Therefore, both the stirring of thought and the cessation of thought both lead back to delusion and confusion.

The explanation states: "stirring of thought" refers to the previous [truths of] suffering and its origin; "cessation of thought" refers to the previous [truths of] cessation and the path. This consists of two parts: first, the inquiry.

Why is this? The explanation is as follows: if one allows thoughts to stir, it is a departure from awakening; if one ceases thoughts, one accords with the truth. Why then are both stirring and cessation called delusion?
This explanation is divided into two parts: first, a direct explanation.
Because they take the beginningless, primordial ignorance as their own sovereign.
The explanation says: because they take the fundamental ignorance of the beginningless dwelling-place as their own master, movement is "my movement" and stillness is "my stillness.
Since the characteristic of self already possesses both movement and stillness, both are deluded; yet this is the primordial ignorance.

This arises first from the fundamental root and further arises from the primal source. As the Sūtra says, "Solitary ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) serves as the seed of afflictions," which is likewise the case here.
Because it does not depend on external objects or conditions, it is termed "solitary.
Therefore, the text first designates the substance of the self (*ātman*), and subsequently explains the successive production of delusions, karma, and suffering through two stages of transformation.
All sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom; the nature of their body and mind is entirely ignorance, just as a person cannot sever their own life.
*Explanation:* The preceding was an explanation in response to a challenge; this, moreover, is a detailed explanation regarding the original text’s initial premise.
Regarding the meaning within this, first is the explanation by way of Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). Its purport is as follows:

because sentient beings have never attained awakening since beginningless time, it is said that "beings lack the eye of wisdom. This is like a person who becomes blind only at the age of ten or twenty;
although they cannot see colors such as blue or yellow before their eyes, they can still understand them when they are described. However, if one is born without eyes while in the womb...
If one is blind from birth, then even when explaining the various qualities of forms at the time of encountering them, it will ultimately be of no benefit;

therefore, one must first use a golden probe to remove the cataracts before explaining what is right and wrong. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a person born blind who does not know the color of milk.

Others explain it for him through successive metaphors: [the sound of] a conch shell (white), [the texture of] rice (soft and pleasant), [the temperature of] snow (cool and pure), and [the color of] a crane."
Because one ultimately cannot discern the color of their own milk, it is said that the nature of body and mind, etc., is entirely ignorance.

If one is to accord with the awakened mind, taking awakening as the foundation, then everything is awakening; thus, at the end of the previous section on the universal purification of the sense organs and their objects, it concludes:
"Because all is awakening. Furthermore, since the preceding attainment of the source has already established the ground of practice...
All that is cultivated is the Buddha; because this arises from fundamental ignorance, all of it is the work of Māra.
It is like gold being fashioned into a thousand vessels: every vessel is gold.
Later, the analogy explains that because one’s body is obtained through craving, if the body is severed, it opposes craving—just as with a human body.
Even those who are base, lowly, or afflicted by illness preserve their own lives and cannot bring about their own severance;

though others might sever them, it is truly difficult to recognize this. I am likewise such that while it may be possible for some to sever all afflictions and evil karma, how could it be possible to sever "me"?
Why is this? Because "me" can never, in the end, sever itself. Furthermore, there is...
Therefore, I certainly do not perceive a self, for just as the eye cannot see itself, so too must emotional delusions be exhausted.
When awakening is one with the essence, this awakening is the true self, and thus the deluded self is fundamentally non-existent; only then can it be called "severed. It is like a dream-body:
however inferior or painful it may be during the dream, one would never consent to its severance until awakening arrives and one merges back into the original body.

Now, one might resent the suffering of the dream yet find nothing to sever; furthermore, this metaphor can also illustrate the subsequent passage concerning the words "loving me" and the expression of "ignorance regarding nurturing.

Since the preceding and succeeding sections are linked in a continuous chain, this single metaphor applies throughout both the preceding and succeeding parts, forming an obstruction to the Path in all four instances.
Therefore, one should know that for those who love me, I accord with them; yet toward those who do not accord with me, resentment and enmity arise.
Because the mind of love and hatred nourishes ignorance, their continuous pursuit of the Path fails to achieve fulfillment.

The commentary states: "Therefore, one should know" refers to the preceding implication that from the very moment aversion and attachment arise directly from the substance of the self, up until the point of not severing life and so forth—this is summarized as a whole to constitute an obstruction to the Path.

Thus, the next two phrases clarify the self in relation to the arising of attachment toward what is favorable, while the subsequent two phrases clarify the self in relation to the arising of aversion toward what is adverse.
The first two lines point back to the previous two [lines], showing that they only nourish ignorance;

thus we know that when the deluded mind cultivates the path, even if one exerts oneself through various gates of practice with great hardship, these merely assist ignorance—how then could they produce the fruit of Buddhahood? The latter two lines correctly clarify the obstacles to the path:
as for "continuity," it originally arises from ignorance, and this hatred and love in turn perfumes ignorance.
The seeds and their active manifestations continue in an uninterrupted succession, whereby the ultimate attainment of the path will not be accomplished. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"If one conceives a precious attachment toward the body and does not abandon the notions of 'self' and 'person,' practicing in such a manner, one will thereby fall into the evil destinies.
Second, the separate explanation of the four characteristics: however, these characteristics of "self" and so forth are distinct; as for "permanence," it refers merely to—
Having already eliminated the deluded attachment to the first fruit, one now proceeds directly to the cultivation and realization of arhatship.

Within the text, this is divided into four sections: (1) examining the self through phenomena; (2) realizing that the person is composed of the self; (3) understanding the arising of traces from traces;

and (4) the latent continuity like life itself. The first section—examining whether the spontaneous functioning [of the mind] distinguishes between self and other—is the passage concerning the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).

The second part [of the middle section] has two sub-sections: first, the indication and explanation of the coarse characteristics; second, the summary pointing to the subtle characteristics. Within the first of these, there are two further points:
first, the inquiry and the general indication. "Good son, what is the mark of self? It refers to that which is realized by the minds of all sentient beings."

The commentary states: "Mind" refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). That which is realized by it is the objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

All sentient beings spontaneously and habitually grasp this as the internal self; therefore, this characteristic is difficult to perceive directly for oneself. One may know it through inferential realization based on phenomena:

simply by verifying that one's own state differs from that of others, one realizes that within oneself there exists a self. Even if one practices the path, abandons delusion, and realizes the truth, [this grasping persists].
To summarize, whatever is perceived as having a mind is collectively termed the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*).
To explain this by means of analogy: Good son, it is like a person whose hundred limbs are in perfect harmony who suddenly forgets his own body.

When his four limbs become slack and his nourishment and care are neglected, even the slightest application of needle or moxa makes him aware that a self exists; thus, the substance of the self manifests only upon being verified through such experience.

The commentary states: "The string being slack" refers to the state where tension is loose and movement is sluggish; this is the condition of the four limbs being uncoordinated and the hands and feet losing their proper measure.

The rest can be understood by analogy. As for the practitioner of the Way: whether dwelling in a quiet room or secluding themselves in deep mountains, they sever all worldly striving and find no distinction between adverse or favorable circumstances.
Through practicing tranquility, it becomes their nature; they momentarily attain the forgetting of emotions, unaware of themselves.
Others say that when one realizes non-self (*anātman*), if one is oppressed by either what is favorable or unfavorable, the mind still arises;

since the mind has not yet been stilled, one knows that a "self" exists. Therefore, it is said below: "If there is another person who praises or slanders the Dharma, one immediately feels joy or resentment.

Ke (Mingke) says: "Harmony and suitability mean being in accord with principle. To be empty and quiescent, yet suddenly forgetful, is to approximate the fusion of the True Ruler (*zhizai*). How much more so when the strings are slack, let alone when they are out of tune!"
Truly, when one bears illness and deviates from the proper method, the luminous nature of reality (dharmatā) contradicts the ordinary;

yet through the application of acupuncture and moxibustion as contemplative observation, the remedy manifests, revealing that the capable mind is preeminent—these two points indicate the subtle characteristics.
"Good son, even the mind that realizes the ultimate, thoroughly understood, and pure nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata is still the mark of self. Commentary:
"Realizes" and those above it refer to the subject; "Tathāgata" and those below it refer to the object. Furthermore, within the object, there is again the Tathāgata.
To think that this is nirvana is what is called the mark of self (*ātman*). It is not only the case that understanding the nirvana of the two vehicles constitutes the mark of self;
even if one understands the nirvana of the Tathāgata, it is likewise the mark of self. For nirvana is merely the essence of awakening and there is nothing else to be realized apart from it.
Now, if upon realizing nirvana one does not forget the subject and object—that is, the one who realizes and that which is realized—this is the mark of self. (2)
To awaken to the self as being the person and to awaken to one's former errors—this is the characteristic [of the person-view]. Section Two, Part One: The Gross Characteristic.
Good son, what is the person-characteristic? It refers to those sentient beings whose minds have attained realization.
Good son, one who awakens to the existence of a self no longer identifies with "what belongs to me. Awakening to the non-self is also like this; having awakened, one transcends all things.
"Those who realize [it] all possess the mark of a person.
The commentary says: To speak of "awakening to and realizing" as being the realization that one's prior state was wrong—this term precisely clarifies the mark of a person;
no longer identifying with it, one does not form a mind of realization. Awakening is also like this, being the same as the prior error. These are the two subtle marks.

"Good son, if the mind—even up to the point of perfectly awakening to nirvāṇa—considers both [the subject and object] to be the self, and if the mind retains even a slight trace of awakening while claiming to have fully exhausted the realization of principle, this is all termed the 'mark of person' (pudgala-nimitta).

*Explanation:* Because one does not grasp at the duality of subject and object (*grāhaka-grāhya*), one experiences perfect awakening; because there is nothing that is not fully exhausted, it is said "to have fully exhausted" (*bei dan*; *dan* meaning "exhausted").
This wisdom does not eliminate [the object] in order to preserve awakening; because it is not variously differentiated, it is said to be "slight.

It is as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-prayoga-gāthā*: "When a slight object is established before one, that [object] is merely empty; this wisdom is what is different. Third, "understanding the traces":
this means understanding that the two preceding marks are both traces of the mind, and by not grasping at them collectively, one is liberated.
I and others have likewise clarified this mind, yet this too is a trace; therefore, it is called "clarifying the trace. Regarding the arising of these traces, the text has three parts:
first, the inquiry and the formal indication.
"Good son, what is the mark of a sentient being? It refers to that which the minds of all sentient beings cannot personally realize or awaken to."

The commentary says: "Understanding" (*jue*) refers to the subject that can awaken; "awakening" (*wu*) is that which is awakened to. Once awakening has become the object of awakening, it is further named the subject.

This process continues infinitely, such that wherever there is a subject and an object, they are all mutually dependent. Because one realizes this lack of fixedness, one departs from the aforementioned [view].
To claim that what is not reached by calculation is the escape from all faults—yet failing to realize this very calculation is itself a mass of [delusions].
"To say that 'sentient beings are born' means not to fixate determinately upon a single [identity]. Second, an analogy is raised to investigate and explain this.

Good son, it is like a person who says, 'I am a sentient being. One should know that when such a person speaks of 'sentient beings,' they are neither 'I' nor 'another. Why are they not 'I'? If 'I am a sentient being,' then that which is 'I' is not [the same as] the sentient being."
"Why is it that 'it is not they' and 'it is I' [indicates] that sentient beings are not 'they' or 'I'?
The explanation says: One borrows the linguistic conventions of worldly people to establish the force of the meaning and manifest the characteristic of sentient beings.
To say 'not I' is because one is oneself a sentient being; to say 'not they' is because one says 'I am a sentient being,' rather than saying 'they are.'"
Because sentient beings [arise] from this, it is revealed that one does not conceive of a self or a person in relation to oneself or others; therefore, there is neither "that" nor "I.
As for the later statement "neither that nor I," "that" refers to the self of another person. This is a threefold analysis in contrast to what preceded.
Good son, all sentient beings who have realized or awakened to [the truth] do so within the framework of "self" and "person";
that which transcends the characteristics of self and person yet still retains the existence of something realized is called the characteristic of the sentient being.
The commentary states: First, the preceding two characteristics are pointed out; subsequently, from "I" onwards, these are contrasted to distinguish the characteristics of sentient beings.

When one realizes that [the self] is empty, the "I" does not reach [emptiness]; when one realizes that [the person] is empty, the "person" does not reach [emptiness]. Because one does not cling to a sovereign master, one is free from the notions of "I," "self," and "person.
Furthermore, one does not forget that this is the characteristic of a sentient being. These four [characteristics] continue secretly like a life-force, which means:
There is no grasping at all, but one merely intends to practice; by not giving rise to the mind, one avoids the three aforementioned faults.
Since this karma of non-grasping continues uninterruptedly without being forgotten, yet is not produced intentionally through the arising of the mind, it is said to "continue secretly.
The text has two parts: first, the inquiry and the presentation of the topic.
Good son, what is the characteristic of life-span? It refers to that which is perceived by the clear illumination of the minds of all sentient beings and understood through awakening;
it is that which all karmic wisdom cannot see for itself, being like the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
The commentary states: Because it is the illumination of the mind itself, it is called "pure," which refers to self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana*).

Because it perceives the traces of what was previously awakened to, it is called "that which is perceived," which refers to awakening others (*parasaṃbodha*). Since realization and enlightenment are entirely exhausted within the true source and there is no further separate capacity, it is simply called "the illumination of the mind.
One intends to cultivate all untainted (*anāsrava*) karmas by means of this wisdom; therefore, it is so named.
"Knowledge of all karma" (*sarvakarma-jñāna*) refers to the knowledge of all functional activities, which are the operations of karma;
because it perceives only the continuous flow of the latent mind, it is called "not-self.

Being like an illusion or a transformation, when not a single thought arises, this is what is meant in the treatise by the "spontaneous worldly karma-knowledge" and the "inconceivable aspect of karma. Now, by means of this—
Although it can eliminate delusion, it does not eliminate itself; therefore, it is called that which cannot see itself. Because it cannot see itself, it is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
That which is "like the life-faculty" also carries the sense of a continuous succession that is never interrupted. Second, the detailed explanation of the text in two parts:
first, the correct explanation according to the meaning.
"Good son, if the mind perceives and illuminates all cognitions, they are all defilements; for that which is cognized does not depart from defilement.

The explanation says: "The mind perceiving and illuminating" is the characteristic of this gate. "All cognitions" collectively refers to the three preceding characteristics. By means of... [text truncated]

Because this mind perceives other cognitions, it is entirely defiled; since the mind has not yet forgotten its objects, the conclusion states that "that which perceives and that which is perceived do not depart from dust.
Second, the explanation is reversed by means of an analogy.
It is like hot water melting ice: there is no separate "ice" that knows the ice has melted. The commentary explains:
when the hot water melts the ice until it is exhausted, they become one and the same water; there is nothing further capable of knowing that the exhaustion has occurred.

By contrast, this clarifies that once the wisdom of this karma illuminates the previous three marks as all being exhausted, then my own illness is not yet exhausted, just like the ice. If one says... [text ends]
When I say "exhaustion," it refers to the exhaustion of this very ice; thus, it is not that [the water] itself is inexhaustible.

If one aligns the beginning and the end, then water is a metaphor for the True Mind, ice for the four marks [of conditioned existence], and hot water for wisdom. To boil water is called "hot water" (tāng); to awaken to the mind is called "wisdom" (zhì).
Therefore, when water freezes to become ice, one must boil that very water to melt it away; once both the ice and the hot water have vanished, the moist nature alone remains.

"Existence" is used as a metaphor for the true mind; when the deluded mind forms the "self," one awakens the mind to dissolve it, until both self and wisdom are exhausted, leaving only the independent essence of illumination.
Third, this accords perfectly with the Dharma.
"Existence" and "self" are likewise applied to "awakening" and "self-awakening. Thus it is also the same.
The commentary states: If one were to apply the analogy in its inverse form, it should say, "There is no separate self that knows the exhaustion of the self.

However, here the force of the analogy is reversed to accord with the preceding formal explanation; therefore, it says, "Correctly applying [the analogy], three [factors] remain, while the self loses the Way. This section has two parts:
first, a general indication of losing the Way.

Good son, if sentient beings in the final age do not understand these four marks, even if they undergo diligent and arduous cultivation of the Way for many kalpas, it will be merely conditioned and will ultimately fail to achieve any of the fruits of sainthood; therefore, this is called the "final age of the True Dharma."
The commentary says: It is simply because that which is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) arises from the four preceding characteristics, all of which involve an object of realization.

Since one is now practicing with this mind, every practice carries with it the duality of subject and object; therefore, it does not constitute the state of a sage. This is exactly the same as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s statement that for many kalpas of practicing the six perfections, one is not yet called a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the phrase "the final age of the True Dharma": this refers to the final age of the orthodox Buddha-dharma.
During the time of the True Dharma (Saddharma), practice leads to universal realization; in the time of the Final Dharma (Paścimasaddharma), people mostly grasp at signs.

Now, if one grasps at the signs of realization, then even the True Dharma becomes the same as the Final Dharma. If, upon encountering this teaching, one thoroughly understands the source of the ailment, then even in the Final Dharma it remains identical to the True Dharma.
Hereafter, the text will be explained extensively in four parts: first, identifying the self as real.

Second, stating that illness is the Dharma; third, conflating ordinary beings with sages; fourth, being deluded regarding causes while pursuing results. Regarding the first two [of these four], there are two parts: first, questioning and explaining their faults;

second, concluding that they constitute obstacles to awakening. Regarding the first of these six [sub-points], there are six sections: (1) questioning how one who has practiced for a long time fails to realize [the truth];

(2) explaining that identifying with the grasping of a self constitutes a non-authentic realization; (3) questioning how such grasping obstructs the Path; (4) [attachment to] craving... [and so forth].

[The Master] explains that being secluded from hatred and noise is not liberation. First, [he asks]: "How can one know for certain that it is not liberation? Second, [he provides] the challenge. Third, [he offers] the praise of joy and the refutation of anger.
Fourth, [he provides] the verification. Fifth, [he provides] the explanation. Now, regarding the first: Why is this so?
The commentary states: Since the number of kalpas has been vast and their practice has been diligent and arduous, for what reason do they not realize the fruit of sainthood?
Within the explanation, there are two points regarding the Dharma:
first, because they take all forms of self as nirvāṇa, there is realization and awakening, which is termed "attainment."
The commentary states: This is precisely because one mistakes the self for *nirvāṇa*; thus, even if one practices diligently for many kalpas, it will ultimately be of no benefit.
It is like mistaking a dream-body for one's own self and laboring tirelessly at domestic affairs;
despite all such exhaustion, not a single thing will benefit one's actual assets. These are the two analogies.
For example, it is like a person who mistakes a thief for his son; the family’s wealth and treasures will never be secured. The commentary explains:
if the thief were outside, one might still be able to guard against him. But how can one exercise caution while raising him as a son?

Furthermore, even if one knows the thief is a thief, he can do no harm [if kept at a distance]; yet if one raises him as a son, how could there not be ruin? This is used as a metaphor for the six [sense bases].
While the sense organs grasping their objects can still be controlled, the false self within the *ālaya-vijñāna* is difficult to discern;

thus, the jewels of merit within the *tathāgatagarbha* waste away moment by moment. Because of this poverty, it is difficult to accumulate merit and wisdom. What obstacle does the "threefold grasping" (*trividhā-upādāna*) pose to the realization of the Path? This is the inquiry.

Why is this? The explanation says: the previous inquiry asked why one does not realize [enlightenment] over many kalpas; the response states that it is because one realizes [enlightenment] by clinging to a self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).

Furthermore, there is another inquiry: even if one were to realize [enlightenment] through clinging to a self-grasping, how could this possibly obstruct the Path? [The answer is: because the four types of craving are stilled and hatred is extinguished.
The clamor is not liberation.
Those who love me also love nirvana; by subduing the root of my craving, they take nirvana as their mark.
Those who hate me also hate birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); yet they do not realize that what they love is truly birth-and-death. To separately hate birth-and-death is called non-liberation.
The commentary states: Now, the cycle of birth and death fundamentally arises from hatred and attachment; if one seeks liberation, these two sources must be exhausted.
Yet, if one now loves *nirvāṇa*, this is still the same fundamental attachment; if one now hates *saṃsāra*, this is likewise the same fundamental hatred.

Although rejecting suffering and rejoicing in bliss differ in form, they are originally rooted in hatred and attachment—the very habits carried over from the past. If one practices the Way while harboring these, how could the fruit of Buddhahood ever be achieved? This would merely serve to suppress me.

Regarding the claim that the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā-mūla*) constitutes the characteristic of nirvāṇa: it is because one suppresses it that it does not arise; this non-arising is a semblance of the characteristic of nirvāṇa, and because this semblance is taken for the real, it is said so.
Those who do not understand [the nature of] craving and the like take nirvāṇa as their fundamental craving and intend to eliminate the craving for saṃsāra.

Since the craving for existence already resides within them, how can the root of craving—which is the very root of saṃsāra—be called liberation? For the root of craving is the seed of hatred toward nirvāṇa; how could such a state be termed understanding?
Since they have not escaped [saṃsāra], it is said that they do not know [the truth]. Regarding the five [fetters] such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*), how can one be certain that they are not liberated?
This is a challenge [to the position]. How, then, should one know that dharmas are not liberated?

The explanation is as follows: "Dharmas" refers to *nirvāṇa*. Based on the previous explanation, it was stated that those who crave *nirvāṇa* are called "unliberated. Therefore, [if one craves it, one does not know it].

This inquiry states: "If you admit that craving for saṃsāra constitutes bondage, then by what sign do you know that awakening to nirvāṇa as the dharma of quiescence is likewise identical to that original craving, such that one remains unliberated?
The sixth praise refutes [this] through the evidence of hatred and joy, explaining: "One who has realized the truth is necessarily without a self;
because there is no self, there is consequently no hatred or joy. Now, it is for the sake of the Dharma that one feels hatred."

Xī immediately knew that the Dharma he had realized was not the ultimate truth because his own realization was not yet complete. Within the text, there are two parts; first, it marks that his realization was not yet complete:
"Good son, those sentient beings in the final age who practice for Bodhi take their slight personal realization as being pure."
One has still not been able to exhaustively eliminate the root of the mark of self (*ātman*).

The explanation says: "Subtle realization" means that externally one knows the sense organs and their objects are a false conjunction, while internally one awakens to the essence of nature as quiescent;
yet, because one has not yet applied the formal standard [of investigation], one has not exhausted the second point: knowing through testing by means of the objective realm.
Furthermore, if someone praises that Dharma, one immediately feels joy and desires to deliver them; yet if someone slanders what they have attained, one immediately gives rise to resentment.

From this, one should know that the mark of self (*ātman*) is firmly grasped and persists, lying latent within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), playing among the sense faculties without ever ceasing.

The commentary states: Regarding "praise, blame, and so forth," while worldly circumstances of adversity and favor are coarse and easy to perceive, they are most difficult to discern within the gateway of the Dharma.

To simply say that one feels anger toward another for the sake of the Dharma, without realizing that this mind is fundamentally the mark of self-attachment, is to know that the underlying cause—the stubborn, latent attachment to a self within the inner mind—is being verified through external objects. Thus, one perceives the hidden characteristics of the ego-clinging still firmly entrenched.

Although his army of wisdom repeatedly raised its banners (as mentioned above, through diligent cultivation over many kalpas and hearing the three preceding contemplations), he frequently crushed the hosts of Māra (as mentioned above, by detesting birth-and-death, subduing self-love, and attaining slight realization).
Yet, the city of the *ālayavijñāna* is difficult to assault, for its sovereign is firm; (the verse says "City of Awakening," which should be translated as the opposite of this city).

The *manas* constantly serves as its guard, providing a strong defense; the *manovijñāna* acts as a minister, managing both internal and external affairs, while overseeing the five sense-consciousnesses as subordinate inspectors.

This is intended to suppress the gates of the six thieves; thus, the King of Thieves (the mark of selfhood) frequently enters and sports, repeatedly stealing titles (calling greed "compassion" and anger "subduing demons"), deluding my Dharma King (the Master of Transformation) and often encroaching upon his borders (the untainted wisdom).

He disturbs my contemplative realm (the practitioner); though he externally fears Prajñā and remains hidden by day (during the time of contemplative observation), he wanders abroad at night (when delusions arise), yet internally he harbors no [fear].
It is clear that day and night [the seeds] do not cease, and these two fetters form an obstruction to awakening.
Son of good family, because those who cultivate the path do not eliminate the mark of self, they are unable to enter pure awakening.

It should be understood that there are two explanations regarding the teaching of illness as a dharma: first, the direct explanation of its incorrectness; second, the conclusion establishing it as an obstacle to awakening.
Within the first [section], there are two parts: the initial retrospective inquiry.
"Good son, if you know that the self is empty, then there is no one who destroys the self; yet because there is a self that preaches the Dharma, the self has not been severed."
The life-force (*jīvita*) is also like this.

The commentary explains: "To investigate by turning back" means to take what preceded as the method; that is, following the sequence of anger and joy, one investigates thoroughly to establish the discourse.
The fault in taking illness as the method is the fear that, upon hearing "anger and joy are the self," one might then simply endure them and fail to employ non-anger as the means of transcendence.
Therefore, I have raised this inquiry: "If one sees that it is another who insults me, and though insulted by them one does not feel anger, this too is because of my [realization of] emptiness.

Furthermore, it is said: "If one knows that the self is empty, there is no one to be insulted. Since one has already seen those who insult me, it follows that one has not yet attained the emptiness of the self;
thus, it should also be said: "Because one knows the self is empty, there is no self to whom the Dharma is taught. Next...

Because making conceptual judgments constitutes a disease, there are two kinds of decisive judgment.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age who proclaim disease to be the Dharma are therefore called "those worthy of pity";
though they exert themselves with diligence, they only increase their various ailments.
The commentary states: "To explain 'taking illness as the Dharma' refers to the faults previously deduced, which are precisely the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).

If these four characteristics persist, they are collectively termed 'illness. Because sentient beings do not understand this and instead regard them as the Dharma, they are called 'those who are to be pitied.
To 'augment all illnesses' means that by practicing while carrying illness, one increases all illnesses; the opposite of this is [the way to cure them]."
In speech, one refers only to reality; in practice, one cultivates only that which benefits true virtue.

Just as medicinal herbs have seeds that are either sweet or bitter, and are nourished by earth and water such that each only increases its inherent quality—where bitterness is a metaphor for the ego-identity (*ātman*) as the root, and sweetness is a metaphor for pure awakening (*bodhi*) as the root, while earth and water are metaphors for the myriad practices (*samskāra*)—the second [point] establishes the obstruction to awakening.
Therefore, one cannot enter pure awakening.

It should be understood that there are three sections concerning how ordinary people confuse the sacred; the text has two parts: first, the actual clarification of this confusion, and second, the conclusion regarding the obstruction of the sacred.
Within the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, suppressing the sacred to equate it with the self.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks; taking the Tathāgata’s understanding and his sphere of practice as their own cultivation, they ultimately achieve nothing.

The commentary states: The Buddha taught the definitive dharma-gates that accord with principle, all of which declare that the mind and objects are fundamentally empty, and that delusions and karma are fundamentally...
The purity of ordinary beings and sages is not different; when the cause and fruit are perfectly luminous, the principle as seen from the perspective of a Buddha is indeed thus.

Furthermore, sentient beings have been deluded for a long time, and their habitual tendencies are deeply rooted; even if they possess faith and understanding of the Dharma-gates and employ them in the present, these originally follow after mental recollection.
They merely take the unimpeded verbal teachings of others to be understood through their own discriminating consciousness, claiming that this is the intent of the Buddha.

If one merely takes the burning of the mind as being "thought," then because one does not awaken to thought and remains ignorant of its dark penetration and realization, this differs from the mind of faith and understanding.
Such talk of recognizing the equality of the Buddha cannot sever delusions or seek realization;
thus, the *Sūtra-seal* says that one will ultimately achieve nothing, and the *Avataṃsaka* also says, "Like a poor man counting another's treasures," and so forth—these two cases are already equal.
Before the Sage, one must suppress the high to conform to the low; this is to level the low with the high. In the second part, one recognizes his sage-like wisdom.
There may be sentient beings who have not attained yet claim to have attained, and who have not realized yet claim to have realized.
The commentary states: "Attainment" refers to the principle, and so forth; "realization" (sākṣātkriyā) refers to the wisdom possessed by the sages.

Thus, it is the body of wisdom through which the sages realize [the truth] in profound stillness. Now, regarding "realization," if one who possesses overweening pride (*adhimāna*) claims to have realized it when they themselves know they have not, this constitutes the fundamental precept of great falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*). This is not the intended meaning of the present text. II.
Examining this reveals that ordinary people give rise to jealousy when they see those who have attained superior progress.

The commentary states: "Thus, for all sages, physical forms and appearances are not fixed; whether they attain [realization] or not, their internal realization resides within the mind. How [is this so]?
Because one distinguishes what others have not yet attained or realized, one observes the signs of what is seen to verify its reality or falsity.
Now, when a sage applies his mind, there is no duality between himself and others; seeing another’s superior progress or the circulation of the Dharma teachings, he rejoices in every thought-moment.
He must certainly be able to accord with this and verify it within his own mind. Thus, either [the other] has indeed realized awakening without falsehood, or [he himself] has attained self-awakening.
When one's own [virtue] declines while another's flourishes, one feels envy; when one's own [virtue] flourishes while another's declines, one feels joy.

Even if one has a profound understanding of the sublime realm, it is merely an object of the mind; do not mistake this for attainment or realization, as these two fetters will form obstacles to awakening.
Because those sentient beings have not yet severed their attachment to self, they are unable to enter pure awakening.
The commentary states: "Those who have not yet severed their attachment to self" refers to both categories of people mentioned previously.

Although the preceding section explained the realm of equality between ordinary beings and sages, it did not permit the view that one's own understanding is identical to that of a Buddha; thus it was said that [such a person] will ultimately not achieve success.

Because the Buddha is free from self-love while ordinary beings possess self-love, and because envy toward seeing others' excellence arises from self-love, they are ultimately unable to enter pure awakening;
they are deluded regarding the causes that lead to the fruits of the four destinies.
"Good son, in the final age, sentient beings who hope to achieve the Way must not seek only awakening; this will only increase their learning and grow their self-view.
The commentary explains: "Hoping to achieve the Way" refers to the pursuit of the fruit [of enlightenment]. The subsequent two phrases refer to the causes of delusion; therefore, the Sūtra says:
The śrāvakas contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate the cause; they are like a dog chasing a clod of earth rather than chasing the person who threw it.
One who wishes to practice and study must first awaken to the mind. Once the mind is thoroughly clarified, one then seeks broad understanding.

Yet people in this degenerate age are mostly deluded by this point, adhering only to names and categories while failing to strive for the realization of the mind. Since their minds remain unpenetrated, their understanding merely increases [their confusion].
Therefore, I say that the view of self increases; the *Avataṃsaka* also states that failing to understand one's own mind leads to the increase of all evils.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Much learning without wisdom is to not know the true reality (*dharmatā*), like having a lamp in great darkness but lacking eyes.
Regarding the four types of abandonment of delusions (only at this point), they form the cause (the Buddha’s teaching below) due to the preceding sections.
The sutra text states that within the practice there are many faults and afflictions, all of which are summarized by concluding that one does not enter pure awakening;

therefore, this admonition urges one to abandon such faulty mental application so that the true cause may be perfected. The text consists of two parts, the first of which provides a sequential explanation.
One should simply apply oneself with diligence to subduing the afflictions and arouse great valor so that what has not been attained may be attained and what has not been severed may be severed.
When greed, hatred, craving, pride, flattery, deceit, jealousy, and the notions of "self" and "other" do not arise toward objects, and when all such attachments are completely extinguished—
the Buddha says that such a person will gradually achieve accomplishment, seek out virtuous friends, and not fall into wrong views.
The commentary states: Regarding the previous discussion on severing delusions, the phrase "one should simply" is specifically intended to mark words of exhortation and admonition.

"Diligence" and "arousing great heroic vigor" apply generally to both cultivation and severance. "Causing what has not yet been attained to be attained" refers to all the meritorious qualities and wondrous functions within the realm of reality (*tattva*).
"Severing what has not yet been severed" refers to all obstructive phenomena within the realm of perversion (*viparyāsa*). That is to say:

Although there are frequent passages concerning the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) both before and after [this section], I shall now comprehensively collect them here and briefly open two gates:

first, the afflictive hindrances to be abandoned; second, the mode of practice for abandoning them; and third, the sequence of stages for abandonment. Regarding the first, the afflictions to be abandoned, there are both general and specific types.
The general refers to what is taught in this Sūtra, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Awakening of Faith*—each of which speaks of two kinds of five [afflictions].
The nature of the text has already been explained in its entirety at the beginning; however, there are distinct aspects regarding its root and its branches. As for the root, there are two kinds:
first, the fundamental non-awakening within the treatise, by which the ālayavijñāna is established; this refers to what is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) in the Mañjuśrī chapter.
Second, as extensively clarified at the beginning of the Maitreya chapter, craving is the root of saṃsāra. Each [of these] is distinct.

The explanation is now complete. (First is the root of the cognitive hindrance; second is the root of the afflictive hindrance. Regarding the "branches," both the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Ratnagotravibhāga* each explain nine types, all of which have been explained as before.

In the root verses of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, six types are stated in general. In the ninth chapter of that treatise, ten types are further explained in relation to the hindrances to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
These ten types have already been explained as before. As for the six types, the verse says: "Afflictions..."
This refers to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views. The long prose commentary explains:

"Because their nature is subsumed under the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), they receive the designation 'affliction' (although they are called 'root' in contrast to the secondary afflictions, they are considered 'branch' in relation to the delusion regarding ultimate truth). These have already been briefly analyzed in the Chapter on the Eight Consciousnesses;
now they will be further explained to clarify the scriptural text. The text states: "Greed, hatred, craving, and pride. In that treatise, "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is not included among their number.
Because they are subsumed under craving (*rāga*) which has no distinct nature, these are only three factors; this is the position of that treatise.

Craving has the nature of being stained attachment toward existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence (*bhavopakarana*); its function is to obstruct non-craving and to produce suffering, for it is through the power of craving that the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) arise.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) has the nature of malice and resentment toward suffering and the instruments of suffering; its function is to obstruct non-hatred.
Its function is to serve as the basis for unwholesome conduct; that is, because hatred necessarily causes affliction and distress to body and mind, it gives rise to various unwholesome karmas.
As for pride (*māna*), its nature is to exalt oneself in relation to others by relying on one's own qualities; its function is to obstruct non-pride and to produce suffering;
that is, if one possesses pride, the mind does not become humble toward those possessing superior virtues or toward those who have attained such virtues.

Because of this, the cycle of birth and death revolves without end, and one undergoes various sufferings; thus, these types of pride (*māna*) are distinguished as seven or nine kinds. Specifically, there are seven based on the three grades of objects regarding self and qualities:

namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of "I" (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*). 1. Pride (*māna*): considering oneself superior to those who are inferior, or equal to those who are equal. 2. Excessive pride (*atimāna*): considering oneself equal to those who are superior, or superior to those who are equal.

3. Pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*): considering oneself superior to those who are already superior. 4. The pride of "I" (*asmimāna*): self-reliance and haughty exaltation. 5. Overweening pride (*adhimāna*): claiming to have attained much when one has attained little. 6. Inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*): [considering oneself only slightly inferior to those who are vastly superior].

(To falsely reckon oneself as superior when one is actually inferior) is *mithyāmāna* (false pride). (To claim attainment when none has been attained) is the ninth, namely: "I am superior" (*mānātimāna*), "I am equal to those who are my equals" (*māna*), "I am inferior" (*ūnamāna*);

"there is one superior to me" (*adhimāna*), "there is one equal to me" (*māna*), "there is one inferior to me" (*ūnamāna*); "there is no one superior to me" (*asmimāna*), "there is no one equal to me" (*abhimāna*), "there is no one inferior to me" (*ūnamāna*).

Thus, while the seven types of pride are broad and the nine are narrow—since the nine are merely three sub-categories within the seven—the seven and the nine are each divided into three to form nine, which correspond as explained in the commentary. *Śāṭhya* (deceit), *īrṣyā* (envy), and *mātsarya* (avarice).

Envy (*īrṣyā*) is a minor derivative affliction (*upakleśa*). It is called "minor" because it arises individually; it is called a "derivative" because it is a concordant outflow (*niṣyanda*) that is a specific state of greed (*lobha*) and so forth.
Deceit (*māyā*) consists of feigning unusual conduct in order to deceive others; its nature is crookedness and its function is to obstruct honest instruction.

Its essence is a portion of greed and delusion (*moha*). As for jealousy (*mātsarya*): [the text continues as follows:]... [The remainder of the passage defines jealousy as a portion of greed that is unable to endure the prosperity of others.]
To pursue fame and profit for oneself while being unable to endure the glory of others, having envy and jealousy as one’s nature, which acts as an obstacle;

to have non-envy and freedom from sorrow as its function, and to take a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*) as its essence—yet among the six fundamental afflictions, ignorance (*moha*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are currently absent [from this definition].
Ignorance is already included in the verse; furthermore, because doubt has been resolved through three successive interrogations and explanations, the verse states: "My body is itself the body."

When the view of a self (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) is severed, the other views are naturally eliminated; "the others" refers to the two views of extremes and wrong views, as these all arise based upon the view of a self.

Furthermore, the term "craving for that self" is repeated because craving is associated with the notion of a self. This section specifically aims to eliminate the notion of a self, as it separately clarifies the compassionate affection for oneself and others (hence the term "endearment").
Since this is the root of birth and death and is most difficult to uproot, one should contemplate its exhaustion.

Because both self and other are quiescent, and because the enumerations of afflictions in various sūtra teachings—whether increasing or decreasing, being adopted or discarded—cannot be standardized according to a single intent, we shall here establish ten categories based on this [system].

Regarding the total number of one hundred twenty-eight afflictions to be abandoned through the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) across the three realms, there are five different systems of teaching concerning the modes of abandonment (*prahāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). First, the Small Vehicle...

Regarding the "Vehicle," this has already been explained in the Chapter on Vajragarbha. Second, the Initial Teaching (Śāstra) holds that the noble path eliminates delusions not by means of the three periods of time, but rather that when wisdom arises, the delusions are immediately absent.

This is because light and darkness cannot coexist, and just as the two ends of a scale rise and fall simultaneously, so too, by principle, wisdom and hindrances cannot coexist. Third, the Final Teaching (Śāstra)... [self...]

There are two meanings: first, the reversal according to characteristics; second, the reversal according to continuity. Regarding the reversal according to characteristics: the meaning does not differ from what preceded, but that previous explanation was incomplete.
That is to say, when the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) correctly severs the afflictions (*kleśa*), does wisdom arise first and the affliction perish later?
Or do the affliction perish first and wisdom arise later? Or do they arise simultaneously? Within this context, if the affliction and wisdom were to occur sequentially...

The latter [position] each has two faults that fail to establish the meaning of abandonment: namely, if wisdom arises first, there is the fault that wisdom would spontaneously become untainted (*anāsrava*), and the fault that it could not extinguish afflictions;
furthermore, there is the fault that afflictions would spontaneously be extinguished, and the fault that they would not obstruct the Noble Path.

If afflictions were extinguished first, these same four faults would likewise apply; the names are identical, but their meanings differ according to how they are mutually related. Taken together, they constitute [the full set].

This is the eighth fault. The preceding explanation—that light and darkness are simultaneous—is based on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* (Verse 6.2), which states that light cannot destroy darkness whether it reaches it or does not reach it, because these two are mutually non-existent;
they are contradictory when simultaneous, and do not interact when occurring at different times. This is the application of the principle (*dharma*).
The failure to achieve the severance of delusions and the attainment of nirvāṇa is also illustrated by this same analogy; likewise, vipaśyanā does not sever afflictions.
Furthermore, while a scale is a single entity where the lowering and raising occur simultaneously, knowledge and delusion are not so—how then could one avoid the aforementioned fault?

If, according to this school, the severance of delusions must necessarily involve the realization that delusions lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, and that there is no obstruction [between them], then if they were definitively existent...
If one falls into the view of permanence, there would be nothing to be severed; if it were definitively non-existent, there likewise would be nothing to be severed.
Now, because the true principle accords with conditions, wisdom arises without arising, and delusion is severed without severance.

Because its self-nature accords with conditions, wisdom arises while being without arising, and delusion is severed while being without severance. As for what is called "continuity," this does not refer to the relationship between delusion and wisdom.
Regarding the wisdom that can sever [the afflictions] through contrast, there are three periods; within these three periods, there are two ways of categorizing them:

first, by distinguishing the three periods according to the initial mind and the ultimate culmination; second, by distinguishing the three moments within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Now, based on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, both of these [interpretations] are applicable. That treatise states: "This wisdom exhausts the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*); it is the primary wisdom for severing [them]."

The middle [section] provides the subsequent answer, stating that it is not severed by the initial wisdom, nor by the middle or subsequent [wisdoms]. A verse from the Sūtra (as cited in the Śāstra) states: "Because it is neither at the beginning, the middle, nor the end.
If there is no severance during these three periods, how can there be severance? The Śāstra says: "It is like the flame of a lamp;

it is not severed solely at the beginning, middle, or end, because it is grasped throughout the beginning, middle, and end. This citation of a simile serves to explain and establish the point. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also says: "For example, when lighting a lamp, it is not by the initial flame..."

The burning wick does not exist apart from the initial flame, nor does it exist apart from the subsequent flames, yet the wick is indeed consumed by fire. This means that while the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*) clarifies both the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the mind in its severance of delusions, the scriptural passage primarily reveals that realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is based solely on the ineffable meaning of profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Since the Master [Vasubandhu] also elucidates the severance of delusions, he distinguishes both nature and characteristics;
thus, neither at the beginning, the middle, nor the end, does one discern the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) as the cause and condition for severance.

If one does not sever the grasping at the preceding, middle, and subsequent [moments], then the characteristic of conditions is not destroyed. This "severing that is non-severing" means: if a single thought-moment can sever [grasping], why rely on three thoughts?

Since it is only through their simultaneous grasping that [the object] is established, one clearly knows it has no intrinsic nature. Because it lacks intrinsic nature, there is no beginning, middle, or end;
yet it is only by virtue of the subsequent [moment] being established that the severing of the beginning, middle, and end occurs. Thus, because it arises from conditions, it is non-existent.
Because nature is non-nature, it arises from conditions. Fourth, regarding the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), there are three gates: 1. The gate of severing only the root:

when the root is severed, the branches are eliminated (as explained above regarding "root and branch"). Thus, the preceding text states, "Permanently sever ignorance," and also says, "First sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
2. The gate of awakening to emptiness before it can be called "severance": this is like dreaming of shackles; upon waking, they vanish.
Because it is liberation itself, the text says: "This ignorance has no real substance," and so forth, up to:

"Knowing it to be like a flower in the sky, there is no cyclic existence. The Treatise says: "To perceive that thoughts differ from awakening, yet that thoughts lack any differing characteristics," and so on.

These three views hold that the nature of these delusions is neither severed nor not severed, because the nature of this delusion is true awakening. As the Treatise says: "One is deluded by depending on awakening; if one were apart from it..."

The nature of awakening is such that there is no non-awakening; as the sutras state: "All obstacles are ultimate awakening," and "Because all things are awakening. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī instructs sentient beings to give rise to the mind of *ātman-dṛṣṭi* (self-view), because self-view is itself bodhi.

Therefore, one should not sever awakening, which is why it is said to be "not severed. As the text says: "Knowing illusion is itself liberation; no further expedient means are required," and "One does not even extinguish the various deluded minds.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Do not sever afflictions," and so forth. Because this is true awakening, one should not mistake it for delusion; thus, it is "not not-severed. As the text says: "When all illusions are exhausted and extinguished..."

The awakened mind is unmoving; it is further said that because illusion is extinguished through extinction, that which is not illusory does not cease. It is also said that by clarifying all thoughts, adventitious dust is forever extinguished. This meaning is like waking from a dream:

one does not say it is "severed" because one has removed the objects within the dream, nor does one say it is "not severed" because one has left those objects behind. Being neither severed nor not severed is the true severance of delusions.
As for the Fivefold Perfect Teaching, this refers to the Huayan school, which holds that the essential nature of all afflictions is ineffable, for the dharmas obstructed must ultimately be exhausted.
The limits [of reality] penetrate the ten directions; the one is identical to all, and the primary and its attendants are inexhaustible.

These possess the four dharma realms, yet they are not merely True Suchness (as explained in detail previously). Therefore, the delusions that can obstruct are such that the obstruction of one obstructs all obstructions (hence, in the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra," a single moment of anger possesses a million doors of obstruction).

The wisdom that can sever them is such that the severing of one severs all severings (hence, in the "Chapter on the Minor Marks," those in the Avīci Hell suddenly realize the Ten Stages). Realizing...

When the Dharma-realm is realized once, all is realized (as already explained above in the section on the stages of realization). When the Buddha-fruit is accomplished once, all is accomplished (as stated in the "Appearance Chapter":

when the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings as having attained perfect enlightenment and entered parinirvāṇa). Third, regarding the sequence of the stages of abandonment: in the Hīnayāna, it is as previously described;
in the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s first turning of the wheel), each of the two obstacles consists of both the manifest and the seeds of the discriminative and innate [afflictions].
Regarding the two types of seeds of the [afflictive] views abandoned at the beginning of the Path of Seeing:

as for those whose innate seeds of afflictions were already suppressed prior to the stages (bhūmi), they are able to abandon them with mastery from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward because they have retained [the capacity to do so]; yet they do not abandon them [at that time]. As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:

"The Bodhisattvas on the ten stages cultivate only the path that counteracts the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), not the path that counteracts the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). This is because [the Bodhisattva] does not fall into the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) due to taking rebirth through the power of moistening [karma] and gathering [beings] for conversion.

For the sake of severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and for the sake of attaining great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), [the Bodhisattva] retains the afflictions until they are exhausted, thereby realizing the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

This means that by employing wisdom to govern their activity, one does not give rise to faults and instead accomplishes superior practices, just as one restrains a snake—as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
This continues until the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, at which point all manifest [afflictions] belonging to the stages are suddenly severed at once.

Regarding the gradual subduing prior [to the first bhūmi]: from the first bhūmi upward, the seeds of the innate cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are gradually severed at each stage until they are forever exhausted by the vajra-like concentration.
As for their manifestation, they are permanently subdued and exhausted from the stages prior to the first bhūmi up through the tenth bhūmi.
From the eighth bhūmi upward, those associated with the six consciousnesses no longer function; however, those associated with the seventh consciousness still persist.

Regarding the arising of the first five [consciousnesses], although the *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) has not yet occurred, because they are suppressed by the untainted (*anāsrava*), the obstacles do not manifest.

In the *Zhengjiao* (Definitive Teaching), the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are not differentiated as innate (*sahaja*) or discriminative (*vikalpita*); there are only the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) along with their latencies (*vāsanā*). This means that before the stages (*bhūmi*), one suppresses the active manifestations;

at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), one cuts off the seeds of the active afflictions; from the subsequent stages onward, one eliminates the latencies; and at the Buddha-stage, ultimate purity is attained. However, regarding these three...
Because these sages have already avoided falling into the stages of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*), they possess mastery over the afflictions (*kleśa*) and are able to sever them;

however, they do not sever them entirely because they intentionally retain them to eliminate the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). (The *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that from the "Ten Understandings" (*daśajñāna*) onward, one attains supramundane pure mind; it further states that those who attain the name of "sage" (*ārya*) supramundane do not fall into the stages of the two vehicles.

The *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that those prior to the [first] stage realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) but do not take realization as their goal. The *Awakening of Faith* also says that they see a small portion of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and are able to manifest the eight signs, etc. For this reason, these Bodhisattvas fear only...
Because of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one practices the contemplation of *vijñaptimātratā*, *tathatā*, and so forth, to suppress and sever it;

since this portion of the hindrance is severed from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, and because the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is no longer retained thereafter, the two hindrances are not distinguished as being [severed] by either the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Upon reaching the first stage, the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of both are entirely exhausted. As the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "Within the paths of seeing and cultivation, all afflictions that can obstruct the benefit of sentient beings..."

Because they arise from active formations (*saṃskāra*), all [afflictions] are severed simultaneously within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). As for the afflictions of the *manas*, their coarse aspects are severed in the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*), while their residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are eliminated later.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "By transforming the defiled *manas*, one attains the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). At the time of the initial clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one has already realized the transformation and subduing of the purified state during the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This clarifies the removal of the habitual tendencies; since these were already severed previously, it speaks only of "transforming into purity" rather than "severing. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* also states that on the grounds (*bhūmi*), one relies upon those two types of obstacles consisting of habitual tendencies. Furthermore, within the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), this is for the purpose of attracting the two...

Because of this vehicle, when explaining from the higher perspective down to the lower, it is said that the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are exhausted only at the stage of Buddhahood according to the teachings of the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, when explaining from the lower perspective up to the higher, it is granted that the Two Vehicles completely sever the afflictive hindrances while partially severing the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Now, according to the definitive discourse of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-deśanā*), even those Śrāvakas who follow the limited Dharma lack the vast mind and are thus unable to ultimately uproot the afflictive hindrances.

If one can merely subdue them, how much more so can one sever them? As stated in the *Commentary on the Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, regarding those who follow the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*), if they are to awaken to the principle and harmonize their vow with that awakening by turning their backs on sensory dust, they do not practice in stages.

As the text says: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts," and "Because the mind does not produce falsehood. Thus, at the stage of Faith (*xinwei*), it is said: "Exhaustive toil and anxiety are forever severed, and the purity of the Dharma-realm is attained. However...
Although delusions are false and vain, their sudden arising through arbitrary grasping cannot be eliminated all at once;

rather, they are exhausted gradually as a natural process, just as when the wind suddenly ceases, the waves gradually subside (as the text says: "Within the midst of effortful activity regarding what has ceased and what has not yet ceased, distinctions are revealed").
This corresponds to the four stages of awakening to delusion within the treatise, as already explained by citing the *Avataṃsaka* Perfect Teaching’s fifty-two stages among the grounds (*bhūmi*).

Because the stages are perfected through abandonment, there are scriptural passages stating that one attains Buddhahood at every stage; this has been briefly explained as before, while the details are as set forth therein.
Having concluded the meaning of the abandonment of afflictions, we shall next explain the remaining text. Regarding "not arising in relation to objects" and "the total quiescence":

these refer to the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) whereby the afflictions have already been subdued. Nevertheless, according to this school, this is also termed "abandonment" from the very first inception.
Because the mind abides in the same manner as the first stage (*bhūmi*), the Buddha taught the following four lines as the "Buddha-seal" that establishes the cause.

Regarding the term "gradual" used therein: although one may have attained awakening at the time of previously eliminating the mind that clings to a self, one still fears that it will be difficult to abandon the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the self over a long period.
Therefore, the Buddha cautioned: "Having attained sudden awakening to the emptiness of the self, you must diligently sever the afflictions and the habitual tendencies of the view of self."

As one's vital energy gradually wanes, the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood is naturally and progressively accomplished. Regarding the phrase "seeking a spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth:
just as a merchant entering the sea must rely upon a guide, a student practicing cultivation must necessarily depend upon a virtuous friend. This is the second [of two] analogies.
If one gives rise to separate feelings of aversion or attachment toward what is sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.

The commentary states: the statement that "giving rise to separate feelings of aversion or attachment prevents entry into awakening" conversely clarifies that by not giving rise to aversion or attachment, one enters awakening;
therefore, it is explained through inversion that the non-arising of aversion and attachment is the severing of delusions and entering awakening, which is precisely the accomplishment [of the path].
For this reason, within this section, I shall briefly divide this passage. I say with sincerity: Alas! Those practitioners of the present age take their ailments as a merit;

they vainly recount empty labors that will surely invite a fall into the depths. Clearly, these are the Buddha’s warnings; I pray you examine your own minds with discernment and do not let a single lifetime pass in vain.
To roam idly through the ocean of meaning—this is the first verse among the four verses of praise which follow in sequence to summarize what preceded.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Pure Karma, you should know: All sentient beings Arise entirely from grasping at a self and attachment."
Within the two lines that separately explain the four characteristics of beginningless false transmigration:
"As long as these four characteristics have not been eliminated, one cannot attain Bodhi."
Among these three, one verse states: "I have lost the Way because of clinging to a self.
Love and hatred arise within the mind, and crookedness persists in every thought. For this reason, there is much delusion and distress, preventing entry into the City of Awakening."

The commentary states: The city is a metaphor for the awakened one (*bodhi*). There are three meanings to this city: first, it defends against external enemies; second, it sustains the multitude of people; and third, it opens its gates to welcome and guide others.
Now, because one has not entered the city of awakening, various thoughts of love and hatred invade and press upon one.

If one realizes that the nature of the mind is empty, then the myriad delusions will not enter; seeing the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the ten thousand practices become perfect, and the path of cultivation increases.
When there is nothing that is not penetrated, one is able to attract and gather both self and others, thereby attaining the fruit; by severing the hundred negations, one achieves liberation;

by nurturing all virtues, one perfects the *dharmakāya*; and by opening up *prajñā*, one becomes all-penetrating. The three preceding sections are all extensive verses, while the four [subsequent] sections are concise;
among these, two and a half verses concern the severance of delusions and the formation of causes.
If one can turn toward awakening the realm, first eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion; when attachment to phenomena no longer dwells in the mind, gradual accomplishment is possible.
Since my own body is fundamentally non-existent, from what cause could love or hate arise?
This person seeks a virtuous friend and shall never fall into false views; regarding that which is sought, do not give rise to a separate mind.

The ultimate non-attainment of realization is called awakening to the *kṣetra*. A *kṣetra* refers to a world-system; just as when one enters the country of Tang, all the territory belongs to Tang, so it is with the realm of awakening.

Thus we know that if one reaches the state of awakening, then every phenomenon (*dharma*) belongs to awakening. The same applies to the state of delusion; even phenomena of attachment to the Dharma [belong to delusion].
This refers to hating birth-and-death and loving nirvana. "My body fundamentally does not exist" means that my body is the very basis of hatred and love;
if one wishes to eliminate hatred and love, one must not cling to this delusory body. Since that which is relied upon is empty, how can that which relies upon it exist?
Furthermore, one loves that which moistens the body and hates that which opposes me. If my body did not exist, hatred and love would not arise. Thus, I awaken to the moment.

Good son, when sentient beings in the final age are about to resolve their great aspiration and seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to practice the path, they should seek one who possesses all correct knowledge and vision;
whose mind does not dwell on signs (*nimitta*) and does not cling to the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
