none of those perceived objects that one hears of should ever be grasped.

The meaning follows from what was stated previously. Although these three contemplations each have their own realized marks (*lakṣaṇa*), in principle, one must practice them in a complete, integrated manner to realize Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), as explained in the preceding text.

Furthermore, regarding the realization of the Three Stills and Three Contemplations in the Tiantai school (the tenth section), it is also said that only through complete cultivation does one reach the ultimate;
that is, by understanding that all phenomena are empty and false due to causes and conditions, one enters emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Next...

From emptiness one enters the provisional, and through this one enters the Middle Way, illuminating both truths simultaneously. Mind after mind becomes quiescent, naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Within a single thought-moment, one possesses all Buddha-dharmas; clearly seeing one's nature, one dwells securely in the Mahāyāna.
One's gait is level and upright, as swift as the wind; one practices the conduct of the Tathāgata, entering the chamber and donning the robes.
Sitting upon the seat, the six sense faculties become pure; within a single pore, one encompasses all things, even unto the attainment of the eightfold marks of enlightenment.

This is precisely the state of the Bodhisattva at the first stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), as taught in the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras.
As for the realm of realizing the fruit through the final mind, it is inconceivable; yet by inferring what is clarified in the scriptures, it is not separate from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The fruit of this is as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa* sūtras; the marks of realization in the present sutra correspond to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, regarding the marks of realization in the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-sūkṣma-dvārāṇi*), it is said that there are two kinds of realization:

first, realization through understanding (*adhigama-prativedha*), which is unimpeded, skillful wisdom that does not depend on mental deliberation, but spontaneously and perfectly cognizes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); second, realization through integration (*samudāgama-prativedha*), wherein wondrous wisdom is brilliantly opened.
The illumination that reveals and penetrates the dharma-realm without obstruction is further divided into two types:
first, the semblance realization, such as the purification of the six sense faculties described in the *Lotus Sūtra*; second, the true realization, which is further divided into three levels:

first, the initial realization, namely the stage of the first resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), wherein one opens the Tathāgatagarbha through right wisdom to manifest the true Dharmakāya; this is also termed the "essence" (*tattva*). Second, the middle... [text continues]
Having realized the various intermediate stages, one subsequently attains the wisdom of a single thought-moment in correspondence with reality;

the wondrous enlightenment manifests before one, exhaustively illuminating the dharma-realm, and its functional capacity becomes universally complete. The realization described in this sutra corresponds to that [stage].

Because he knows all that exists within the three thousandfold world-system, and because he knows the mental thoughts and raindrops across hundreds of thousands of worlds, it is either identical to [that stage] or similar to it.
In the initial realization of the truth, because stillness reaches its ultimate limit and awareness is all-pervasive, the worlds of the known transcend the three thousandfold world-systems;
thus, it was previously stated that "the Buddhas of the ten directions appear as the mind," and it will be stated below that "the Tathāgata appears in the world.

Within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (Yuan-dun jiao), cause and effect interpenetrate, and the characteristics of realization are not restricted to a fixed sequence of before and after. This is the third section: the summary.
This is called the initial skillful means (*upāya*) of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

The commentary explains: since the previous question asked what constitutes the beginning of the three types of pure contemplation, this has now been fully answered and concluded with the words "this is called," etc.

Thus, one should understand that although the various wheels of the three contemplations in the preceding section have been explained in detail regarding their characteristics, it is only now that they are truly entered into.
This refers precisely to the two types of universal cultivation and the three contemplations explained here.
If all sentient beings universally cultivate these three kinds with diligent and vigorous effort, this is called the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.

The commentary states: The birth originally manifested by the Tathāgata was solely for the purpose of exhorting sentient beings to practice cultivation. Now that the three contemplations are complete, the myriad practices are perfected;

therefore, with respect to this person, it is called the "emergence of a Buddha. Furthermore, when this person’s original enlightenment (benjue) is free from discursive thought, it is called the "emergence of a Buddha.
However, while it was previously stated that freedom from the four maladies constitutes the realization of enlightenment and parinirvāṇa, here we speak of cultivation.

The three contemplations are called "the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world. Now, they are explained through the contrast between appearance in the world (*saṃsāra*) and *nirvāṇa*, which has two gates:
first, according to the ultimate meaning; second, according to the adaptation to capacities. Regarding the ultimate meaning, there are three points:

first, the ultimate truth of dependent origination as emptiness is neither appearance nor cessation; thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor does he pass into extinction."

There is the conventional truth of the two-fold Nirvāṇa and True Suchness as dependent origination, which manifests moment by moment and in every place, and enters Nirvāṇa moment by moment and in every place.
A Great Sūtra further states: "A Bodhisattva should know that within their own mind, there is always the attainment of perfect enlightenment by a Buddha;
as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings. (This refers to the thought-moment...)
Furthermore, it is said: "One should know that there is not even the slightest place that is empty and devoid of the Buddha-body" (that is, everywhere).
Nirvāṇa is precisely this Buddha-body appearing universally in all places as described above.

Since this is a conditioned phenomenon arising through dependent origination, its four characteristics—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—are simultaneous; now, one takes this very arising-as-ceasing to be mindfulness.

Regarding the thought of attaining *parinirvāṇa* in every place, there are three points concerning the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): it is eternally abiding in the world and eternally in *nirvāṇa*.
This means that because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it dwells in the world; and because it illuminates while remaining constantly quiescent, it is *nirvāṇa*.

For those with the capacity [to respond], when the conditions for their capacity are stirred, he appears beneath the Bodhi tree; when the conditions for their capacity are exhausted, he [manifests] at the twin *śāla* trees.
Because he entered *nirvāṇa* between the trees, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "O Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgatas appear in the world in order to inspire joy in sentient beings;
they manifest *nirvāṇa* in order to engender longing and devotion in sentient beings.
It is like the rising sun that shines universally upon the world, appearing within all vessels of pure water. This corresponds to the intent of the present sūtra.
The explanation may be understood through three sections on the mutual cultivation of the three contemplations: first, clarifying that the cultivation of contemplation is not accomplished;
if, in the future末法 (mofa) age, sentient beings of dull faculties desire to seek the Way but fail to achieve accomplishment.
The commentary states: This is the lowest of the middling grades; one’s power does not fulfill one’s heart’s desire. Second, one should repent to eliminate delusions and karma.

Because of past karmic obstructions, one should diligently practice repentance and constantly give rise to aspiration. First, sever hatred and love, jealousy and envy, flattery and crookedness, and seek a superior, exalted mind.
The commentary states: "To reiterate one's vows and resolve with determination to realize [enlightenment], one should apply effort and exert the will to repent and sever delusions.

The *Treatise* also says: 'If a person practices with confidence, yet faces numerous obstacles due to the karmic offenses of previous lives, they should vigorously perform the three practices—prostration, repentance, and so forth—cultivating them as appropriate and interchangeably.'"

Regarding the practice of one of the three types of pure contemplations (*śubha-vipaśyanā*) according to the instructions: once this contemplation has been attained, one must not revert to practicing the other contemplations; rather, with the mind never letting go, one should gradually seek realization.

The commentary explains: there are those hindered by perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), for whom the contemplation of emptiness and stillness is difficult to accomplish. First, one contemplates the illusion of form; [the form] is illusory...

Only when one observes the totality of emptiness and stillness does [the contemplation] truly succeed. Furthermore, there are those who cling to fixed, substantial form, which obstructs the mind-consciousness and makes it difficult to contemplate the provisional and illusory.
One must first know that its substance is fundamentally non-existent, yet not hindered by perceiving its provisional appearance; only then does the contemplation of illusion truly succeed.

Furthermore, there are those who find it difficult to accomplish the Middle Way because it is beyond all dependence. One must first know that the provisional is entirely empty, yet without [a separate] "emptiness of the provisional," and that the empty is entirely provisional.
Furthermore, when both emptiness and emptiness-of-emptiness are absent through their mutual negation, one transcends all opposition and perceives quiescence.

Moreover, there are those who directly perceive the source of the mind and thereby know that all phenomena are empty because they are identical to the nature, yet provisional because they do not destroy their characteristics;

or that they are provisional because they manifest from the nature, and empty because there is nothing separate from what is manifested. These aspects alternate sequentially, as explained in the verses on the wheels.
Within the section of praise, there are two parts; within the first, the site of enlightenment, there are three sections.
The first verse sets the time limit. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Perfect Enlightenment, you should know: All sentient beings Who seek the unsurpassed path..."
First, one should establish the three periods;
next, the characteristics of the three phrases are as follows:
Repent of karma from beginningless time, passing through twenty-one days, and thereafter engage in correct contemplation.
"Right reflection" refers to the passage following the section on "collecting the mind.

The latter two phrases, "it is certainly not the object heard by him" and "it is ultimately ungraspable," constitute the general and specific characteristics respectively; these four sections are here combined into one within the second stage of application (*prayoga*).
The first verse of the three [verses] concerns the distinct cultivation [of the three samādhis]:
Śamatha is ultimate stillness; Samādhi is correct mindfulness and retention; Dhyāna is clarity regarding the gates of counting— these are called the three pure contemplations.
The next two lines concern universal cultivation.
If one can diligently practice them, these are called the five lines for mutual cultivation after the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Those of dull faculties who have not yet attained accomplishment should always repent with a diligent mind.
When all sins and obstacles from beginningless time are extinguished, the realm of the Buddha will manifest before one.

[The preceding section and the rules for the summer retreat (vassa) are concluded. [The following verse concerning the manifestation of the Buddha-realm is omitted; the preceding verse is placed after it.]
The remainder is merely abbreviated in the text.
The third major section, the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) division, refers to the point where the exposition of the Dharma and its meaning in the *śarīra* (main body) division has been completed;
it exists so that [the teaching] may extensively benefit others, reach far into future generations, and circulate with unimpeded continuity in an endless succession.
I. No one transmits it; non-transmission means it does not flow, yet non-stagnation means it does not dwell.
Transmission meets with obstacles, yet this non-obstruction means it is neither blocked nor congested. (Section 51) II. Qing hears of the profound Dharma and requests its circulation.

(1) Praising and granting permission to listen establishes a resonance that facilitates circulation. (2) III. Based on the request, the teaching is proclaimed to provide internal protection for circulation. (3)
Fourth, receiving the mandate to provide external protection for the circulation [of the teaching]; fifth, the conclusion of the circulation through the assembly’s reception and upholding.
The first section of this [fifth part] has three divisions, as above. Now, for the first:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him to the right.
Having circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, they knelt for a long time with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It should be known that, within the second section of the correct exposition, the first part celebrates the hearing of what is expressed:
'The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has extensively opened our understanding and that of sentient beings in the final age to such inconceivable [truths].'"

Section on the Matter. The commentary states: "The near celebration of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) encompasses the entire canon from afar. Second, regarding the inquiry into the expressive designation:
'World-Honored One, what is the name of this Mahāyāna teaching, and how should it be upheld? What do sentient beings obtain by practicing its cultivation?'"
"How may my merit cause me to protect and uphold those who transmit this sutra, so that these teachings reach their ultimate destination?

The explanation says: Indeed, within the section on the Correct Teaching (samyak-dharma), one merely asks about the principles and meanings (dharma-artha) that are expounded. Although these principles and meanings are already complete and perfect, it is difficult for the ordinary mind to maintain them.
While they are clearly understood at the moment of hearing, there is fear that they will be forgotten once that time has passed.

One must maintain the teachings so as to penetrate them thoroughly; since the text must not be omitted, one explains the meaning according to the text and gives rise to contemplation based on that meaning, only then achieving authentic practice.
Therefore, this question concerns the scriptural teachings. Regarding "names": in order to understand the meaning, one must first recognize the names;

if one is deluded regarding the names, one will not comprehend the meaning. Regarding "upholding": although the upholding of the Dharma was already explained previously, the present inquiry concerns the upholding of the teachings.
Regarding "merit": based on the principle of practice, one realizes the merit of the noble ones (*ārya*) as being boundless;

yet, fearing that merely upholding the names and teachings might lack benefit, one asks how to protect and uphold those who circulate the sūtra-holders and so forth—this summarizes the ten types of Dharma-practice (*dharmaparyāya*).
That is to say: making offerings to this sūtra, copying it, giving it away, listening to it, receiving it, and reading it.
Recite, explain, contemplate, and practice; thus distributed and transmitted, where will it ultimately lead? At the end of the third section, prostrate with utmost sincerity.
Having spoken these words, cast down the five limbs upon the ground. Thus make this request three times, beginning again and again until the end.
Second, the praise and approval.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You have been able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the merit of such scriptural teachings for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age."
“O Virtuous One, listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.

The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla and the great assembly waited in silence, listening with focused attention. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
Regarding the threefold exposition based on the inquiry, there are two parts. First, the brief identification of the one who speaks and the one who protects:
"Good son, this sutra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers;
it is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, it is the refuge of Bodhisattvas in the ten directions, and it is the pure eye of the twelve divisions of scripture."

The commentary states: Since the Buddha who preached this sutra is the True Body (*dharmakāya*), and the True Body is unimpeded and of the same essence as the sands of the Ganges, what is spoken by one is simultaneously spoken by many.
As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share a single Dharma-body;
their single mind, single wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are likewise so. Furthermore, in sutras of provisional meaning, [the teachings] vary according to the region.
Regarding the teaching that is neither provisional nor definitive, there is no Buddha who does not speak it; as the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"I have never seen a buddha-field where this sutra is not taught. As for its protection, it is also as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"We, the Buddhas, shall protect and uphold this Dharma so that all bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it shall [all hear it]."
Among those who have heard and taken refuge, there are none among whose causal practices the Eye of Buddhahood is not attained from this;
for by investigating the root of delusion and illuminating the source of awakening, the principle penetrates all scriptures and its meaning is nowhere exhausted herein.
If one understands this, all teachings will shine forth clearly; if one does not comprehend it, how can one know the Right Path? Thus it is said:
Regarding the two primary answers concerning the Dharma that was taught and protected, there are five sections: first, the answer regarding the name; second, the answer regarding the destination;
third, the answer regarding upholding; fourth, the answer regarding merit; and fifth, the answer regarding protection. This is the first [section].

This sutra is titled "The Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Dharani," and it is also titled "The Sutra of Definitive Meaning," "The King of Secret Samadhis," "The Determinate Realm of the Tathagata," and "The Distinctions of the Self-Nature of the Tathagatagarbha.
You should uphold it with reverence.
The commentary states: The sutra has five names, two of which have already been explained. Regarding "the Samādhi of the Secret King":

it is not heard by those who are not suitable vessels, hence it is called "Secret" (Guhyaka); it is heard differently according to the capacity of the vessel, hence it is called "Mysterious" (Guhya). As for the name "Samādhi," its enumerations are immeasurable.
The *Samādhi of Perfect Enlightenment* is the root source of these, and is therefore called the "King. "The Tathāgata’s Decisive Realm" refers to the ultimate realization.
Regarding the distinctions within the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgatagarbha: the Tathāgatagarbha is the name for Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) while still enmeshed in afflictions;
that it cannot be altered by delusion is called its "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), and that it gives rise to delusion according to conditions is called its "distinction" (*viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, the "empty Tathāgatagarbha" and the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha" constitute these distinctions. "You should uphold this" is the command.

Regarding the question of how to uphold [the teaching] based on its name and meaning: if one proceeds by way of the explicit text, there is no impediment to answering by means of explaining the title of the sutra, as it follows naturally from the textual momentum;

if one seeks it by way of the meaning, it is found in the two answers given later in the section on the sudden and gradual teachings. This section has two parts: first, indicating the basis upon which the practice relies.
"Good son, this sutra reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata; only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, can fully proclaim it.
*Explanation:* The preceding passage spoke of "the ground of pure awakening of all sentient beings," and further mentioned ignorance, craving, the four marks, and the four illnesses.
Now, stating that "it reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata," the latter phrase itself provides the explanation: only a Buddha can [fully proclaim it].
Because it is taught that ignorance and so forth are all non-existent, this is precisely the realm of the Buddha.
If the realm of the Buddha were not manifest, how could sentient beings all realize emptiness? If sentient beings did not realize emptiness, how could they penetrate the ground of awakening?

Therefore, the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is itself the realm of the Buddha. Although "wisdom" (*jñāna*) and "knowledge" (*vidyā*) differ, both are the Buddha’s realm; this is the intended meaning.
Second, regarding the destination reached through cultivation:
if all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely on this practice, they will gradually advance until they reach the stage of Buddhahood.

The commentary states: For those who practice in reliance upon this, it encompasses ten types of dharma-practice; since the sutra reveals exclusively the realm of the Buddha, practicing these will necessarily lead to the stage of Buddhahood.
Third, the response regarding the text on "receiving and upholding" has two parts: first, the dharma.

"Good son, this sutra is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahayana; sentient beings with sudden faculties attain awakening through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice the gradual path.

The commentary explains: "The principle is the Sudden Teaching, while the phenomena include the gradual gate. Since both the gradual and the sudden are gathered therein, both the slow and the quick [attain realization]."

For those who have already attained awakening, the nature of words is detached; yet for those who have not yet awakened, one must uphold the meaning without detaching from the words—this is the mark of upholding [the Dharma].
Whether one has entered [the path] or not, one may in all cases apply the mind; therefore, within the orthodox teaching, two analogies are distinguished: superior and inferior.
For example, the great ocean does not refuse even small streams, nor even the drinking of its water by mosquitoes, gadflies, or asuras, yet it remains fully filled.
The explanation says: gradual teaching contradicts sudden teaching; the gate of the sudden must necessarily possess the gate of the gradual, just as mosquitoes and gadflies drink from the ocean.
The analogy of the two vehicles receiving and upholding [the teaching] is like the asuras drinking from [a vessel];

the analogy of the bodhisattvas receiving and upholding [the teaching] is like the great ocean containing immeasurable water, which they drink according to the capacity of their own bellies. In the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, there are boundless dharma-gates;
one receives them according to whether one’s vessel is gradual or sudden. Part Four: The Text on the Merits, Section One: Revealing the Hearing [of the Teaching] by Comparing it to Bestowing Jewels.
The superior intention of the sutra clarifies its merit by comparing it with [ordinary] merit;

second, it clarifies its superior intention by comparing it with the salvation of others to reveal its wisdom (for without wisdom one cannot save others, and furthermore, while a listener might not understand and yet still generate merit, a speaker necessarily understands—thus it is solely a matter of wisdom).

Third, it reveals faith in the superiority of the sutra through the verification of past causes, thereby clarifying both merit and wisdom. Regarding the first of these two [sections on merit and wisdom], the inferior is first presented.
"Good son, suppose there were someone who filled the trichiliocosm entirely with the seven treasures and used them for giving.
The commentary explains: the first [part] shows that the accumulation of merit can be known; the second reveals its superiority."
It is not as good as someone hearing the name of this sutra or even a single phrase of its meaning.

To explain: according to the textual examples used for comparison in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is said that while worldly treasures filling the entire universe may serve as the resources for the fruits of outflows (*āsrava*), a single word of the wondrous Dharma will surely yield the reward of Bodhi. Second, when compared in terms of delivering sentient beings...
Regarding "measure" (*mātra*): this means that whereas previously inferior merit was used to manifest superior merit, here inferior wisdom is used to manifest superior wisdom. The text has two parts;
first, the presentation of the inferior:
"Good son, suppose there were a person who taught as many sentient beings as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers to attain the fruit of Arhatship."
The explanation says: "By accumulating merit, one may know [the former]; this reveals its superiority.
It is not equal to someone who proclaims this sutra and analyzes even half a verse.
The explanation says: Generally, a full verse consists of four lines. There are two kinds of lines: namely, word-lines and meaning-lines.

If one considers the literal phrasing, two lines constitute a half-verse; however, if one considers the meaning of the phrases, the statement that "all phenomena are originally empty and quiescent" constitutes the half-verse.
To reveal that the essence of emptiness is not empty constitutes the full verse.

Alternatively, impermanence and true permanence constitute the half and the full [verses]. Third, the superiority of faith in the sutra is revealed through past causes (the text itself clarifies both merit and wisdom).
[This] clarifies [the following]. Part One: Explaining Hearing and Belief.

"Good son, if there is another person who hears the name of this sutra and their mind of faith is free from delusion," [this shows that] one may know [this as] a second verification of past causes. Part Two: A Counter-illustration.
It should be known that such a person has not merely planted roots of merit and wisdom under one or two Buddhas;
it should be understood that they have followed the light in this way,
even unto planting all roots of goodness and hearing the teachings of this sutra in the presence of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
The commentary states: This is also like the phrasing of the *Vajra* [Sūtra]; those who have faith in this school must possess a faith that is simultaneous with understanding.
Since this faith encompasses the ocean of fruition and is not a minor cause, it is verified that their past causes were likewise no ordinary matters.
(5) Answering the protection and maintenance.

"O son of good family, you should protect those practitioners in the final age so that evil Māras and various heterodox teachers do not afflict their bodies and minds, causing them to fall into despondency and retreat. The commentary explains:
The previous question asked how to provide protection and support; the meaning of the present answer is simply that one must ensure that evil Māras and heterodox teachers [do not cause such harm].
That which afflicts the body and mind is precisely what is protected and maintained. Now, such affliction of body and mind applies to both Māras and externalists (*bāhyaka*).
If we correlate this according to their respective meanings: externalists delude people with false wisdom, causing them to harbor doubts; this is the affliction of the mind.
Māras, by means of their supernatural powers, cause people various forms of unease, even illness and the like; this is the affliction of the body. Therefore, the sutras speak of "the various Māras."

Those who delight in birth and death and those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who are attached to various views (the "etc. includes necklaces, right and wrong, victory and defeat)—both of these cause beginners on the path to retreat and become disheartened.
Truly relying upon protection, they receive the fourfold external support for their lives. Section Three:
The Multitude of Mallas.
At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty thousand Vajras—including Agnīśikhara-vajra, Vajra-vidāraṇa-vajra, and Nīlambā-vajra—along with their retinues.
They rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, if in the future final age there are sentient beings who are able to uphold this definitive Great [Dharma]...”
Relying on us, you shall be protected as if we were guarding our own eyes, even at the site where you practice for the sake of the path;
we, the Vajras, leading our own retinues, will protect you morning and evening so that you do not regress.
Your household shall be forever free from calamities and obstacles, pestilence shall be extinguished, and your wealth and treasures shall be abundant, never lacking.
The commentary states: "Vajra" refers to those who grasp this *kīla* (ritual dagger). If one takes the name [of the deity], it is called *Nogenta* in Sanskrit, which means "Exposed-Shoulder";
he is the Exposed-Shoulder Deity (*Aṃsadhṛk*). "Head" (*śiras*) means the top of the head; because there is a flame upon his head, he is named "Crusher" (*Pramardana*) based on his function.
*Nilamba* has not yet been translated [into Chinese]. When these deities first generated the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*),...
He constantly vows to act as a powerful protector for those householders who practice the path; these "householders" refer to the assembly of lay followers.
Generally, all who resolve upon the Great Mind encounter obstacles and difficulties, and while such obstacles are manifold, they are summarized here by citing calamities and illnesses.

Thus it is said, "up to having sufficient wealth and treasures," meaning that one need not be opulent to be called "abundant"; rather, it refers to being fully equipped with the necessary provisions and conditions for the Path. Therefore, it follows with the words "always [sufficient]."
Because they are neither deficient nor abundant, they advance toward the sublime gateway without falling back or being cowed.

At that time, the assembly of the two heavenly kings—the Great Brahmā King, the twenty-eight heavenly kings, Sumeru the King of Mountains, the Heavenly Kings who protect the lands, and others—rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we too..."
"To protect" means to constantly ensure that those who uphold this sutra remain peaceful and secure, so that their minds do not regress.
The commentary explains: "Mahābrahmā" specifically refers to the King of the First Dhyāna; "Lord of the Sahā World" generally refers to the twenty-eight heavens of the triple world;
"King of Mount Sumeru" specifically clarifies Śakra; and "Protector of the Nation" specifically reveals the [Four Great Kings].
The King separately designates three categories because when Brahmā, Śakra, and all the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, they all act as the presiding patrons;
furthermore, the World-Protectors and the Guardians of the Nation ensure that calamities do not arise. Therefore, beyond the general listing, he further clarifies these three groups of ghost kings.

At that time, there was a great powerful ghost-king named Kumbhāṇḍa, together with one hundred thousand ghost-kings, who rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we too shall protect those who uphold this sutra, attending them morning and night so that they do not fall back or become disheartened. Within a distance of one yojana of where such a person dwells, if there should be..."
"If spirits and ghosts invade my domain, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust.
The commentary explains: *Kumbhāṇḍa* is also called *Ghuṇḍaka*; they consume the vital essence and blood of humans, moving as swiftly as the wind and possessing many powers of transformation.
Dwelling in forests and wilds, they preside over the hosts of ghosts; therefore, they are titled "King" and have come to the Way.
They act as leaders in their assemblies, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, each being like this. They dwell in deep mountains or inhabit rock caves;
their forms are fearsome, and they possess an extreme capacity for transformation. They do not belong to the realms of humans or devas, but reside in the realm of ghosts.
One *yojana* is forty *li* (or sixteen *li*). Their followers accept and uphold [the teachings] during the five periods of the day.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the eight classes of attendants, as well as the various heavenly kings, the Brahma kings, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The commentary states that the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* explains three kinds of meaning for "rejoicing and practicing accordingly":
first, the purity of the speaker, because they are not defiled by attachment to fame or profit; second, the purity of what is spoken, because of knowing the essence of phenomena as they truly are;
and third, the purity of attaining the fruit, which refers to the benefit of the teaching.
Reflecting upon myself, from time immemorial I have wandered in the ocean of deluded mind, drifting and sinking amidst the waves and dust of birth and death through vast eons.
Though Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges appear among humanity, they are as difficult to encounter as a blind turtle finding a floating log.
How fortunate that this body has met the definitive teaching; my thousandfold doubts and obstructions have melted away like ice.
Having sought through many lifetimes and accumulated the熏 (xūn) of hearing the Dharma, Possessing shame and remorse, he has long served as a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This superior being, out of compassion for the final age, Has requested these teachings in their proper sequence from beginning to end.
The Benevolent One, responding to this inspiration, has proclaimed the source of the mind; From its root to its branches, he has expounded it all at once without obstruction.
Having gathered all explanations to strike at true stillness, I interpret this text in accordance with the Sage’s intent.
May these merits be universally dedicated to all sentient beings, That they may together enter the Great Treasury of Supernatural Power and Radiance.
The Fourth Part of the Lower Scroll of the Great Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment. (End)
Phonetic Explanations:

*Lǔhù* (the character *lǔ* is pronounced as *luò*, meaning "to plunder"; the character *hù* is pronounced as *yòu*, meaning "to stop" or "to follow along"). *Cī* (pronounced as *cí*, meaning "disease" or "blemish"). *Dì* (pronounced as *dì*, meaning "a drop of water").

On behalf of the late Shen Yunsoqi, former Official of the Ministry of Rites, this was carved by a group of people performing repentance rites and cultivating merit, who contributed their funds for this purpose.
In this entirety of the Great Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra, may all deceased spirits, by virtue of this spiritual power, swiftly awaken to the pure nature of perfect enlightenment,
distance themselves from the empty flowers of birth and death, behold the Buddha, realize the fruit, and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. Excluding the topical outlines (ke-wen),
the total count for the entire commentary in twelve fascicles is one hundred thirty-one thousand one hundred and sixty characters.
The total calculated labor cost is sixty-eight taels, four mace, and six candareens. From this, having deducted forty-five taels, three mace,
and five candareens received from the venerable elders, relatives, friends, brothers, nephews, daughters, concubines,
and family members who assisted in the repentance ritual for use at the carving workshop, there remains a deficit of twenty-three taels, two mace, and one candareen.
Carved to completion with the assistance of his biological younger brothers, Pyeong and Sun.
